q.explanation: The sphincter pupillae is smooth muscle in the pupillary zone, supplied by parasympathetic fibres through the short ciliary nerves (oculomotor pathway). The dilator lies in the ciliary zone and is made of myoepithelial cells from the anterior iris epithelium. Its supply is postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion, reaching it through the long ciliary nerves.

q.stem: How many anterior ciliary arteries normally feed the major arterial circle of the iris, together with the two long posterior ciliary arteries?
q.explanation: Each rectus gives two anterior ciliary arteries except the lateral rectus, which gives one, making seven. They join the two long posterior ciliary arteries in the major arterial circle. Radial branches from this circle form the incomplete minor circle near the pupil.

q.stem: How do the blood vessels of the iris and the ciliary body differ?
options: Iris vessels are non-fenestrated with tight junctions, whereas ciliary body vessels are fenestrated
Iris vessels are fenestrated, whereas ciliary body vessels are non-fenestrated
q.explanation: Iris vessels are non-fenestrated and have tight junctions, but they form only a 'pseudo' barrier because they leak protein and cells when inflamed. Ciliary body vessels are fenestrated, unlike those of the iris.

q.stem: The ciliary body is anchored to the sclera at only one site. Where?
options: The scleral spur, where its longitudinal muscle fibres insert
q.explanation: The base of the ciliary body is its only fixed anchor to the sclera, where the longitudinal ciliary muscle inserts into the scleral spur. Choroidal attachments to the sclera are at the vortex vein exits and the optic nerve head, and Schwalbe's line ends Descemet's membrane.

q.stem: Why is an intravitreal injection given through the pars plana?
options: The pars plicata is avascular and lies 8 mm behind the limbus
The pars plana contains the major arterial circle
The retina extends to the limbus, so no posterior route is safe
The pars plana is a relatively avascular region, making it the safest route into the vitreous, about 3-4 mm behind the limbus
q.explanation: The pars plana is about 4 mm wide, pigmented and relatively avascular, lying between the ciliary processes and the ora serrata. Entry about 3-4 mm behind the limbus is the safest way into the vitreous cavity. The pars plicata is highly vascular because of its ciliary processes.

q.stem: Where do most lens zonules attach on the ciliary body?
options: In the troughs (valleys) between the ciliary processes
On the tips of the ciliary processes
q.explanation: Zonules attach mainly in the troughs between the ciliary processes, with some on the pars plana. Non-pigmented epithelial cells in the valleys are adapted to anchor zonules, whereas those at the process tips are specialized for fluid secretion.

q.stem: Which feature of the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium forms part of the blood-aqueous barrier?
options: Tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between adjacent cell apices
Its continuity with the retinal pigment epithelium
q.explanation: The tight junctions between neighbouring non-pigmented epithelial cells form part of the blood-aqueous barrier. These cells have few melanosomes. The non-pigmented layer's basal lamina is continuous with the retina's internal limiting membrane; it is the pigmented layer's basal lamina that is continuous with the RPE.

q.stem: What is the largest group of ciliary muscle fibres?
q.explanation: The ciliary muscle has longitudinal, radial and circular fibre groups. The longitudinal fibres (Brücke's muscle), running between the scleral spur and the choroid, are the largest. The circular fibres lie furthest forward and nearest the lens. All three groups contract together during accommodation.

q.stem: Contraction of the ciliary muscle during near focusing results in:
options: Backward movement of the ciliary body, tightening the zonules to flatten the lens
Forward and inward movement of the ciliary body, slackening the zonules so the lens becomes more convex
q.explanation: The ciliary muscle pulls against the fixed scleral spur and moves the ciliary body forward and inward. The zonules slacken and the lens takes on a more convex, more powerful shape. For distance viewing the zonules are under maximum tension and the lens is flatter. The muscle is supplied by parasympathetic fibres via the short ciliary nerves.

q.stem: Which statement about Bruch's membrane is correct?
options: Its outermost layer is the basement membrane of the RPE
It has five layers, its innermost layer is the basement membrane of the RPE, and it is 2-4 micrometres thick
It consists of a single elastic layer about 20 micrometres thick
It lies between the choroid and the sclera
q.explanation: Bruch's membrane has five layers and is 2-4 micrometres thick: the RPE basement membrane on the inside, three middle layers containing elastic fibres, and the choriocapillaris basement membrane on the outside. It lies between the RPE and the choriocapillaris. A break in it in AMD lets choroidal new vessels grow under the retina.

q.stem: Which feature describes the choriocapillaris?
options: Small non-fenestrated capillaries with tight junctions
Vessels with an internal elastic lamina and a smooth muscle media
Wide-bore capillaries (about 40-60 micrometres) with fenestrations, mainly on the side facing the RPE
The outermost vascular layer of the choroid
q.explanation: The choriocapillaris is the innermost layer of the choroid, just outside Bruch's membrane. It is a continuous network of large capillaries (40-60 micrometres) with thin, heavily fenestrated walls, especially on the RPE side, and pericytes on the outer surface. An internal elastic lamina and smooth muscle media are features of the medium and large vessel layers.

q.stem: Choroidal blood flow is so high that only about 2-3% of arterial oxygen is extracted. What extra function is this rapid flow thought to serve?
options: Removing heat produced by light absorption
q.explanation: Very fast choroidal flow, with only 2-3% oxygen extraction, is thought to carry away heat produced as light is absorbed, so the choroid acts as a heat sink. Its dense pigment also traps light. The inner retina is supplied by the central retinal artery, and aqueous is made by the ciliary body.

q.stem: The short ciliary nerves carry which type of fibres?
options: Sensory and sympathetic fibres only, from the nasociliary nerve
Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres, arising from the ciliary ganglion
Parasympathetic fibres only, from the pterygopalatine ganglion
Somatic motor fibres from the oculomotor nucleus
q.explanation: The short ciliary nerves arise from the ciliary ganglion and carry both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres. The long ciliary nerves are branches of the nasociliary nerve (V1) and carry sensory and sympathetic fibres. Both groups enter the sclera around the optic nerve head and run forward in the suprachoroidal space.

q.stem: What is a rough clinical landmark for the position of the ora serrata?
options: The insertions of the medial rectus medially and the lateral rectus laterally
q.explanation: The front edge of the retina, the ora serrata, roughly lines up with the medial rectus insertion on the medial side and the lateral rectus insertion on the lateral side. The vortex veins exit behind the equator, further back.

q.stem: Counting the retinal layers from the vitreous outwards, which layer lies between the inner nuclear layer and the outer nuclear layer?
q.explanation: From the inside, the order is ILM, nerve fibre layer, ganglion cell layer, inner plexiform, inner nuclear, outer plexiform, outer nuclear, ELM, photoreceptors and RPE. The outer plexiform layer therefore separates the two nuclear layers. The inner plexiform layer lies between the ganglion cell layer and the inner nuclear layer.

q.stem: The external limiting membrane of the retina is formed by:
options: The outer foot processes of Müller cells, with adherens junctions to the photoreceptors
The basement membrane of the RPE
Astrocyte processes in the nerve fibre layer
The inner foot processes of Müller cells
q.explanation: The ELM is formed by the outer processes of Müller cells joined to photoreceptors by adherens junctions. Their inner foot processes and basement membranes form the inner limiting membrane. Neither membrane is part of the blood-ocular barrier.

q.stem: Which statement about midget (P) ganglion cells is correct?
options: They pool input from a large receptive field of many photoreceptors
They project to the magnocellular layers of the lateral geniculate nucleus
They are absent from the central retina
They often carry the signal of a single cone and are most common near the fovea
q.explanation: Midget (P) ganglion cells each connect with a single midget bipolar cell, so their signal often comes from one cone, giving fine detail. They are most common near the fovea and project to the parvocellular layers. Parasol (M) cells have large receptive fields and project to the magnocellular layers.

q.stem: Why is the optic nerve head conical in shape?
options: Retinal ganglion cell axons are myelinated only after they leave the globe
The lamina cribrosa is thickest centrally
The central retinal vein widens at the disc
Müller cells are absent at the disc
q.explanation: Within the eye, ganglion cell axons are wrapped by glial cells but have no myelin. They gain myelin only after leaving the globe, so the nerve widens behind the lamina, giving the nerve head its conical shape. The fibres next synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus.

q.stem: The cell bodies of which cell type are NOT found in the inner nuclear layer?
q.explanation: The inner nuclear layer contains the cell bodies of bipolar, amacrine, horizontal and Müller cells. Ganglion cell bodies lie in their own ganglion cell layer, nearer the vitreous.

q.stem: Retinal horizontal cells improve contrast and spatial resolution by releasing which neurotransmitter onto bipolar cells?
q.explanation: When stimulated by photoreceptors, horizontal cells release GABA, which inhibits bipolar cells and sharpens contrast and spatial resolution. Cone horizontal cells contact about seven cone pedicles, and rod horizontal cells contact 10-12 rod spherules.

q.stem: Which bipolar cell type connects one cone cell to one ganglion cell?
q.explanation: Midget bipolar cells link a single cone to a single midget ganglion cell. Rod bipolar cells gather several rods onto one to four ganglion cells. Flat or diffuse bipolar cells link many cones to many ganglion cells, and amacrine cells are not bipolar cells.

q.stem: Where is rod density highest?
options: In the juxtafoveal zone, about 160,000 cells/mm2
q.explanation: There are about 120 million rods. None are at the fovea; density rises to a peak of about 160,000/mm2 just around it and falls to about 30,000/mm2 in the peripheral retina. Cones, about 6-7 million, are most concentrated in the fovea.

q.stem: Which statement about rod photoreceptor structure is correct?
options: The connecting cilium has nine doublet microtubules with no central pair
Each outer segment contains about 50 discs
The myoid contains the basal body and most of the mitochondria
Rods are shorter than cones, about 40 micrometres long
q.explanation: The connecting stalk has a modified cilium of about nine doublet microtubules with no central pair. Each rod outer segment holds 600-1000 discs. The ellipsoid, not the myoid, contains the basal body and mitochondria; the myoid holds the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi. Rods are 100-120 micrometres long, longer than cones at 65-75 micrometres.

q.stem: Histologically, how is the macula lutea defined?
options: The area with no ganglion cell layer and only cones
The area where the ganglion cell layer is more than one cell thick
The 500 micrometre zone without retinal capillaries
The area 1.5 mm in diameter at the centre of the optic disc
q.explanation: The macula is about 4.5 mm across, lies about 3 mm lateral to the disc and is defined by a ganglion cell layer more than one cell thick. The fovea (1.5 mm) is defined by an absent ganglion cell layer and a cone-only receptor layer. The foveal avascular zone is about 500 micrometres across.

q.stem: Before laser treatment for diabetic maculopathy, the clinician identifies the foveal avascular zone on fluorescein angiography. Roughly how wide is it?
q.explanation: The foveal avascular zone is about 500 micrometres across, shows up on fluorescein angiography and must be avoided during laser. The figures 1.5 mm and 4.5 mm are the diameters of the fovea and the macula.

q.stem: Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segment tips by the RPE follows a daily rhythm. When does most of the shedding happen, and what is the end product of digestion?
q.explanation: RPE microvilli continuously remove and phagocytose the tips of the outer segments over a 24-hour cycle, with most shedding in the morning. Lysosomes digest the phagosome contents, leaving lipofuscin granules.

q.stem: The outer blood-retinal barrier is formed mainly by:
q.explanation: The blood-retinal barrier depends on zonulae occludentes between the non-fenestrated retinal capillary endothelial cells (inner barrier) and between RPE cells (outer barrier). The choriocapillaris is fenestrated, and neither limiting membrane forms part of the barrier.

q.stem: Where does the central retinal artery enter the optic nerve?
options: On its superolateral side, about 2 mm behind the globe
On its inferomedial side, about 12 mm behind the globe
q.explanation: The central retinal artery is the first branch of the ophthalmic artery. It runs along the dural sheath and enters the nerve on its inferomedial side about 12 mm behind the eyeball, picking up coverings from the dura, arachnoid and pia as it passes through.

q.stem: An occasional larger connection between the posterior ciliary and central retinal arterial systems is called the:
q.explanation: Small anastomoses commonly link posterior ciliary branches with the central retinal artery, and sometimes a larger vessel, the cilioretinal artery, joins the two systems. The anterior ciliary arteries and the minor arterial circle belong to the anterior segment circulation.

q.stem: Which statement about the retinal arterial circulation is correct?
options: Arteriovenous anastomoses are common in the retina
The arteries lose their internal elastic lamina after branching at the disc and behave as end arteries
Retinal capillaries supply the photoreceptor layer
q.explanation: After branching at the optic disc, retinal arteries lose their internal elastic lamina and act as end arteries, with no arteriovenous anastomoses. Retinal capillaries reach only as far out as the inner nuclear layer, with non-fenestrated endothelium. The retina outside the outer plexiform layer, including the photoreceptors, depends on the choroid.

q.stem: Which is the principal secreted mucin of the tear film?
q.explanation: MUC5AC, made by conjunctival goblet cells, is the main tear mucin. TFF1 (with TFF3) is a trefoil protein co-secreted with it rather than a mucin. MUC1 and MUC16 are not the secreted gel-forming mucin described as dominant.

q.stem: Aggregations of conjunctival goblet cells on the bulbar conjunctiva nasal to the limbus are known as:
q.explanation: Goblet cells cluster on the bulbar conjunctiva nasal to the limbus as Manz's glands. Henle's crypts are the equivalent clusters in the tarsal conjunctiva. Wolfring glands are accessory lacrimal glands and Moll glands are apocrine sweat glands of the lid margin.

q.stem: A researcher samples lacrimal fluid while flow is very low. Compared with a sample taken during brisk reflex tearing, the low-flow sample is most likely to be:
q.explanation: The electrolyte content of lacrimal fluid depends on flow: at low flow it is hypertonic and at higher flow rates it becomes isotonic. It is never described as hypotonic, and K+ and Cl- are prominent electrolytes.

q.stem: What is the approximate basal rate of tear secretion?
q.explanation: Basal tear secretion is about 1.2 μl/min and rises with mechanical and psychological stimuli. 2–3 μl/min is the rate of aqueous humour formation, not tear secretion.

q.stem: Most of the nerve supply to the main lacrimal gland acinar cells is:
options: Purely sensory from the ophthalmic nerve
Parasympathetic, using acetylcholine and vasoactive intestinal peptide
q.explanation: The lacrimal gland is under autonomic control and most of its nerves are parasympathetic (acetylcholine and VIP), acting on acinar and myoepithelial cells. Sympathetic and sensory fibres are present but are the minority. Hormones have a role, but secretion is not purely hormonal.

q.stem: Which statement about secretion of the aqueous tear layer is FALSE?
options: The conjunctiva can secrete electrolytes and water under sympathetic control
Accessory lacrimal glands have sparse innervation, supporting their role as the source of basal tears
The corneal epithelium contributes water and electrolytes under sympathetic control
Testosterone increases secretion of some tear components such as IgA
q.explanation: The accessory lacrimal glands are in fact well supplied by parasympathetic nerves, which argues against the old idea that they produce basal tears. The other statements are true: corneal epithelium and conjunctiva add water and electrolytes under sympathetic control, and testosterone boosts some components such as IgA.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the lipid layer of the tear film?
options: Stopping skin lipids from spreading onto the ocular surface
Preventing tears overflowing the lid margin
Delivering lysozyme and lactoferrin to the ocular surface
q.explanation: Lysozyme and lactoferrin are proteins of the aqueous layer from the lacrimal gland. The oily layer slows evaporation, stops tears spilling over the lid margin, keeps skin lipids off the ocular surface and helps give a clear optical medium.

q.stem: The meibomian glands release their lipid by holocrine secretion. Lipid synthesis in these glands is mainly regulated by:
q.explanation: Androgenic sex steroids control meibomian lipid synthesis and secretion. Nerves around the acini can also alter synthesis, and blinking expresses stored lipid from the ducts. The other hormones are not identified as the main regulators.

q.stem: Roughly what proportion of secreted tear volume is normally lost by evaporation?
q.explanation: About 10–25% of tear volume evaporates; the remainder drains via the nasolacrimal system to the nose, with some absorption along the way.

q.stem: The epithelium lining the lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct is:
q.explanation: The sac and duct are lined by non-ciliated columnar epithelium. Stratified squamous epithelium lines the canaliculi, which are surrounded by orbicularis muscle.

q.stem: During the closing phase of a blink, which event helps draw tears into the lacrimal sac?
options: Gravity pulling tears from the canaliculi into the sac
Opening of the puncta as the lids meet
Lateral displacement of the sac wall by the deep heads of preseptal orbicularis
Lengthening of the canaliculi by Horner's muscle
q.explanation: On blinking, the deep preseptal orbicularis pulls the sac laterally, while the pretarsal deep heads (Horner's muscle) shorten the canaliculi; the puncta close and canalicular tears are pushed medially and sucked into the sac. Gravity mainly affects flow from sac to duct, not into the sac.

q.stem: What is thought to stop retrograde flow of tears from the lacrimal sac back into the canaliculi?
options: Closure of the valve at the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct
The anterior angulation of the common canaliculus as it enters the sac
Tonic contraction of the inferior oblique
Ciliary beating in the sac epithelium
q.explanation: The common canaliculus (present in about 90%) bends anteriorly as it joins the sac, giving a valve-like effect against reflux. The sac is lined by non-ciliated epithelium, and a valve at the duct's nasal end would not prevent sac-to-canaliculus reflux.

q.stem: Aqueous humour is actively secreted mainly by:
options: Non-pigmented ciliary epithelium of the anterior pars plicata
Pigmented ciliary epithelium of the pars plana
q.explanation: Active secretion is carried out by the non-pigmented epithelium covering the ciliary processes of the anterior pars plicata. The pigmented layer takes up NaCl from the stroma but does not release aqueous into the posterior chamber, and the pars plana has no processes.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT a recognised role of the ciliary body?
q.explanation: The ciliary body is involved in accommodation, aqueous production, zonule production, vitreous glycosaminoglycan and collagen production and non-conventional outflow. Crystallins are made by lens fibre cells.

q.stem: Approximately what fraction of aqueous outflow leaves by the uveoscleral route?
q.explanation: About 10% of aqueous drains by the uveoscleral pathway; most leaves through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal into episcleral veins.

q.stem: The normal rate of aqueous humour formation is about:
q.explanation: Aqueous is formed at about 2–3 μl/min by diffusion, ultrafiltration and, mainly, active secretion. The other values are too low or too high by an order of magnitude or more.

q.stem: What proportion of total aqueous humour formation is normally due to active secretion?
q.explanation: Active secretion accounts for 80–90% of aqueous formation. Diffusion and ultrafiltration are passive and mainly produce a stromal pool of plasma ultrafiltrate from which aqueous is secreted.

q.stem: Where in the ciliary epithelium is Na+–K+-ATPase mainly located?
options: Basolateral infoldings of the non-pigmented epithelium
Apical membrane of the pigmented epithelium
q.explanation: Na+–K+-ATPase is concentrated on the basolateral infoldings of the NPE, where it pumps sodium into the posterior chamber. Pigmented cells take up NaCl from the stroma and pass it to NPE through gap junctions; the ciliary capillaries are fenestrated and leaky.

q.stem: Acetazolamide lowers intraocular pressure mainly because reduced bicarbonate formation in the ciliary epithelium:
options: Reduces active Na+ transport into the posterior chamber
Closes gap junctions between epithelial layers
q.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase makes HCO3- and H+ from CO2 and water; less HCO3- reduces active sodium movement across the NPE, so less water follows and aqueous formation falls. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act on secretion rather than outflow or venous pressure.

q.stem: Compared with plasma, the protein and ascorbate concentrations of aqueous humour are approximately:
options: Protein 20 times lower; ascorbate 200 times higher
Protein 200 times lower; ascorbate 20 times higher
q.explanation: The key differences are a protein concentration about 200-fold lower and ascorbate about 20-fold higher than plasma. The high ascorbate is thought to protect against UV-related oxidative damage.

q.stem: Which constituent is present at a HIGHER concentration in aqueous humour than in plasma?
q.explanation: Lactate is raised in aqueous because the cornea, lens and other structures rely on glycolysis. Glucose, bicarbonate and calcium are all lower in aqueous than in plasma.

q.stem: In the three-step model of aqueous secretion, how does NaCl move from pigmented to non-pigmented ciliary epithelial cells?
options: By Na+–K+-ATPase on the pigmented cell apex
Across tight junctions by paracellular flow
q.explanation: NaCl is taken up from the stroma into pigmented cells by electroneutral transporters, passes to non-pigmented cells via gap junctions, then leaves through Na+–K+-ATPase and Cl- channels. Tight junctions between NPE cells block paracellular flow.

q.stem: What is the approximate water content of the normal cornea compared with the sclera?
q.explanation: The cornea is about 80% water and the sclera about 70%. Despite this, the cornea readily takes up more water if available, as seen at a laceration.

q.stem: The corneal stromal swelling pressure is principally attributed to:
q.explanation: Glycosaminoglycans, notably lumican, attract water and generate the swelling pressure, which also tensions the fibrils into their normal arrangement. The endothelial pump opposes rather than creates this pressure.

q.stem: Which feature of the stromal collagen best explains corneal transparency?
options: Fibrils whose diameter is greater than the wavelength of visible light
Widely varying fibril diameters that cancel scattering
Fibrils of narrow, uniform diameter with short-range order in a quasi-random arrangement
Fibrils arranged in a perfect crystalline lattice throughout the stroma
q.explanation: Fibril diameters vary little and are a fraction of the wavelength of light; they are not in a regular lattice but quasi-random, with local order over about 200 nm, which is enough for transparency.

q.stem: The trans-endothelial potential of the cornea is approximately:
options: 0 μV, as the endothelium is leaky
q.explanation: Intracellular bicarbonate produced by carbonic anhydrase gives a potential of about –500 μV across the endothelium, the aqueous side negative relative to stroma. –60 mV is closer to the ocular resting potential at the RPE.

q.stem: If bicarbonate is omitted from a solution irrigating the corneal endothelium, the most likely result is:
options: Increased endothelial pump activity with deturgescence
No effect, as glucose is the only essential component
q.explanation: Removing bicarbonate from the irrigating fluid causes bicarbonate to move from stroma to aqueous and the cornea swells. That is why irrigating solutions contain a buffer such as bicarbonate alongside an energy source such as glucose.

q.stem: In an intraocular irrigating solution, which component is added specifically to maintain mydriasis?
q.explanation: Adrenaline keeps the pupil dilated. Glucose provides energy, bicarbonate acts as a buffer, and glutathione and calcium help junctional stability and the blood–aqueous barrier.

q.stem: In corneal epithelial metabolism, the pentose phosphate pathway mainly helps to:
options: Generate most of the cell's ATP
q.explanation: About 85% of glucose-6-phosphate goes through glycolysis, mostly to lactate, with some entering the citric acid cycle. The pentose phosphate pathway handles the rest and helps the cell cope with free radicals.

q.stem: During sleep with the eyes closed, the corneal epithelium receives its oxygen mainly from:
q.explanation: When the eye is open, oxygen comes from the atmosphere via the tear film. During sleep it is supplied by the palpebral conjunctiva. The aqueous and limbal vessels contribute only minor amounts to the epithelium.

q.stem: Which statement about corneal endothelial metabolism is FALSE?
options: It obtains its oxygen from the aqueous humour
It is less metabolically active than the epithelium
It uses the citric acid cycle more than epithelial cells do
It relies mainly on anaerobic glycolysis
q.explanation: The endothelium is about five times as metabolically active as the epithelium. It mainly uses anaerobic glycolysis but, because of its high activity, uses the citric acid cycle more than epithelium, and it gets oxygen from the aqueous along with the deep stroma.

q.stem: During contact lens wear, the hypoxia and acidosis produced lead to increased endothelial oxygen consumption chiefly because:
options: Na+–H+ exchange is activated, which stimulates Na+–K+-ATPase
q.explanation: pH-regulating mechanisms such as Na+–H+ exchange are activated by acidosis and in turn drive Na+–K+-ATPase activity, raising oxygen use. Endothelial cells do not undergo mitosis.

q.stem: Corneal epithelial cells are renewed chiefly from:
options: Central basal cells, with a mitotic rate of about 1% per week
Limbal stem cells, with a mitotic rate of about 10–15% per day
q.explanation: Most mitotic activity is in limbal stem cells, which give rise to basal cells; the epithelial turnover rate is about 10–15% per day.

q.stem: Firm long-term attachment of healing corneal epithelium to its basement membrane is achieved by:
options: Anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen and the lamina densa
Type II collagen fibrils from Bowman's layer
q.explanation: Hemidesmosomes make the initial attachment, and later attachment depends on the lamina densa and anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen. Type II collagen is a vitreous collagen.

q.stem: Which of the following does NOT occur in migrating corneal epithelial cells during wound healing?
options: GLUT1 mRNA rises within about 2 hours
q.explanation: Migration is energy-dependent, so glycogen falls in migrating cells. Protein synthesis rises, vinculin is newly made, CD44 is increased, and GLUT1 mRNA increases within 2 hours with transporter protein up within 4 hours to supply glucose for anaerobic glycolysis.

q.stem: After loss of corneal endothelial cells, the defect is covered by:
options: Enlargement and migration of neighbouring cells, which stay in contact as they move
Epithelial cells growing through the stroma
Migration of keratocytes onto Descemet's membrane
q.explanation: Corneal endothelium does not divide. Neighbouring cells change size and shape and slide in (up to 80–100 μm/day early on) without losing contact, then remodel to hexagons; pump and barrier function return once a confluent monolayer forms.

q.stem: Opacity in a large healed corneal stromal wound is mainly because keratocytes:
options: Undergo apoptosis and leave acellular gaps
Act as unspecialised fibroblasts laying down irregular collagen and GAGs
Secrete excess hyaluronic acid that crystallises
q.explanation: In the healing stroma, keratocytes behave like ordinary fibroblasts and produce collagen and GAGs of irregular size and arrangement, causing opacity, particularly in larger wounds. Smaller wounds come closer to restoring normal matrix.

q.stem: Crystallins, which make up about 40% of the wet weight of the lens, belong to which protein family?
q.explanation: Crystallins belong to the heat shock protein family and act as chaperones, stabilising partly unfolded proteins and preventing aggregation. Aquaporins (such as MIP), connexins (gap junctions) and cadherins (adhesion) are other lens membrane proteins.

q.stem: Major intrinsic polypeptide (MIP) of the lens fibre membrane:
options: Is the main cytoskeletal intermediate filament
Is an aquaporin family protein making up about half of fibre membrane protein
Is a connexin forming gap junctions
q.explanation: MIP accounts for about 50% of fibre cell membrane protein and belongs to the aquaporin family; it is thought to be important in lens fluid and ion flow. Gap junctions are built from connexins, and vimentin is an intermediate filament.

q.stem: Lens fibre plasma membranes are unusually rigid. Which lipid composition contributes most?
options: Very low cholesterol with abundant polyunsaturated fatty acids
The highest cholesterol content of any plasma membrane, plus abundant sphingomyelin
q.explanation: Fibre membranes have the highest cholesterol proportion of any plasma membrane, rising with age, and a high sphingomyelin content; both stiffen the membrane.

q.stem: The lens has the highest density of gap junction plaques of any tissue. This is best explained by:
options: Its cells lying far from a nutrient supply
The need to conduct action potentials
q.explanation: Gap junctions (made of connexins) allow communication and passage of nutrients between cells that are far from any nutrient source. The lens is avascular, ectodermal in origin, and deep fibres do not divide.

q.stem: Lens fibres are bound to each other along their length by which adhesion molecule linked to the actin cytoskeleton?
q.explanation: N-cadherin links adjacent fibres along their length and is attached to actin. Close adhesion minimises extracellular space and so reduces light scatter.

q.stem: Which intermediate filament protein, usually seen in cells of mesodermal origin, is found in lens fibres?
q.explanation: Lens fibres contain vimentin intermediate filaments, typical of mesodermal cells, along with microtubules and actin microfilaments. Vimentin filaments disassemble with ageing.

q.stem: How does glutathione reach the deep nuclear lens fibres?
options: It is synthesised locally by deep fibres
Only by diffusion, which becomes less effective with age
By active transport across each fibre membrane
q.explanation: Glutathione is made by superficial fibres and the epithelium and imported from aqueous, but diffusion is the only way it reaches deeper fibres, and this declines with age. Deep fibres lack organelles and do not synthesise it.

q.stem: What protective role does transferrin in the aqueous humour play for the lens?
options: It catalyses breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
It transports glucose into the lens epithelium
It binds iron, preventing it reacting with hydrogen peroxide to release free radicals
q.explanation: Transferrin binds iron so it cannot react with hydrogen peroxide to generate free radicals. Hydrogen peroxide itself is broken down by lens catalase and glutathione peroxidase.

q.stem: Which enzyme in the lens converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen?
q.explanation: Catalase splits hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Glutathione peroxidase also reduces hydrogen peroxide, linked to the oxidation of glutathione.

q.stem: Main energy source of the deep lens fibres:
q.explanation: Deep fibres lack mitochondria and diffusion is slow, so glycolysis provides most energy, with lactic acid lowering the pH deeper in the lens. Superficial fibres and epithelium use both glycolysis and oxidative pathways.

q.stem: Which describes normal human lens growth?
options: Rapid in utero and the first year, slower from 1 to 10 years, then slow and linear for life
Growth stops completely at about 10 years of age
q.explanation: The lens grows quickly before birth and in the first postnatal year, slows between 1 and 10 years and then grows slowly and linearly throughout life by adding new fibre layers.

q.stem: A rise in cytoplasmic calcium in lens fibres would be expected to cause:
options: Cytoskeletal breakdown, uncontrolled proteolysis, swelling and opacity
Activation of mitosis in deep fibres
Improved transparency due to tighter packing
q.explanation: Lens fibres actively pump calcium out and normally keep cytoplasmic levels below those of other cells. High calcium leads to cytoskeletal degradation, proteolysis, cell swelling and opacification.

q.stem: The refractive index gradient of the lens (higher centrally than at the surface) helps to:
q.explanation: Deep fibres have a higher refractive index than the surface layers, and this gradient partly corrects spherical aberration. UV absorption is from chromophore accumulation and is unrelated.

q.stem: In the model of the lens internal circulation, the outward positive current at the lens equator is thought to be carried by:
q.explanation: Na+–K+-ATPase draws Na+ into cells, creating the positive current at the sutures, while the outward positive current at the equator is attributed to K+. Water is thought to follow these ion flows.

q.stem: With age, why does the lens become less able to protect its proteins from aggregation?
options: MIP converts to a chaperone-inhibiting form
α-crystallin becomes less soluble centrally and is used up binding altered proteins
Lens epithelial cells stop producing glutathione at puberty
q.explanation: α-crystallin becomes less soluble towards the lens centre, and the functional α-crystallin binds hydrophobic regions of modified proteins, leaving less for chaperone duty. Crystallins are also truncated and aggregate as fibres age.

q.stem: The gel structure of the vitreous is mainly due to:
options: Type I collagen with chondroitin sulphate
Long unbranched type II collagen fibres with hydrated hyaluronic acid
q.explanation: Vitreous is about 99% water; its gel comes from long unbranched, mostly type II collagen fibres and highly hydrated hyaluronic acid. The gel hinders solute movement, which occurs by diffusion or bulk flow.

q.stem: The opsin of rhodopsin has which structure?
options: 149 amino acids spanning the membrane twelve times
349 amino acids spanning the membrane seven times
349 amino acids spanning the membrane once
A soluble cytoplasmic protein of 500 amino acids
q.explanation: Rod opsin has 349 amino acids and crosses the disc membrane seven times. Cone opsins differ but share the seven-helix arrangement.

q.stem: After a photon is absorbed by rhodopsin, which intermediate is the catalytically active form that activates transducin?
q.explanation: Isomerisation of 11-cis to all-trans retinal changes rhodopsin into metarhodopsin II (R*) within about 10 ms, and this form activates transducin. The other intermediates are part of the bleaching sequence but are not the active species.

q.stem: Which step in the phototransduction cascade is NOT an amplification step?
options: Activation of transducin by metarhodopsin II
Activation of phosphodiesterase by transducin α
Diffusion of R* in the disc membrane to meet many transducins
Hydrolysis of cGMP by active phosphodiesterase
q.explanation: Two transducin α subunits are needed to fully activate one PDE, so this step does not amplify. One R* activates several hundred transducins, and each active PDE hydrolyses many cGMP molecules, which are the amplification steps.

q.stem: What happens to a rod photoreceptor when light falls on it?
options: cGMP falls, channels open and the cell depolarises
cGMP rises, channels open, the cell depolarises and glutamate release rises
cGMP falls, cation channels close, the cell hyperpolarises and glutamate release falls
Calcium influx rises and glutamate release increases
q.explanation: Activated PDE lowers cGMP, closing cGMP-gated cation channels, reducing the dark current and hyperpolarising the cell. Voltage-gated calcium channels close and, with less calcium, glutamate release falls.

q.stem: Which protein binds phosphorylated rhodopsin, competing with transducin and speeding rhodopsin inactivation?
q.explanation: Phosphorylation by rhodopsin kinase greatly raises rhodopsin's affinity for arrestin, which then outcompetes transducin and speeds recovery. Recoverin regulates rhodopsin kinase, phosducin aids transducin regeneration, and calmodulin acts on the cGMP channel.

q.stem: At high intracellular calcium (dark), recoverin:
options: Binds arrestin and accelerates rhodopsin shut-off
Binds rhodopsin kinase, inactivating it and prolonging the life of activated rhodopsin
q.explanation: When calcium is high, rhodopsin kinase associates with membrane-bound recoverin and loses activity, so activated rhodopsin is not phosphorylated and stays active longer. When light lowers calcium, kinase is released and shut-off is faster.

q.stem: Transducin activity is terminated mainly by:
options: Intrinsic GTPase activity of its α subunit
q.explanation: Transducin α hydrolyses its own bound GTP to GDP, halting its action. Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates rhodopsin rather than transducin, and PDE hydrolyses cGMP.

q.stem: During light adaptation, the fall in intracellular calcium helps extend the operating range of photoreceptors mainly by:
options: Releasing calmodulin from the cGMP channel and increasing cGMP synthesis
Increasing recoverin binding to rhodopsin kinase
q.explanation: Lower calcium makes calmodulin dissociate from cGMP channels and increases the rate of cGMP synthesis, opposing saturation and speeding responses. Low calcium releases rhodopsin kinase from recoverin rather than increasing binding.

q.stem: Which step is thought to be rate-limiting in the visual (chromophore) cycle?
options: Reduction of all-trans-retinal to all-trans-retinol by retinol dehydrogenase
q.explanation: Reduction of all-trans-retinal to all-trans-retinol by RDH is thought to be rate-limiting, because all-trans-retinal is the only intermediate that builds up after bleaching. Photoisomerisation is very fast.

q.stem: After bleaching, all-trans-retinal is moved from the luminal to the cytoplasmic side of the disc membrane by:
q.explanation: ABCR, a member of the ATP-binding cassette family, shuttles all-trans-retinal across the disc membrane. IRBP carries retinoids in the subretinal space, and transthyretin is a plasma carrier.

q.stem: Within the RPE, all-trans-retinol is esterified to all-trans-retinyl ester by which enzyme?
options: Retinol dehydrogenase of the rod outer segment
q.explanation: LRAT forms all-trans-retinyl esters, which are stored or converted by the isomerohydrolase (thought to include RPE65) to 11-cis-retinol. 11-cis-retinol dehydrogenase then oxidises this to 11-cis-retinal.

q.stem: In plasma, retinol (vitamin A) delivered to the basolateral RPE is carried by:
q.explanation: Circulating retinol is bound to retinol-binding protein complexed with the larger transthyretin. CRBP binds retinol inside RPE cells, and IRBP is in the subretinal space.

q.stem: Which statement about cone visual pigments is correct?
options: Cone pigment is stored in free-floating discs like rhodopsin
Blue and red opsins are almost identical
Cones use a different chromophore from rods
Red and green opsins are highly homologous; the red opsin probably arose from a recent gene duplication
q.explanation: Red and green opsins have close spectra and high homology, with red thought to derive from a recent duplication; blue opsin is distinct. Cone pigment sits in infoldings of the plasma membrane, and the chromophore is still 11-cis-retinal.

q.stem: Which comparison of cones with rods is FALSE?
options: Cones saturate at normal daylight levels
Cones are 25–100 times less sensitive to a single photon
q.explanation: Cones do not saturate at normal environmental light levels and adapt better to background light. They are less sensitive to single photons, catch fewer photons, have faster kinetics and faster calcium clearance.

q.stem: Photoreceptors release glutamate at specialised synapses that contain an electron-dense bar and have a high release rate. These are called:
q.explanation: Ribbon synapses have an electron-dense bar perpendicular to the membrane and release transmitter faster than conventional synapses; endocytosis keeps pace. Both exocytosis and endocytosis are regulated by calcium.

q.stem: ON bipolar cells depolarise to light because their glutamate receptor is:
options: Metabotropic, closing a cation channel when activated
Ionotropic, opening a cation channel when activated
q.explanation: ON bipolars use a metabotropic glutamate receptor that closes a cation channel, giving a sign-inverting synapse: they hyperpolarise in the dark when glutamate is high and depolarise in light. OFF bipolars use ionotropic, sign-preserving receptors.

q.stem: Horizontal cells and most amacrine cells are thought to use which transmitters?
q.explanation: Horizontal and most amacrine cells release GABA or glycine as inhibitory transmitters. Glutamate is the transmitter of photoreceptors and bipolar cells.

q.stem: Which statement about retinal glucose metabolism is correct?
options: The retina cannot make ATP without oxygen
Aerobic metabolism yields only 2 extra ATP per glucose
In the inner retina light greatly increases glucose oxidation
In the outer retina most glucose becomes lactate, and light reduces glucose use there
q.explanation: In the outer retina about 80% of glucose becomes lactate and light reduces this consumption; in the inner retina about 70% is oxidised and is unaffected by light. Under anaerobic conditions glycolysis can supply about 75% of normal ATP, and the TCA cycle adds about 36 ATP per glucose.

q.stem: Glucose crosses the RPE and retinal vascular endothelium mainly by:
q.explanation: Glucose enters the retina by facilitated diffusion using GLUT1 in the RPE (over fenestrated choroidal vessels) and in retinal endothelial cells. Tight junctions prevent significant paracellular passage.

q.stem: Which retinal cells are the main glycogen store and supply lactate as a fuel to neurons?
q.explanation: Müller glia store glycogen, get most of their energy from glycolysis and release lactate, which retinal neurons prefer as a fuel. Some neurons such as rod bipolars and cones also hold glycogen.

q.stem: Mitochondria are absent from rod outer segments, and ATP diffusion through the connecting cilium is slow. Energy is transferred from inner to outer segment by:
options: A phosphocreatine shuttle using creatine kinase
q.explanation: A phosphocreatine shuttle carries high-energy phosphate from inner to outer segment, where creatine kinase passes it from creatine phosphate to make ATP. ABCR carries retinal, not ATP.

q.stem: In the rod outer segment, the pentose phosphate pathway is particularly important because it:
options: Supplies NADPH for retinol dehydrogenase during rhodopsin regeneration
Produces most of the ATP for the dark current
q.explanation: Retinol dehydrogenase in the ROS uses NADPH to reduce all-trans-retinal, and the pentose phosphate pathway is thought to provide this NADPH as well as protecting against oxidative damage.

q.stem: In the dark-adapted retina, oxygen consumption is greatest in which layers?
options: Photoreceptor inner segments, outer plexiform layer and outer IPL
Nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell layer
q.explanation: Oxygen is mainly used in the photoreceptor inner segments (full of mitochondria), the OPL and the outer IPL where OFF bipolar terminals lie. These are terminals of neurons depolarised in the dark with continual calcium entry and glutamate release.

q.stem: Rods synapse with which type of bipolar cell?
options: Both ON and OFF midget bipolar cells
q.explanation: Rods connect only to depolarising ON bipolar cells through a metabotropic glutamate receptor. The ON/OFF split in the scotopic pathway appears later, when AII amacrine cells feed into cone ON and OFF channels.

q.stem: How does the AII amacrine cell pass rod signals to the ON pathway?
options: Via gap junctions with ON cone bipolar cells
Via chemical synapses onto ON ganglion cells
Via horizontal cells in the OPL
Via a direct rod-to-ganglion cell synapse
q.explanation: AII amacrines make gap junctions (electrical synapses) with ON cone bipolar cells, which then drive ON-centre ganglion cells. Their chemical synapses go to OFF-centre ganglion cells in sublamina a.

q.stem: The approximate convergence of a rod pathway onto a single ganglion cell is:
options: 75,000 rods → 5000 rod bipolars → 250 amacrine cells → 1 ganglion cell
q.explanation: About 75,000 rods drive 5000 rod bipolars and 250 amacrine cells before converging on one large ganglion cell. This high convergence gains sensitivity at the expense of resolution, unlike the foveal midget system.

q.stem: The antagonistic surround of a bipolar cell receptive field is mainly generated by:
options: Inhibitory feedback from horizontal cells onto photoreceptors in the OPL
AII amacrine cells in the IPL
q.explanation: Centre responses come from the direct photoreceptor–bipolar–ganglion pathway; the surround comes from horizontal cell inhibitory feedback onto photoreceptors in the outer plexiform layer.

q.stem: For colour opponent channels in the retina, ON and OFF ganglion cell pathways have been identified for red and green cones. What is different for blue (S) cones?
options: They connect only to rod bipolar cells
No ON ganglion cell channel has been identified
They have no bipolar cell connection
No OFF ganglion cell channel has been identified
q.explanation: Red and green cones have both ON and OFF channels, but no OFF ganglion cell channel has been identified for blue cones.

q.stem: Which describes the foveal midget system?
options: Many cones converge on one large parasol ganglion cell projecting to magnocellular LGN
Foveal cones signal through AII amacrine cells
Each cone feeds one ON and one OFF midget bipolar and ganglion cell, projecting to parvocellular LGN
Foveal cones connect only to ON bipolar cells
q.explanation: For high resolution, each foveal cone connects to an ON and an OFF bipolar and so to an ON and an OFF midget ganglion cell, with minimal convergence; midget cells project to parvocellular LGN cells and carry red or green information.

q.stem: Which statement about RPE cells is FALSE?
options: Their nuclei and mitochondria are basal
They are hexagonal cuboidal cells in a monolayer
Their pigment granules are in the apical cytoplasm
They divide regularly to replace lost cells
q.explanation: RPE cells do not undergo mitosis. They form a monolayer of hexagonal cuboidal cells with basal nuclei and mitochondria and apical pigment granules that make the layer look black.

q.stem: Subretinal fluid is reabsorbed after a retinal break is closed. The RPE can absorb fluid at up to approximately:
q.explanation: The RPE can reabsorb up to about 2 ml per 24 hours, more than half the aqueous secreted in that time. This pumping may also help keep the neurosensory retina attached by suction.

q.stem: Which pairing of RPE protein and disease is correct?
q.explanation: Myosin VIIa is linked to Usher syndrome, bestrophin to Best disease and OA1 to ocular albinism. RPE65 is part of the isomerohydrolase of the visual cycle.

q.stem: What is the most abundant glycoprotein of the interphotoreceptor matrix?
q.explanation: IRBP is the most abundant IPM glycoprotein, and retinol can bind it in the subretinal space. Conventional matrix proteins such as collagen may be absent from the IPM.

q.stem: At light onset, which change occurs in the subretinal space?
options: K+ concentration rises and pH falls
K+ concentration falls and pH rises
Na+–K+ pumping in inner segments increases
q.explanation: Light reduces the dark current and inner segment Na+–K+ pumping, so subretinal K+ and lactate fall and pH rises. The fall in K+ hyperpolarises the RPE apical membrane.

q.stem: Which is NOT a function of retinal Müller cells?
options: Storing glycogen and supplying glucose to neurons
Covering the vitreal surface of retinal blood vessels in place of astrocytes
Uptake of glutamate from the extracellular space
Buffering light-evoked changes in extracellular K+
q.explanation: Müller cells buffer K+, take up glutamate, store glycogen and insulate neuronal processes; they cover intraretinal vessels, but vessels on the vitreous side are covered by astrocytes.

q.stem: In the ciliary body, the blood–aqueous barrier is formed by:
options: The basement membrane of the ciliary muscle
Tight junctions between pigmented epithelial cells
Tight junctions between non-pigmented ciliary epithelial cells
q.explanation: Ciliary capillaries are fenestrated and leak into the stroma; the barrier is the tight junctions between NPE cells. In the iris, by contrast, the barrier is formed by non-fenestrated endothelium with tight junctions.

q.stem: Tight junctions of both iris vessels and ciliary epithelium contain which proteins?
q.explanation: Iris and ciliary body tight junctions share the proteins occludin and cingulin. Connexins form gap junctions, such as those linking pigmented and non-pigmented ciliary epithelium.

q.stem: About what proportion of ocular blood flow passes through the choroid?
q.explanation: About 85% of ocular blood flow goes through the choroid and about 7% through the ciliary body. The very high choroidal flow means venous blood in the vortex veins has lost only 5–10% of its oxygen.

q.stem: Blood leaving the choroid through the vortex veins has lost only 5–10% of its oxygen. This is mainly because:
options: Choroidal vessels are impermeable to oxygen
Oxygen is mostly supplied by retinal vessels
The retina uses very little oxygen
Choroidal blood flow is very high
q.explanation: The very high choroidal flow means little oxygen is extracted per unit of blood. The retina actually uses more oxygen per gram than the brain, and lipid-soluble gases cross endothelium easily.

q.stem: Where is there a natural deficiency in the blood–retinal barrier?
options: At the ora serrata, where the RPE lacks tight junctions
At the fovea, where retinal capillaries are fenestrated
At the optic disc, where substances diffuse from the choroidal extravascular space into the anterior optic nerve
q.explanation: At the optic disc, water-soluble substances can diffuse directly from the choroidal extravascular space into the anterior optic nerve. Elsewhere, retinal endothelial tight junctions and RPE tight junctions maintain the barrier.

q.stem: Retinal capillary pericytes:
options: Form a continuous layer outside the endothelium joined by tight junctions
Lie within the basement membrane and may regulate permeability, endothelial growth and microcirculation
Are the main cells of the blood–retinal barrier
q.explanation: Pericytes form a discontinuous layer within the capillary basement membrane, contact endothelium by peg-and-socket junctions, adhesion plaques and gap junctions, and are contractile. They may affect permeability, angiogenesis and blood flow; the barrier itself is due to endothelial tight junctions.

q.stem: Which mediators can rapidly increase blood–ocular barrier permeability, thought to be by contracting endothelial cells?
q.explanation: Histamine, bradykinin and serotonin cause rapid increases in permeability, thought to be by endothelial contraction that widens intercellular clefts. Occludin and cingulin are tight junction proteins.

q.stem: Why do choriocapillaris vessels need to be fenestrated?
options: To keep a high glucose concentration at the RPE and supply substrates for vitamin A production
To form the outer blood–retinal barrier
To prevent albumin reaching Bruch's membrane
To allow lymphatic drainage of the choroid
q.explanation: Fenestrated choriocapillaris lets through small molecules and even albumin, keeping glucose high at the RPE and supplying amino acids needed for vitamin A production for the retina. The outer barrier is the RPE, and the choroid has no recognised lymphatics.

q.stem: Contraction and relaxation of the ciliary muscle are mediated respectively by:
q.explanation: Parasympathetic stimulation through M3 receptors contracts the ciliary muscle, and sympathetic stimulation through β2 receptors relaxes it. This is why pilocarpine causes accommodation and atropine-like drugs cause cycloplegia.

q.stem: An emmetropic, non-presbyopic eye shifts focus from infinity to a target at 25 cm. How much accommodation is used?
q.explanation: Accommodation in dioptres is the reciprocal of the fixation distance in metres: 1/0.25 m = 4 D. By the same rule, 1 m needs 1 D and 0.5 m needs 2 D.

q.stem: In the absence of a stimulus (for example in darkness), the eye rests at a tonic accommodation of about:
q.explanation: Resting or tonic accommodation is about 1.5 D, not zero. The eye has no accommodation only when focused at infinity.

q.stem: Which change occurs during accommodation?
options: The ciliary body moves forwards and inwards, zonular tension falls and the anterior chamber shallows
The lens becomes less curved on its posterior surface only
The lens capsule is stretched outwards and becomes flatter
The ciliary body moves backwards, zonules tighten and the lens flattens
q.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction moves the ciliary body anteriorly and inwards, relaxing the zonules. The elastic capsule then moulds the lens into a rounder shape, steepening both surfaces, and the anterior chamber shallows.

q.stem: What provides the main force making the lens more spherical during accommodation?
q.explanation: Once zonular tension is released, the capsule provides the major force reshaping the lens. Zonules are passive elastin-based fibres and lens fibres have no contractile mechanism for this.

q.stem: Why do even older presbyopic patients often appear to retain about 1 D of accommodation?
options: Convergence alone produces 1 D of accommodation
The lens keeps growing and becomes more elastic
Depth of focus, aided by smaller pupils, leads to an overestimate of true amplitude
q.explanation: Depth of focus inflates measured amplitude, and small pupils (which come with ageing) increase depth of focus, so about 1 D of apparent accommodation remains. True accommodative amplitude has declined.

q.stem: Ciliary muscle differs from other smooth muscle in which way?
options: Its ultrastructure resembles skeletal muscle, and it has large motor neurons
It is innervated only by sympathetic fibres
q.explanation: Ciliary muscle is smooth muscle with parasympathetic (M3) and sympathetic (β2) supply, but it has large motor neurons, a long nerve–muscle distance and an ultrastructure resembling skeletal muscle.

q.stem: Simple (physiological) anisocoria with no underlying pathology is found in about what proportion of people?
q.explanation: About a quarter of the population has simple anisocoria. The pupil also shows a normal physiological oscillation called hippus.

q.stem: The pupillary light reflex has a latent period of 0.2–0.5 s. As a consequence:
options: The pupil cannot follow light stimuli flickering faster than about 5 Hz
The pupil reacts more slowly than accommodation
Pupil constriction stops above 1 log unit of stimulus intensity
The direct and consensual responses differ in timing
q.explanation: Because of this latency, the pupil cannot respond to stimuli faster than about 5 Hz. The light reflex is much faster than accommodation, and constriction increases with stimulus intensity up to about 9 log units above threshold.

q.stem: When the pupil is dilated, light entering through the peripheral pupil is less effective at stimulating photoreceptors because of its oblique incidence. This is the:
q.explanation: The Stiles–Crawford effect describes the reduced effectiveness of light striking photoreceptors obliquely through the edge of a dilated pupil. The Purkinje shift concerns change in spectral sensitivity with adaptation, and Troxler's phenomenon is image fading.

q.stem: Which of the following is a consequence of pupil constriction?
options: Less depth of focus and less diffraction
More peripheral light reaching the retina
Greater depth of focus but more diffraction
q.explanation: Miosis increases depth of focus and reduces chromatic aberration, but diffraction increases. Dilation has the opposite effects and lets more peripheral light in.

q.stem: The first-order sympathetic neuron to the pupil synapses in the:
options: Ciliospinal centre of Budge at C8–T2
q.explanation: The first-order neuron runs from the hypothalamus to the ciliospinal centre of Budge (C8–T2). The second-order neuron goes to the superior cervical ganglion, and the third-order neuron follows the internal carotid artery. The ciliary ganglion and Edinger–Westphal nucleus are parasympathetic.

q.stem: In the cavernous sinus, third-order oculosympathetic fibres lie close to which cranial nerve before joining the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal?
q.explanation: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres ride on the internal carotid adventitia through the cavernous sinus close to the sixth nerve, then join the ophthalmic division of V to reach the dilator pupillae and Müller's muscle.

q.stem: Light shone in one eye causes equal constriction of both pupils. The anatomical basis is that:
options: The superior cervical ganglia are linked
Each pretectal nucleus receives input from both eyes and projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei
All retinal fibres cross at the chiasm
The ciliary ganglia are connected across the midline
q.explanation: Each pretectal nucleus receives input from both eyes, and pretectal outputs reach both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, so the direct and consensual responses are equal. Only nasal fibres cross at the chiasm.

q.stem: Pupils that react to a near target but not to light can occur because:
options: Near stimuli are processed only in the retina
The light reflex bypasses the Edinger–Westphal nucleus
The near response uses sympathetic fibres
The near-response pathway reaches the Edinger–Westphal nuclei without passing through the pretectal nuclei
q.explanation: The near triad is organised in pre-occipital cortex (areas 19 and 22) and converges on the Edinger–Westphal nuclei, bypassing the dorsal midbrain pretectal nuclei. Lesions affecting the pretectal pathway can therefore spare the near response.

q.stem: A patient has left miosis and ptosis. Topical cocaine dilates the right pupil but not the left. Topical hydroxyamphetamine later dilates the left pupil. The lesion is most likely:
options: Preganglionic or central (first or second order)
q.explanation: Cocaine blocks noradrenaline reuptake, so the Horner's pupil fails to dilate. Hydroxyamphetamine releases noradrenaline from an intact postganglionic neuron, so dilation means the lesion is preganglionic or central; pharmacology cannot separate those two.

q.stem: In Horner's syndrome, the anisocoria is:
q.explanation: In dim light the normal pupil dilates while the Horner's pupil cannot, so anisocoria increases. This is why light reflexes should be examined with the room lights dimmed.

q.stem: Why is facial sweating usually preserved in postganglionic Horner's syndrome?
options: Sudomotor fibres travel with the abducens nerve
Sudomotor fibres to the face run with the external carotid artery
Sweating is controlled by parasympathetic fibres
Sweating fibres leave the chain below T2
q.explanation: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres for facial sweating follow the external carotid artery, whereas pupillary fibres follow the internal carotid, so a lesion beyond the bifurcation spares sweating.

q.stem: Which of the following cannot produce a relative afferent pupillary defect?
q.explanation: A cataract does not cause an RAPD. RAPDs are most commonly due to retinal or optic nerve disease such as glaucoma, which reduces afferent input to the pretectal nucleus.

q.stem: Adie's tonic pupil shows supersensitivity to dilute cholinergic agonists because:
options: It is caused by a dorsal midbrain lesion
It results from a ciliary ganglion lesion causing postganglionic denervation
The iris sphincter is directly damaged by trauma
q.explanation: Adie's pupil arises from a ciliary ganglion lesion; denervation supersensitivity to cholinergic agonists follows. The light reaction is sluggish while the near response is preserved but tonic.

q.stem: Thymoxamine causes miosis by:
options: Blocking α-adrenergic receptors on the dilator pupillae
q.explanation: Thymoxamine is an α-blocker, so it opposes the dilator and causes miosis. Cholinesterase inhibitors (such as physostigmine) and muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, carbachol) cause miosis by cholinergic means; cocaine blocks reuptake and dilates.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: A standard Snellen or logMAR letter chart primarily measures which type of acuity?
q.explanation: Letter charts measure minimum resolvable acuity, the ability to resolve features within a visible target. Minimum visible is detecting a single feature, and hyperacuity is judging the relative position of features.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: At 5° from the centre of the fovea, visual acuity is approximately what fraction of foveal acuity?
q.explanation: Acuity falls steeply with eccentricity; at 5° from the foveal centre it is about a quarter of foveal acuity, because cones are more widely spaced and summation areas grow.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: Vernier (hyperacuity) thresholds are typically:
q.explanation: Vernier acuity involves judgements at 2–10 seconds of arc, well below the 30 seconds to 1 minute resolution limit. It is absent in infancy, best at around 14 years, and thought to be absent in strabismic amblyopia.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: A grating has maximum luminance 60 cd/m² and minimum luminance 40 cd/m². What is its contrast (modulation)?
q.explanation: Modulation M = (Imax – Imin)/(Imax + Imin) = (60 – 40)/(60 + 40) = 0.2. Contrast sensitivity is the reciprocal of the threshold modulation.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: The normal contrast sensitivity function is best described as:
options: Highest at intermediate spatial frequencies, falling at both low and high frequencies
Highest at the lowest spatial frequencies
Highest at the highest spatial frequencies
q.explanation: Both low and high spatial frequencies need more contrast to be seen, so sensitivity peaks in the intermediate range. Sensitivity is also greatest for vertical and horizontal grating orientations.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: Over what range of pupil diameter does visual acuity remain relatively constant?
q.explanation: Acuity is fairly constant for pupils between 2.5 and 6 mm; outside this range minimum angle of resolution and pupil size are reciprocally related.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: The crowding phenomenon is reduced on logMAR charts mainly because:
options: Optotypes are evenly spaced in proportion to their size
Fewer letters are used per line
q.explanation: Crowding happens when targets are too close together. logMAR charts have defined letter sizing and spacing so optotypes are evenly spaced, removing this effect, which is one reason they are standard in clinical trials.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: Ricco's law describes the relationship whereby:
options: Threshold intensity is inversely proportional to stimulus area
Threshold intensity is inversely proportional to stimulus duration
q.explanation: Ricco's law covers spatial summation: threshold intensity varies inversely with stimulus area. Bloch's law concerns temporal summation (intensity versus duration), and ΔI/I constant is the Weber–Fechner relation.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: About how many quanta of light must reach the cornea for a flash to be detected?
q.explanation: Detection needs roughly 50–150 quanta at the cornea, stimulating about 10–15 rods, whose responses are summed at bipolar or ganglion cell level.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: The Weber–Fechner relation states that over a moderate range of background intensities (about 3 log units for cones):
options: Pupil area halves with each log unit
ΔI is constant regardless of I
Threshold is inversely proportional to stimulus area
q.explanation: In the Weber–Fechner range the increment threshold ΔI is proportional to background I, so ΔI/I (the Weber fraction) is constant. At high intensities saturation occurs and the relation fails.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: Peak spectral sensitivity of the light-adapted and dark-adapted eye are approximately:
q.explanation: The light-adapted (photopic) eye is most sensitive near 555 nm, the dark-adapted (scotopic) eye near 505 nm. 434 nm is quoted for melanopsin.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: The diagram shows a normal dark adaptation curve. The kink (X) marks the point at which:
q.explanation: Dark adaptation has an early fast cone component followed by a slower rod component; the break is where rods become more sensitive than cones. Full dark adaptation takes about 30 minutes, much slower than light adaptation.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: If dark adaptation is measured using only a small central white target, the curve:
options: Becomes steeper with an earlier rod–cone break
Flattens, showing only a cone component
q.explanation: A small central target falls on the rod-free fovea, so rods are not stimulated and only the cone branch is seen, with the curve flattening early.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: The rate of recovery of sensitivity after a bleach is limited mainly by:
options: Delivery of 11-cis-retinal to opsin, which depends on a healthy RPE
q.explanation: Rhodopsin regeneration and dark adaptation depend on the supply of 11-cis-retinal to bleached photoreceptors, which relies on the RPE; age-related slowing of dark adaptation may reflect failing RPE.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells that influence circadian rhythm:
options: Project mainly to V1 for image formation
Make up most ganglion cells and contain rhodopsin
Make up about 2% of ganglion cells and contain melanopsin, with a peak sensitivity in blue light
q.explanation: About 2% of RGCs contain melanopsin (peak quoted as 434 nm) and are separate from image-forming cells; they help entrain circadian rhythm via the suprachiasmatic nuclei, which drive pineal melatonin.

q.section: Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, light detection and dark adaptation
q.stem: Melatonin is synthesised in the pineal gland from:
q.explanation: Melatonin is made from tryptophan via serotonin. It is secreted mainly at night and suppressed by light, under control of the suprachiasmatic nuclei.

q.stem: As illumination falls from photopic to scotopic levels, blue-green objects look relatively brighter than red ones. This is the:
q.explanation: The Purkinje shift is the relative brightening of short wavelengths as luminance falls, with peak brightness moving from about 555 nm (photopic) to about 500 nm (scotopic). Colour constancy is a cortical process keeping object colour stable.

q.stem: An object's perceived colour stays the same under different illuminants even though the reflected wavelengths change. This colour constancy is due to:
q.explanation: Colour constancy is a function of higher visual processing in the cortex, not a retinal photochemical effect.

q.stem: Peak sensitivity ranges of human cones are approximately:
options: S 400 nm; M 500 nm; L 650 nm
S 505 nm; M 555 nm; L 600 nm
q.explanation: Short-wavelength (blue) cones peak at 440–450 nm, medium (green) at 535–550 nm and long (red) at 570–590 nm. Blue cones are the rarest in the human fovea.

q.stem: Which theory proposes that colour is coded by paired opponent mechanisms (red–green, blue–yellow, white–black) organised at the ganglion cell level?
q.explanation: Hering's colour opponent theory explains how ambiguity at the bipolar cell is resolved by receptive field organisation at ganglion cell level. The trichromatic theory (Young, Helmholtz, Maxwell) concerns summation of three receptor types.

q.stem: A child has very poor visual acuity, photophobia, nystagmus and no colour discrimination. The most likely diagnosis is:
q.explanation: Rod monochromats (about 1 in 30,000) have true achromatic vision with low acuity, photophobia and nystagmus, sometimes with macular dystrophy. Cone monochromats (about 1 in 100,000) have normal acuity, and the defect is in cortical processing.

q.stem: The most common form of colour vision defect, affecting about 6% of males, is:
q.explanation: Anomalous trichromats use abnormal proportions of the three primaries for matches and are the commonest group, about 6% of males. Dichromats match with only two primaries.

q.stem: A protanope:
options: Lacks red (L) cone function and matches colours with two primaries
Has no cone function at all
Uses more red than normal in colour matches
q.explanation: Protanopes are dichromats missing red; deuteranopes miss green and tritanopes blue. A protan anomalous trichromat (protanomal) uses more red in matches but has all three mechanisms.

q.stem: Cerebral achromatopsia is associated with lesions of:
options: The lingual or fusiform gyrus (area V4)
q.explanation: Cortical colour processing occurs in V4, and lesions in the lingual or fusiform gyri cause cerebral achromatopsia.

q.stem: Colour discrimination on the Farnsworth–Munsell 100 hue test is best at about what age?
q.explanation: Hue discrimination, tested clinically with the Farnsworth–Munsell 100 hue test, peaks at about 19 years.

q.stem: Which retinal neurons produce all-or-nothing action potentials rather than graded potentials?
q.explanation: Ganglion cells fire all-or-nothing action potentials, so their output can only be graded by firing rate. Photoreceptors, bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells give graded responses.

q.stem: There are about 150 million photoreceptors but how many optic nerve fibres per eye?
q.explanation: Around 1 million optic nerve fibres serve about 150 million photoreceptors, requiring convergence and summation of stimulatory and inhibitory inputs.

q.stem: Large receptive fields with high convergence are characteristic of:
q.explanation: M cells are large with large receptive fields reflecting convergence from many bipolar or amacrine cells. P cells and foveal midget cells have small fields with little convergence.

q.stem: Compared with horizontal cells, amacrine cells:
options: Are more numerous and use a wider range of neurotransmitters
Act only at the photoreceptor–bipolar synapse
q.explanation: Amacrine cells outnumber horizontal cells and use dopamine, acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA and glycine, modifying signals at the bipolar–ganglion interface. Horizontal cells act at the receptor–bipolar interface.

q.stem: The standing (resting) potential of the eye is generated mainly at the interface between:
options: The ganglion cells and the nerve fibre layer
q.explanation: The resting retinal potential of about 60 mV arises at the RPE–photoreceptor interface, and is the basis of the EOG.

q.stem: On electro-oculography, a normal Arden ratio (light peak/dark trough) is greater than:
q.explanation: An Arden ratio above about 180% is normal. Recordings use electrodes at the inner and outer canthi after about 20 minutes in the dark followed by light.

q.stem: The light rise of the EOG is thought to result from:
options: Current flow due to changes in potassium concentration in the interphotoreceptor matrix
q.explanation: The light rise reflects extracellular current flow driven by potassium changes in the interphotoreceptor matrix across the RPE. It is lost when the RPE–photoreceptor relationship is disrupted, as in retinal detachment.

q.stem: On the flash ERG, the a-wave and b-wave arise mainly from:
options: Bipolar cells and ganglion cells respectively
Ganglion cells and the optic nerve respectively
q.explanation: The negative a-wave reflects photoreceptor hyperpolarisation (Granit's PIII). The positive b-wave comes from bipolar cells, directly or via Müller cells (PII). The c-wave arises in the RPE.

q.stem: A patient has a 'negative' ERG in which the b-wave is smaller than the a-wave. Which condition is consistent with this?
q.explanation: In congenital night blindness and retinoschisis the rod bipolar contribution to the b-wave is lost, giving a negative ERG. In retinitis pigmentosa the scotopic ERG is reduced overall, while optic neuritis and amblyopia do not affect the full-field ERG.

q.stem: Which ERG stimulus isolates a cone response?
options: A dim blue flash in the dark-adapted eye
A dim white flash after 30 minutes of dark adaptation
q.explanation: Cone responses are obtained with a bright flash on a rod-saturating background or a 30 Hz flicker that rods cannot follow. A dim blue or white flash in the dark gives a rod response, and a checkerboard is used for pattern ERG/VEP.

q.stem: On pattern ERG, selective reduction of the N95 component suggests disease of:
q.explanation: N95 (negative at about 95 ms) is affected by optic nerve damage, while P50 is affected by damage to the inner retina and macula. The pattern ERG helps distinguish maculopathy from optic nerve disease.

q.stem: Which statement about VEP recording is correct?
options: VEP is recorded from corneal electrodes
Optic nerve demyelination shortens P100 latency
Pupils should not be dilated and refractive error should be corrected for pattern VEP
Flash VEP requires full patient cooperation
q.explanation: Pattern VEP needs undilated pupils and refractive correction. Flash VEP can be used in infants, uncooperative or unconscious patients, and demyelination delays P100. VEPs are recorded from scalp electrodes over the occipital cortex.

q.stem: In albinism, both flash and pattern VEPs are abnormal. This is because of:
options: An increase in uncrossed fibres at the chiasm
A reduced number of uncrossed fibres at the chiasm
q.explanation: Albinism has fewer uncrossed (more crossed) fibres at the chiasm, which distorts the cortical VEP distribution. In contrast, an amblyopic eye gives a normal flash VEP but an abnormal pattern VEP.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: UK driving standards require a binocular field of at least:
options: 90° either side and 45° above and below
60° either side of fixation horizontally and 20° above and below the horizontal
q.explanation: The UK standard is a binocular single vision field extending 60° either side of the vertical meridian and 20° above and below the horizontal meridian.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: The normal monocular visual field extends approximately:
q.explanation: The monocular field reaches about 100° temporally, 60° nasally, 60° up and 75° down. The binocular field is about 120° wide, and the total field about 200° by 135°.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: In perimetry, what stimulus intensity corresponds to 40 dB on a Humphrey perimeter?
q.explanation: Decibels are attenuation from the maximum: 40 dB is 4 log units below 10,000 asb, which is 1 asb, regarded as the minimum perceivable stimulus. The Goldmann maximum is 1000 asb.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: A spiral-shaped field on Goldmann perimetry most strongly suggests:
q.explanation: Goldmann kinetic perimetry is useful when malingering is suspected because it gives a classic spiral field. It is also useful for neurological defects and patients with poor fixation.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: Which is a standard Humphrey perimetry parameter?
options: Moving target from periphery to centre
Goldmann size V stimulus on a 10 asb background
Goldmann size III stimulus on a 31.5 asb background
q.explanation: Humphrey uses a static Goldmann III stimulus presented for 0.2 s on a 31.5 asb background, typically testing the central 30°. Moving targets belong to kinetic (Goldmann) perimetry.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: Which Humphrey threshold strategy advances in 3 dB steps without reversal, being about 70% quicker than the original full threshold?
q.explanation: FASTPAC uses 3 dB steps with no reversal; it is quicker but has lower resolution and more variability. Full threshold uses 4 dB steps then reverses in 2 dB steps, and SITA uses statistical modelling to halve test time while keeping reliability.

q.section: Visual fields, eye movements and stereopsis
q.stem: The centre of rotation of the eye lies approximately:
options: 13.5 mm behind the corneal apex and 1.6 mm temporal to the geometric centre
7 mm behind the corneal apex at the lens
24 mm behind the corneal apex at the posterior pole
13.5 mm behind the corneal apex and 1.6 mm nasal to the geometric centre
q.explanation: The fixed centre of rotation is about 13.5 mm behind the corneal apex and 1.6 mm nasal to the geometric centre of the globe.
