q.explanation: Histamine opens the tight junctions between endothelial cells. Leukocytes can then pass into the tissue and, together with complement, phagocytose the offending organism. It does not act by destroying the basement membrane or killing endothelial cells.

q.stem: In the chemotaxis of neutrophils, which substance is an example of a chemotactic factor that binds receptors on the neutrophil surface?
q.explanation: Chemotactic factors such as C5a and PGE2 bind neutrophil receptors. This triggers phospholipase A2 activity, calcium influx and microtubule activation, so the cell migrates down the gradient. Histamine mainly raises vascular permeability, IgE sensitises mast cells, and thromboxane A2 drives platelet aggregation.

q.stem: Epithelioid cells, the characteristic cells of granulomatous inflammation, are derived from:
q.explanation: Epithelioid cells come from monocytes or macrophages. They have plentiful eosinophilic cytoplasm, can phagocytose and interact with T cells, and often palisade around necrosis. Neutrophils, fibroblasts and plasma cells do not transform into epithelioid cells.

q.stem: A skin nodule biopsy from a child with juvenile xanthogranuloma shows giant cells in which a ring of nuclei is surrounded by an outer zone of foamy cytoplasm. These are:
q.explanation: Touton giant cells have foamy cytoplasm outside a ring of nuclei and are typical of lipid disorders such as juvenile xanthogranuloma. Langhans' cells have homogeneous eosinophilic central cytoplasm with nuclei around the periphery and are typical of tuberculosis. Foreign body giant cells contain the material that provoked them.

q.stem: Which giant cell is classically associated with tuberculosis and has a homogeneous eosinophilic centre with a peripheral rim of nuclei?
options: Plasma cell with a Russell body
q.explanation: The Langhans' giant cell, formed by fused macrophages, has a peripheral horseshoe or rim of nuclei around homogeneous eosinophilic cytoplasm and is typical of TB. Touton cells have peripheral foamy cytoplasm and occur in lipid disorders. A Russell body is an inclusion in a plasma cell, not a giant cell.

q.stem: A chalazion is excised. Which pattern of granulomatous inflammation would you expect to see?
q.explanation: A chalazion shows a zonal pattern: a central area (here lipid-associated necrosis) surrounded by a palisade of epithelioid cells, then lymphocytes and plasma cells. Other zonal examples are caseating TB, a ruptured dermoid cyst and suture granuloma. Diffuse patterns occur in sympathetic uveitis and VKH, and discrete tubercles in sarcoidosis.

q.stem: Which condition typically shows a DISCRETE pattern of granulomatous inflammation, with tubercles of epithelioid cells surrounded by a narrow rim of lymphocytes and plasma cells?
q.explanation: Discrete (tubercle-forming) granulomas occur in sarcoidosis, tuberculoid leprosy and miliary TB. Sympathetic uveitis and VKH show a diffuse pattern, with epithelioid cells scattered among lymphocytes and plasma cells. Toxocara gives a zonal pattern around a necrotic centre.

q.stem: Which of the following is an example of NON-granulomatous chronic inflammation?
q.explanation: The book lists Behçet's disease, most forms of anterior and posterior uveitis, multiple sclerosis, retinal vasculitis and endocrine exophthalmos as non-granulomatous. Sarcoidosis (discrete), sympathetic ophthalmia (diffuse) and chalazion (zonal) are all granulomatous.

q.stem: A conjunctival biopsy shows plasma cells whose cytoplasm is distended by eosinophilic inclusions, pushing the nucleus to one side. Which statement about these inclusions is correct?
options: They are Rosenthal fibres and indicate optic nerve glioma
They are Dalen–Fuchs nodules and indicate sympathetic ophthalmia
They are psammoma bodies and indicate meningioma
They are Russell bodies and are seen in B-cell lymphomas
q.explanation: A Russell body is an eosinophilic inclusion that fills and enlarges the plasma cell cytoplasm, leaving the nucleus eccentric or absent. It is seen in B-cell lymphomas. Dalen–Fuchs nodules are collections of cells at the level of the RPE, Rosenthal fibres are altered astrocyte processes, and psammoma bodies are calcified bodies in meningioma.

q.stem: After a full-thickness corneal laceration, at approximately what time does endothelial sliding cover the posterior wound?
q.explanation: Posterior wound coverage by sliding endothelium happens at about 24 hours. Polymorphs invade the wound at around 30 minutes (leukocytic phase), and at about 1 hour healthy endothelium stops full-thickness epithelial ingrowth. One week is the timescale for new vessel formation and myofibroblast contraction in skin wounds.

q.stem: In the fibroblastic phase of healing of a central full-thickness corneal wound, the wound fibroblasts arise from:
q.explanation: Fibroblasts in a central corneal wound come from stromal keratocytes. They lay down collagen and mucopolysaccharides to form an avascular matrix. Mononuclear cells from limbal vessels are involved in limbal wounds, and endothelium and epithelium cover the wound surfaces but do not form the stromal fibroblasts.

q.stem: Which corneal layer does NOT regenerate after injury?
q.explanation: Bowman's layer does not regenerate. Descemet's membrane also does not regenerate, although it is elastic and recoils at the edge of a defect. Epithelium regenerates from the limbus, keratocytes heal the stroma, and endothelium fills defects by sliding and lays down secondary Descemet's layers.

q.stem: Why do iris wounds, such as a surgical iridotomy, tend to remain patent?
options: Fibrinolysins in the aqueous prevent fibrin clot formation
Iris pigment epithelium undergoes fibrous metaplasia
q.explanation: Fibrinolysins in aqueous humour inhibit fibrin clot formation, so iris defects stay open. Only if the wound edges come together can the iris pigment epithelium proliferate reactively. The iris is vascular, and fibrous metaplasia is the response of lens epithelium, not iris.

q.stem: After retinal injury, the glial cells that replace damaged neurons are derived from:
q.explanation: Damaged retinal neurons are replaced by glial cells derived from perivascular astrocytes and Müller cells. The RPE can separately become metaplastic and form fibrous tissue such as preretinal membranes. Choroidal melanocytes do not proliferate after trauma, and episcleral fibroblasts are involved in scleral scarring.

q.stem: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is an example of which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
q.explanation: Seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis are immediate (type I) reactions. Mast cells carrying IgE on their Fc receptors degranulate when antigen crosslinks the IgE. Type II involves antibodies against self cells, type III immune complex deposition, and type IV sensitised T cells.

q.stem: In type I hypersensitivity, which mediator released by mast cells also acts as a negative-feedback signal that inhibits further mast cell degranulation?
q.explanation: Crosslinking of IgE on mast cells releases histamine, serotonin, platelet-activating factor and eosinophil chemotactic factors. Histamine is singled out as also inhibiting further degranulation through negative feedback. The other mediators are released but are not described as having this feedback role.

q.stem: Myasthenia gravis is an example of which type of hypersensitivity?
q.explanation: In type II hypersensitivity, antibody is directed against antigens on the body's own cells. Examples include myasthenia gravis, incompatible transfusion, rhesus disease of the newborn and hyperacute graft rejection. Rheumatoid arthritis and SLE are type III examples, and Mantoux is type IV.

q.stem: A previously immunised patient develops a local inflammatory reaction a few hours after an intradermal injection of the same antigen. This Arthus reaction is an example of:
options: Type I hypersensitivity, occurring within minutes
Type III hypersensitivity, typically lasting about 4–10 hours
Type IV hypersensitivity, peaking at 48–72 hours
Type II hypersensitivity, mediated by NK cells
q.explanation: The Arthus reaction is an immune complex (type III) reaction. In a person with high pre-existing antibody levels, antigen–antibody complexes deposit locally and cause acute inflammation lasting about 4–10 hours. Peaks at 48–72 hours are characteristic of tuberculin-type (type IV) responses.

q.stem: The Mantoux test produces a dermal reaction that peaks at:
q.explanation: Tuberculin-type (type IV) hypersensitivity after subdermal tuberculin peaks at 48–72 hours. The Arthus reaction (type III) lasts 4–10 hours, and immediate type I reactions occur within minutes. A granulomatous cell-mediated reaction from persistent antigen peaks at about 4 weeks.

q.stem: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis and atopic keratoconjunctivitis are best described as:
options: Mixed type I and type IV reactions
q.explanation: The book groups GPC, VKC and AKC together as partly type I and partly type IV hypersensitivity reactions. Pure type I examples are seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis. These conditions are not described as antibody-cytotoxic or immune complex disorders.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors on which immune complex (type III) deposition depends?
options: Increased vascular permeability due to histamine release
Specific antigen–antibody complexes directed to a single organ
Turbulent blood flow, e.g. in the kidney
Crosslinking of IgE on mast cell Fc receptors
q.explanation: Type III deposition depends on turbulent flow (as in the kidney), raised vascular permeability from histamine release, and specific antigen–antibody complexes targeting a single organ. IgE crosslinking on mast cells is the mechanism of type I hypersensitivity.

q.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a dystrophy from a degeneration?
options: A dystrophy occurs only in the elderly; a degeneration only in children
A degeneration is always inherited; a dystrophy is acquired
A degeneration affects a single matrix component; a dystrophy affects all
A dystrophy is a primary inherited disorder; a degeneration is secondary to previous disease
q.explanation: Degeneration is a secondary change after previous disease in tissue that has finished growing, and it often involves collagen, elastin and proteoglycans. Dystrophy is a primary, inherited disorder that can occur at any age and may involve a single matrix component.

q.stem: Aniridia is given as an example of which tissue reaction?
q.explanation: Hypoplasia is arrested development of a tissue in embryonic life, e.g. aniridia. Aplasia is a complete lack of development, e.g. aplasia of the optic nerve. Atrophy is a reduction in size of cells or tissue, and dysplasia is abnormal growth with increased mitoses and reduced differentiation (e.g. retinal dysplasia).

q.stem: Anterior subcapsular cataract involves transformation of lens epithelium into fibrous tissue. This is an example of:
q.explanation: Metaplasia is the change of one tissue type into another. The book's example is fibrous metaplasia of lens epithelium in anterior subcapsular cataract, and the lens responds to trauma in the same way. Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, hypertrophy an increase in size without more cells, and neoplasia uncontrolled growth that never reaches equilibrium.

q.stem: Which feature distinguishes dysplasia from invasive malignancy?
options: Dysplasia always regresses once the stimulus is removed
Dysplastic tissue has fewer mitoses than normal tissue
Dysplastic tissue does not breach the basement membrane
q.explanation: Dysplasia shows abnormal growth with more mitoses and less differentiation, but it is not invasive and does not cross the basement membrane. Invasion through the basement membrane is a feature of malignancy. The other options contradict the definition.

q.stem: How does neoplasia differ from hyperplasia?
options: Neoplastic growth never reaches equilibrium and persists after the stimulus stops
Neoplasia involves an increase in cell size but not number
Hyperplasia only occurs during embryonic development
Hyperplasia always involves an increase in cell size
q.explanation: Hyperplastic growth increases cell number but reaches an equilibrium and is not indefinite (e.g. RPE hyperplasia after trauma). Neoplastic growth is uncoordinated, exceeds that of normal tissue, never reaches equilibrium, and continues after the provoking stimulus is removed.

q.stem: A corneal biopsy stained with Congo red shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. The deposited material is:
q.explanation: Amyloid is homogeneous pink on H&E and stains with Congo red, showing apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Calcium is deposited as hydroxyapatite in band keratopathy, glycogen infiltration gives lacy vacuolation (e.g. iris pigment epithelium in diabetes), and mucopolysaccharide accumulates in macular corneal dystrophy.

q.stem: Band keratopathy is a form of calcific degeneration affecting:
options: Bowman's layer and the superficial stroma
The corneal epithelial basement membrane only
q.explanation: In band keratopathy, calcium is deposited in Bowman's layer and the superficial stroma. Dystrophic calcification occurs in normocalcaemic states, and metastatic calcification occurs in hypercalcaemic states such as hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D and sarcoidosis.

q.stem: Angioid streaks in pseudoxanthoma elasticum arise from which type of degeneration?
options: Elastotic degeneration with ruptures in Bruch's membrane
q.explanation: Elastotic degeneration results from defective fibroblast function, giving an altered and less elastic matrix. It is seen in ageing skin, pterygia and pseudoxanthoma elasticum, where breaks in Bruch's membrane expose the choroid as angioid streaks. Hyaline change affects arteriolosclerotic vessel walls.

q.stem: Which of the following is classified in the book as a SYSTEMIC form of amyloid deposition with ocular relevance?
options: Solitary amyloid nodule of the eyelid
q.explanation: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is listed as systemic. Its amorphous eosinophilic material deposits on the anterior lens capsule, ciliary processes, iris and trabecular meshwork, causing secondary glaucoma, and also in skin and viscera. Solitary eyelid nodules and the lattice and gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophies are localised forms.

q.stem: Lacy vacuolation of the iris pigment epithelium in diabetes mellitus is due to:
q.explanation: Glycogen infiltration in diabetes causes lacy vacuolation of the iris pigment epithelium. It is also seen in long-standing neural retinal detachment and in proliferating RPE cells. Hydropic change is a reversible cytoplasmic vacuolation seen with infection, intoxication, anaemia or circulatory disturbance.

q.stem: In phthisis bulbi, where is the woven and lamellar bone typically located?
options: On the outer surface of the sclera
On the inner surface of Bruch's membrane, from metaplastic RPE-derived fibrous tissue
q.explanation: In a hypotonic phthisical eye, fibrous tissue formed by proliferating RPE undergoes metaplasia and ossification. The bone sits on the inner surface of Bruch's membrane and can extend into the vitreous and choroid. Calcification in the fibrous lens cortex is a separate entity, cataracta ossea.

q.stem: In chemical carcinogenesis, which statement about 'promotion' is correct?
options: It only occurs with physical carcinogens
A substance capable of promotion can never initiate
It involves long-term exposure that encourages proliferation and is usually not mutagenic
It is a short exposure that causes a mutation
q.explanation: Initiation is a short exposure that causes a mutation. Promotion is prolonged exposure that drives cell proliferation and is usually not mutagenic. Substances that can both initiate and promote are called complete carcinogens.

q.stem: Ultraviolet radiation damages skin DNA mainly by forming:
options: Double-strand breaks with major chromosome deletions
q.explanation: UV mainly affects the skin by forming pyrimidine dimers, which DNA repair mechanisms usually excise. Ionising radiation damages DNA directly, causing anything from single-gene mutations to large chromosome deletions. Hepatic hydroxylation is relevant to chemical carcinogens such as 2-naphthylamine.

q.stem: Epstein–Barr virus is associated with which ocular/orbital tumour?
q.explanation: EBV can cause orbital Burkitt's lymphoma, and intraocular large B-cell lymphoma in immunosuppressed patients. Conjunctival papillomas are linked to papillomavirus type 16 and lacrimal papillomas to type 11. Choroidal melanoma is not given a viral cause.

q.stem: A single point mutation in the ras gene is oncogenic because the mutant protein:
options: Is translocated next to an immunoglobulin gene
Loses the ability to bind E2F
Cannot hydrolyse GTP, leaving signalling permanently on
Is amplified to produce many gene copies
q.explanation: Ras is the book's example of structural change. A point mutation stops the protein hydrolysing GTP, so signalling stays switched on. Translocation (e.g. myc in Burkitt's, abl in CML) and amplification (e.g. myb) are the other mechanisms. Binding E2F is a function of pRB.

q.stem: Which statement about tumour-suppressor genes is correct?
options: Loss of both copies is required for neoplasia to develop
They code for growth factors and their receptors
The NF1 gene is a proto-oncogene on chromosome 13
A single mutated copy is enough to drive neoplasia
q.explanation: Tumour-suppressor genes switch off cell proliferation, and both copies must be lost before neoplasia develops. Growth factors and their receptors are products of proto-oncogenes. The NF1 gene is a tumour-suppressor gene on the long arm of chromosome 17.

q.stem: According to Knudson's 'two-hit' hypothesis, in hereditary retinoblastoma:
options: Both hits are inherited from the parents
A single hit in one allele is sufficient
The first hit is a germline mutation and the second is a somatic mutation in the other allele
Both hits occur in somatic cells
q.explanation: In the inherited form, one allele is already defective in the germ line (first hit) and the second allele later mutates (second hit). In sporadic cases both hits occur in somatic cells. One hit alone is not enough, because tumour-suppressor genes need both copies lost.

q.stem: Which event allows a cell to progress from G1 into S phase in the pRB/E2F pathway?
options: Binding of pRB to E2F promoters
Binding of p16 to E2F, activating transcription
Phosphorylation of pRB by cyclin D1/cdk4, releasing E2F
q.explanation: E2F switches on genes for DNA synthesis, and hypophosphorylated pRB binds E2F to block this. Cyclin D1/cdk4 is most active in G1 and phosphorylates pRB, releasing E2F so the cell enters S phase. p16 is a cdk inhibitor that indirectly prevents pRB phosphorylation, so it holds the cell in G1.

q.stem: The p53 gene is located on chromosome 17p13.1. In response to DNA damage, its major functions are:
options: Suppression of apoptosis via the mitochondrial pathway
Cell cycle arrest and initiation of apoptosis
q.explanation: p53 is the commonest target of genetic change in human tumours. When DNA is damaged it halts the cell cycle and starts apoptosis. Suppression of apoptosis through the mitochondrial pathway is the role of bcl-2, and pRB is phosphorylated by cyclin D1/cdk4.

q.stem: In follicular B-cell lymphoma, the t(14;18) translocation causes neoplasia by:
options: Loss of BAX, which normally suppresses proliferation
Overexpression of bcl-2, which inhibits apoptosis
q.explanation: t(14;18) fuses bcl-2 with the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene. The resulting overexpression of bcl-2 protects B cells from mitochondrial-pathway apoptosis and so prolongs their survival. BAX opposes this by inducing apoptosis, and the balance of BCL-2/BAX homodimers and heterodimers decides whether apoptosis occurs.

q.stem: A hamartoma is best defined as:
options: A benign neoplasm of glandular origin
A malignant tumour of embryonic tissue
A non-neoplastic malformation of tissues normally found at that site
A non-neoplastic malformation of tissues not normally found at that site
q.explanation: A hamartoma is a non-neoplastic malformation made of tissues native to the site; haemangiomas and naevi are examples. A choristoma is a malformation of tissues not normally present at that site (e.g. epibulbar dermoid). A benign glandular tumour is an adenoma.

q.stem: A child has a smooth white nodule at the limbus with fine hairs on its surface. Histology shows fibrous tissue, fat, hair and sweat glands. This lesion is:
q.explanation: An epibulbar dermoid contains tissues not normally found on the bulbar conjunctiva, which makes it a choristoma. Phakomatous choristoma of the eyelid is another example. Haemangiomas and naevi are hamartomas, and a sebaceous adenoma is a benign glandular tumour, typically a yellow caruncular mass.

q.stem: Which statement about periocular haemangiomas is correct?
options: Capillary haemangiomas may regress in childhood, whereas cavernous haemangiomas do not
Cavernous haemangiomas usually regress spontaneously in childhood
q.explanation: Haemangiomas are hamartomas: lobulated proliferations of vascular channels in the eyelid, orbit or choroid. Capillary haemangiomas may regress during childhood, while cavernous haemangiomas (large thick-walled vessels) do not. Extensive haemangiomas occur in Sturge–Weber syndrome.

q.stem: Which benign tumour is given as an example of a benign neoplasm that can nevertheless be locally invasive?
q.explanation: Benign tumours are generally non-invasive and non-metastatic, but meningioma and pleomorphic adenoma are cited as benign tumours that can invade. This is one reason pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland must be excised completely.

q.stem: Platelet dense bodies contain:
options: Factor VIII, factor V and fibrinogen
q.explanation: Dense bodies in the organelle zone hold ADP, calcium and 5-HT. Alpha granules hold factor VIII, factor V, fibrinogen, fibronectin, PDGF and chemotactic factors. Microtubules and microfilaments are in the sol-gel zone, and the dense tubular system belongs to the membrane zone.

q.stem: Factor V Leiden predisposes to venous thrombosis because:
options: Factor V becomes resistant to breakdown by activated protein C
It causes deficiency of antithrombin III
It increases von Willebrand factor production
q.explanation: The factor V Leiden mutation makes factor V resistant to inactivation by protein C. About 5% of white people are carriers. Protein C, with protein S as cofactor, normally inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.

q.stem: What is the role of protein S in the anticoagulant system?
options: Directly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa
Cofactor for activated protein C in inactivating factors Va and VIIIa
q.explanation: Protein S is the cofactor for activated protein C when it inactivates factors Va and VIIIa. Deficiency is autosomal dominant and found in 5–8% of young patients with venous thrombosis. tPA converts plasminogen to plasmin, antithrombin III inactivates thrombin and several factors including Xa, and von Willebrand factor mediates platelet adherence.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of Virchow's triad?
options: Change in blood flow, e.g. venous stasis
Change in the vessel wall, e.g. atherosclerosis
Change in blood constituents, e.g. increased platelets
q.explanation: Virchow's triad is altered blood flow (stasis, arrhythmia, valve disease), altered vessel wall (atherosclerosis, trauma, inflammation, neoplasia) and altered blood constituents (e.g. more platelets or abnormal platelet function). Plasma oncotic pressure is not part of it.

q.stem: In atheroma formation, the main factor stimulating proliferation of intimal smooth muscle cells is:
q.explanation: After endothelial injury, adherent platelets stimulate intimal smooth muscle to proliferate, mainly through platelet-derived growth factor. Lipid then accumulates because endothelial barrier function has failed, forming a fibrolipid plaque. VEGF, histamine and tPA do not have this role.

q.stem: Which of the following is a NON-reversible risk factor for atherosclerosis?
q.explanation: Irreversible risk factors are age, male sex and race. Smoking, hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia can be modified. High levels of high-density lipoprotein are protective.

q.stem: Roth's spots in the retina are associated with which type of embolus?
options: Septic embolus from subacute bacterial endocarditis
q.explanation: Septic emboli from subacute bacterial endocarditis cause Roth's spots. Fat emboli follow severe trauma with multiple fractures, air emboli can occur during thyroid surgery, and amniotic fluid emboli complicate delivery, especially if the fetus is manipulated.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Some weeks after a penetrating injury with uveal prolapse, a patient develops photophobia and blurred vision in the fellow eye. Histology of the injured eye would most likely show collections of macrophages at the level of the RPE known as:
q.explanation: This is sympathetic ophthalmia, a bilateral, diffuse granulomatous, T-cell-mediated panuveitis that can follow penetrating injury by anything from 5 days to many years. Macrophages accumulating at the RPE form Dalen–Fuchs nodules, and mutton-fat keratic precipitates are seen. Russell bodies are plasma cell inclusions, Rosenthal fibres occur in glioma, and Homer–Wright rosettes in retinoblastoma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Sympathetic ophthalmia is thought to be a delayed-type hypersensitivity to antigens on the RPE or uveal melanocytes. Which HLA type is associated with it?
q.explanation: The book lists HLA DRB1*04, DQA1*03 and DQB1*04 as associated with sympathetic ophthalmia. The other HLA types are not mentioned for this condition in the text.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis following lens capsule rupture is characterised by:
options: A zonal granulomatous inflammation around lens material
q.explanation: Phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis is an autoimmune, zonal granulomatous reaction to lens material after capsule rupture, possibly from a loss of T-cell tolerance. Macrophages engulfing lens matter can block the angle and cause phacolytic glaucoma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Panophthalmitis is defined as inflammation of:
options: The anterior chamber and iris only
All three coats of the eye, with possible spread into the orbit
q.explanation: Endophthalmitis is inflammation of one or more coats of the eye and the adjacent cavities. Panophthalmitis involves all three coats and can extend into orbital structures.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Histologically, the term 'suppurative' in suppurative endophthalmitis indicates:
options: Tissue necrosis with polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration
Eosinophilic infiltrate from type I hypersensitivity
q.explanation: Suppurative inflammation means tissue necrosis with infiltration by polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Its source can be exogenous (surgery, penetrating trauma, radiation, chemicals) or endogenous (e.g. Behçet's, spread from neighbouring structures, haematogenous).

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In Sjögren's syndrome, dry eye results from:
options: Lymphocytic destruction of lacrimal acinar tissue and loss of conjunctival goblet cells
Amyloid deposition in the lacrimal gland
Fibrosis of the lacrimal ductules after trachoma
Granulomatous destruction of the meibomian glands
q.explanation: Sjögren's syndrome, primary or secondary (e.g. to rheumatoid arthritis), affects acinar glands of the conjunctiva, lacrimal gland and mouth. A lymphocytic infiltrate destroys the secretory lacrimal acini and conjunctival goblet cells are lost, so tear secretion falls.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Regarding scleromalacia perforans in rheumatoid disease, which statement is correct?
options: It is a brawny scleritis with reactive fibrosis
The sclera thins to expose uvea, but perforation is rare; it is usually due to arteriolar infarction
It typically presents as posterior scleritis with macular oedema
q.explanation: In scleromalacia perforans, the sclera thins and the underlying uvea becomes visible. Perforation is rare despite the name, and the usual cause is arteriolar infarction. Brawny scleritis features inflammation with reactive fibrosis, and posterior scleritis can cause macular oedema.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Histology of extraocular muscles in thyroid eye disease typically shows:
options: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, mast cells and glycosaminoglycan accumulation, later fibrosis
Caseating granulomas with Langhans' giant cells
q.explanation: In thyroid eye disease, lymphocytes infiltrate around vessels, with mast cells and glycosaminoglycan building up in and around the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. In later stages this becomes fibrosis. It can occur in hyperthyroid, hypothyroid and euthyroid patients.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Following blunt trauma, angle recession glaucoma results from:
options: Separation of the ciliary muscle from the scleral spur with trabecular meshwork collapse
q.explanation: Blunt trauma deforms the globe front to back and can separate the ciliary muscle from its attachment at the scleral spur. The trabecular meshwork then collapses, producing angle recession glaucoma. The other options are separate causes of secondary glaucoma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Why are alkali burns generally more damaging to the eye than acid burns?
options: Alkalis coagulate proteins and form a protective barrier
Alkalis penetrate tissue easily, whereas acids coagulate proteins that limit their diffusion
Acids are neutralised by the tear film immediately
q.explanation: Acids coagulate proteins, which limits their spread through cornea and sclera. Alkalis pass through tissue easily, can cause limbal ischaemia that prevents epithelial repair, and their high pH destroys cells of the lens, uvea and retina. Acid burns can still cause conjunctival and corneal fibrosis and scarring.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: What radiation dose range is quoted for treating retinoblastoma with X-rays and γ-rays?
q.explanation: Retinoblastoma is treated with X-rays and γ-rays at 40–60 Gy. Melanoma may receive proton beam or γ-ray therapy at up to 110 Gy. The gray measures the energy absorbed by tissue.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: After panretinal photocoagulation, the pigmented edge around each white laser scar is due to:
options: Deposition of haemosiderin from retinal haemorrhage
Reactive proliferation of RPE at the burn margin
q.explanation: PRP destroys the outer third of the retina along with the underlying RPE. The white scar is formed by glial cells, and RPE proliferating reactively at the edge of the burn produces the surrounding pigment. Choroidal melanocytes do not proliferate after trauma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: An elderly patient with a progressing age-related cataract notices that their glasses prescription is becoming more myopic. Which morphology is most likely?
q.explanation: Nuclear cataract is the commonest age-related type and can cause increasing myopia as it matures. Cortical cataract looks radial in the cortex, posterior subcapsular cataract is associated with corticosteroids, and Morgagnian cataract is a liquefied cortex with the nucleus sunk inferiorly.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: A cataract in which the cortex has liquefied and the nucleus has sunk inferiorly within the capsular bag is described as:
q.explanation: In a Morgagnian cataract the cortical lens matter liquefies and the nucleus drops inferiorly in the bag. A hypermature cataract leaks water so the capsule shrinks, a mature cataract is dense and white and blocks the red reflex, and an immature cataract is incompletely opaque.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which change is characteristic of age-related cataract rather than normal lens ageing?
options: Extensive oxidation of lens proteins with reduced glutathione
Constant post-translational modification of lens proteins
q.explanation: Ageing and cataract are separate processes. The ageing lens shows lifelong post-translational modification, with less γ-crystallin synthesis and more β-crystallin, but little oxidation. Age-related cataract shows extensive protein oxidation, failure of antioxidant defences (mainly reduced glutathione) and increased proteolysis.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In diabetic cataract, water is drawn into lens fibres mainly because of intracellular accumulation of:
q.explanation: High glucose and galactose overwhelm anaerobic glycolysis and upregulate the polyol (aldose reductase) pathway. Sorbitol (a polyol) builds up and draws water into the cells, and later ATP and glutathione fall, causing oxidative damage. The other substances are not part of this mechanism.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: The GLC1A gene, linked to primary open-angle glaucoma, codes for which protein?
q.explanation: GLC1A on chromosome 1 codes for TIGR (trabecular meshwork inducible glucocorticoid response protein), also called myocilin. Carriers present earlier, have higher peak IOP and more often need surgery. Rhodopsin and peripherin are retinitis pigmentosa genes, and ABCA4 is the Stargardt gene.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In primary open-angle glaucoma, which optic nerve fibres are selectively damaged by raised IOP?
options: Fibres entering the disc above or below the horizontal on the temporal side
Nasal fibres entering the disc horizontally
Papillomacular bundle fibres entering the temporal disc at the horizontal
q.explanation: Raised IOP causes ischaemia of the optic nerve capillary bed and mechanically reduces axoplasmic flow at the lamina cribrosa. Prelaminar bundles entering above or below the horizontal on the temporal side are damaged selectively. This causes vertical enlargement of the cup and field defects such as a nasal step or arcuate scotoma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which patient is most predisposed to primary angle-closure glaucoma?
options: An elderly hypermetrope with small eyes
q.explanation: Primary angle closure is partly age-related and more likely in hypermetropes with small eyes, or after blunt trauma. As the lens enlarges with age, it pushes the iris forward and narrows the angle. Myopia appears in the book as a risk factor for POAG instead.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which of the following causes SECONDARY ANGLE-CLOSURE glaucoma?
options: Inflammatory cells and protein in uveitis
Haemorrhage in the angle after trauma
q.explanation: In secondary angle closure the angle is mechanically displaced and closed. Examples are a tumour pushing the lens forward, synechiae causing pupil block and iris bombé, and rubeosis. Phacolytic material, blood and inflammatory cells block an open angle and so cause secondary open-angle glaucoma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In diabetic retinopathy, dot haemorrhages are located in:
q.explanation: Dot haemorrhages come from ruptured capillaries in the outer plexiform layer. Flame haemorrhages come from small arterioles and lie in the nerve fibre layer. Blot haemorrhages are larger, with blood tracking between the photoreceptors and the RPE.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Hard exudates in diabetic retinopathy are found mainly in which retinal layer, and what do they contain histologically?
options: Outer plexiform layer; eosinophilic material with lipid-laden foamy macrophages
Nerve fibre layer; swollen ends of interrupted axons
q.explanation: Leakage of plasma from damaged deep capillaries into the outer plexiform layer forms yellow, well-circumscribed exudates. These are eosinophilic masses containing foamy macrophages with lipid. Swollen ends of interrupted axons in the nerve fibre layer are cotton wool spots.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Retinal microaneurysms in diabetes develop mainly because of:
options: Proliferation of endothelial cells at the edge of ischaemia
Necrosis of pericytes weakening the capillary wall
Thrombosis of the central retinal vein
q.explanation: Ischaemia of the capillary bed causes pericyte necrosis. This weakens the capillary wall, which bulges into a microaneurysm. Endothelial proliferation at the edge of ischaemic retina causes neovascularisation instead.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which best describes the pathogenesis of retinopathy of prematurity?
options: Hyperglycaemia causes pericyte loss and microaneurysm formation
Vessels grow from the periphery towards the disc and overshoot
Emboli from the umbilical artery occlude retinal vessels
Supplemental oxygen reduces the hypoxic drive for vascular growth; on return to normal oxygen the ischaemic avascular periphery drives disorganised neovascularisation
q.explanation: In the fetus, relative hypoxia drives retinal vessels outward from the disc towards the periphery. Supplemental oxygen in a premature infant removes this drive and halts vascular extension. When oxygen returns to normal, the ischaemic avascular periphery drives rapid, disorganised neovascularisation that can lead to bilateral retinal detachment.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In hypertensive disease, lobular infarcts of the choriocapillaris are known as:
q.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis of choroidal vessels in hypertension causes lobular infarcts of the choriocapillaris, called Elschnig's spots. Roth's spots come from septic emboli, Dalen–Fuchs nodules are seen in sympathetic ophthalmia, and drusen are deposits on Bruch's membrane.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In central retinal artery occlusion, the cherry-red spot at the macula is seen because:
options: The thin fovea lacks neuronal tissue, so the choroidal circulation remains visible through it
The cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea
q.explanation: The infarcted retina becomes opaque and hides the choroidal red reflex. The fovea is thin and has little neuronal tissue, so the choriocapillaris still shows through as a cherry-red spot. CRAO is usually embolic, typically from carotid atheroma.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which feature favours central retinal vein occlusion over central retinal artery occlusion?
options: A cherry-red spot at the macula
Extensive retinal haemorrhages with later risk of rubeotic glaucoma, usually within 3 months
q.explanation: CRVO shows extensive retinal haemorrhages and carries a risk of neovascularisation and rubeotic glaucoma, usually within 3 months. Vision may also improve. Neovascularisation is extremely rare after CRAO, which shows the cherry-red spot instead.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: In a U-shaped (horseshoe) retinal tear after posterior vitreous detachment, the base of the retinal flap points:
options: Towards the ora serrata nasally regardless of location
q.explanation: The vitreous separates posteriorly first and tears the retina at a point of adhesion. Continued traction extends the tear forward towards the vitreous base, so the base of the flap lies anteriorly.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which type of drusen is a risk factor for progression to advanced age-related macular degeneration?
options: Soft drusen larger than 63 μm with ill-defined borders
q.explanation: Hard drusen are small and well-defined and do not predispose to advanced ARMD. Soft drusen are larger than 63 μm with poorly defined borders, grow in size and number with age, and are a risk factor. Dry ARMD makes up about 90% of ARMD.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: A basal linear deposit, linked to the onset of neovascular ARMD, lies:
options: Between the RPE cell membrane and its basement membrane
On the inner surface of the internal limiting membrane
Between the photoreceptors and the RPE
q.explanation: A basal linear deposit lies between the RPE cell membrane and the RPE basement membrane and has been linked to the start of neovascularisation (wet ARMD). Drusen lie between the RPE basement membrane and the rest of Bruch's membrane.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: The 'bone spicule' fundus pigmentation in retinitis pigmentosa results from:
options: RPE cells proliferating and migrating into the retina around hyalinised vessels
q.explanation: In RP, RPE cells proliferate and migrate into the retina, gathering around hyalinised vessels in a bone-spicule pattern. Peripherally, Müller cells replace the outer nuclear layer and fuse with the RPE. AD forms are linked to rhodopsin (3q) and peripherin (6p) mutations.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Which of the following causes an EXUDATIVE (non-rhegmatogenous) neural retinal detachment?
q.explanation: Choroidal tumours and posterior scleritis are given as causes of exudative detachment. Lattice degeneration, retinal dialysis and giant retinal breaks cause rhegmatogenous detachments (equatorial and oral types).

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Stargardt's disease is an autosomal recessive macular dystrophy caused by mutation of:
q.explanation: Stargardt's is caused by mutation of ABCA4 (STGD1), the retinal ATP-binding cassette transporter gene on 1p21. Lipofuscin builds up and RPE and photoreceptors are destroyed. About 18.7% of dry ARMD cases also carry ABCA4 mutations. Rhodopsin and peripherin are linked to AD retinitis pigmentosa.

q.section: Additional examples of basic ocular pathology
q.stem: Best's disease is characterised by:
options: X-linked inheritance with peripheral field loss
Autosomal dominant inheritance with lipofuscin accumulation in RPE and a yellow macular disc
Autosomal recessive inheritance with bone spicule pigmentation
q.explanation: Best's disease is an AD macular degeneration with reduced central acuity and a yellow disc of tissue at the macula. Histology shows lipofuscin in RPE cells and atrophy of the photoreceptor layer.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Many corneal dystrophies of Bowman's layer and the stroma are linked to mutations in the TGF-β-induced gene, located on chromosome:
q.explanation: The TGF-β-induced gene is on 5q31. It codes for a membrane protein of corneal epithelium and keratocytes that helps wound healing. Mutations cause protein misfolding with amyloid or non-fibrillar deposits, and these dystrophies are autosomal dominant with complete penetrance. 1p21 holds ABCA4 and 17p13 holds p53.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Reis–Bücklers' and Thiel–Behnke dystrophies look similar on light microscopy. On electron microscopy, Thiel–Behnke dystrophy shows:
options: Curly fibres within superficial fibrous nodules
q.explanation: Both are AD dystrophies of Bowman's layer with fibrous nodules between Bowman's layer and epithelium. On EM, Reis–Bücklers' shows electron-dense rods, while Thiel–Behnke (linked to chromosome 10, usually in older patients) shows curly fibres.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Fine branching lines in the anterior stroma that stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence are characteristic of:
q.explanation: Lattice dystrophy is caused by amyloid deposits in the anterior stroma, with the typical Congo red staining and birefringence. Granular dystrophy has non-birefringent hyaline deposits, macular dystrophy has mucopolysaccharide, and Schnyder dystrophy has cholesterol crystals.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Which stromal corneal dystrophy is autosomal RECESSIVE and features mucopolysaccharide accumulation within keratocytes?
q.explanation: Macular dystrophy is less common, autosomal recessive, starts in the first decade with grey-white axial anterior stromal opacities, and accumulates mucopolysaccharide in keratocytes and between lamellae. Granular, Avellino and lattice type 1 are autosomal dominant.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: A patient with systemic hypercholesterolaemia has fine polychromatic crystals in the anterior stroma and a dense corneal arcus. The most likely dystrophy is:
q.explanation: Schnyder crystalline dystrophy is a rare AD disorder of corneal lipid metabolism, strongly associated with systemic hypercholesterolaemia. Cholesterol crystals are deposited in the anterior stroma and there is a dense arcus.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Which statement about Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy is correct?
options: It is more common in males and presents in childhood
The endothelial cells acquire epithelial features such as desmosomes
Guttata form from abnormal collagen on a thickened Descemet's membrane, usually after age 50
q.explanation: Fuchs' dystrophy is very common, more frequent in women, sporadic or AD, and usually starts after 50. Dystrophic endothelium forms guttata, cell number and pump function fall, and progressive oedema can lead to bullous keratopathy. Epithelial-like endothelium is the feature of posterior polymorphous dystrophy.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: In which corneal dystrophy does the endothelium become multilayered with epithelial-like features such as microvilli and desmosomes?
q.explanation: Posterior polymorphous dystrophy is AD. The endothelium becomes multilayered with epithelial features, and in severe disease it resembles stratified corneal epithelium with prominent desmosomes. It is usually asymptomatic but can cause astigmatism or decompensation.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Which type of congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) is autosomal recessive and presents at birth or within the first few weeks?
q.explanation: CHED1 is autosomal dominant and presents in the second year of life. CHED2 is autosomal recessive and presents at birth or within the first few weeks. In both, primary endothelial dysfunction causes corneal opacification, and Descemet's membrane is finely laminated.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Meesmann's dystrophy is a:
options: Bowman's layer dystrophy with electron-dense rods
Rare AD epithelial dystrophy with onset in early childhood
q.explanation: Meesmann's is a rare autosomal dominant epithelial dystrophy starting in early childhood. Separated, deformed cells form basement membrane loops and microcysts. Cogan's map-dot dystrophy is the other epithelial dystrophy, with onset in the second decade.

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Which of the following is true of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome?
options: It is classified as a corneal dystrophy
It is bilateral and autosomal dominant
It is unilateral and sporadic in adults, and the Cogan–Reese variant is associated with an iris naevus
q.explanation: ICE syndrome is unilateral, sporadic and occurs in adults, and it is not classed as a dystrophy. Abnormal endothelium can grow as a membrane over the angle. Its forms include progressive iris stromal atrophy, Chandler syndrome (glaucoma with a normal iris) and Cogan–Reese syndrome (iris naevus).

q.section: Corneal dystrophies and corneal endothelial dysfunction
q.stem: Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy is more likely to follow which of these?
options: Placement of an anterior chamber lens
Use of a posterior chamber lens in the bag
q.explanation: Aphakic or pseudophakic bullous keratopathy is more likely after surgical complications or when an anterior chamber lens is placed. Other causes include Fuchs' dystrophy, herpetic endotheliitis, graft failure or rejection, chronic anterior uveitis and trauma.

q.stem: What proportion of all eyelid tumours are basal cell carcinomas?
q.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the commonest malignant tumour seen by ophthalmologists and makes up about 90% of eyelid tumours. Squamous cell carcinoma and sebaceous gland carcinoma each account for about 1–5%.

q.stem: Which histological subtype of basal cell carcinoma is well circumscribed, with peripheral palisading, and usually excised successfully?
q.explanation: Nodular BCC forms well-circumscribed islands of basal cells with palisading at the edge, so excision usually succeeds. Infiltrative BCC grows in strands in a fibrous stroma with a poor border. Micronodular BCC may have nodules that cannot be seen clinically. Superficial BCC has gaps between nests of cells.

q.stem: A squamous cell carcinoma of the lower eyelid would be expected to spread first to the:
q.explanation: Lymphatic spread from the lower lid goes to the submandibular nodes, and from the upper lid to the preauricular nodes. Lid SCC is associated with UV exposure and immunosuppression, and the spindle cell form is more aggressive.

q.stem: An elderly woman has had chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis that has not responded to treatment. Biopsy shows tumour cells with foamy, vacuolated cytoplasm spreading within the surface epithelium. The most likely diagnosis is:
q.explanation: Sebaceous gland carcinoma is most common in older women and usually arises from the meibomian glands. It can mimic chalazion or chronic unilateral blepharitis. The diffuse subtype spreads within the epithelium in a pagetoid pattern, and prognosis is poor because of its diffuse nature.

q.stem: Which statement about pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland is correct?
options: It contains tissues from all three germ layers
It contains both epithelial and mesenchymal elements and must be fully excised because of malignant potential
It is a rapidly growing malignant tumour with a Swiss cheese pattern
q.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign mixed tumour, the most common epithelial tumour of the lacrimal gland. It is slow-growing and pseudoencapsulated, with epithelial and mesenchymal elements (myxoid tissue, cartilage, fat, sometimes bone). Incomplete excision risks malignant change to pleomorphic carcinoma. The Swiss cheese pattern belongs to adenoid cystic carcinoma, and the three germ layers to teratoma.

q.stem: A middle-aged patient has rapidly progressive proptosis with pain and paraesthesia. Lacrimal gland biopsy shows a cribriform 'Swiss cheese' pattern. The diagnosis is:
q.explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lacrimal gland grows quickly and invades locally, causing pain, paraesthesia, proptosis and diplopia. The commonest histological pattern is cribriform (Swiss cheese). It is aggressive and needs surgery with radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

q.stem: Which form of primary acquired melanosis (PAM) of the conjunctiva is premalignant?
options: Neither; conjunctival melanoma only arises de novo
q.explanation: PAM with atypia is premalignant and PAM without atypia is not. Conjunctival melanoma can arise from PAM, a pre-existing naevus or de novo. Thickness over 5 mm and a forniceal location indicate a poor prognosis.

q.stem: Uveal melanoma most commonly metastasises to the:
q.explanation: Uveal melanoma spreads mainly by the blood and usually goes to the liver, typically within 2–3 years. Choroidal tumours make up about 80% of uveal melanomas. Spread to regional lymph nodes is a feature of conjunctival melanoma.

q.stem: A choroidal melanoma has a 'mushroom' (collar-stud) shape on imaging. This configuration results from:
options: The tumour breaching Bruch's membrane and spreading in the subretinal space
q.explanation: The mushroom shape forms when the tumour breaks through Bruch's membrane and expands into the subretinal space. Large tumours may necrose spontaneously, and blood-borne spread can occur through collector channels, vortex veins or short ciliary vessels. Trabecular meshwork infiltration is a feature of iris melanoma.

q.stem: Which feature carries a WORSE prognosis in uveal melanoma?
options: Choroidal rather than ciliary body location
q.explanation: Poor prognostic factors are older age, larger size, ciliary body location, epithelioid cells, and closed vascular loops on PAS staining. Tumours made only of spindle cells do better than those with epithelioid cells, and choroidal location is better than ciliary body.

q.stem: Immunohistochemistry of a uveal melanoma would usually be positive for:
q.explanation: Uveal melanomas are usually positive for S100, HMB45 and Melan A. MyoD1 helps diagnose rhabdomyosarcoma. Vascular patterns in melanoma are assessed with PAS staining.

q.stem: An orbital tumour shows palisaded spindle cells (Antoni A) and myxoid areas (Antoni B). The diagnosis is:
q.explanation: Schwannomas arise from Schwann cells around axons and show Antoni A (palisaded) and Antoni B (myxoid) areas. Pigmented schwannomas can be confused with spindle cell melanoma. Neurofibromas come from endoneurium, show spindle cells with wavy nuclei and collagen, and are associated with NF1.

q.stem: Eosinophilic masses representing modified astrocyte processes (Rosenthal fibres) are a histological feature of:
q.explanation: Optic nerve glioma shows myxoid degeneration and Rosenthal fibres. Optic nerve meningioma shows psammoma bodies in a transitional pattern, and retinoblastoma shows rosettes. Adult gliomas are rare and have a poor prognosis because of intracranial extension.

q.stem: Which statement contrasts optic nerve meningioma with optic nerve glioma correctly?
options: Meningiomas grow slowly in adults but are more aggressive in children
Meningiomas are more aggressive in adults than in children
Meningiomas only arise primarily within the optic nerve sheath
q.explanation: Optic nerve meningioma can be primary or extend from an intracranial meningioma. It tends to grow slowly in adults and more aggressively in children. Histology shows psammoma bodies in a transitional pattern. Rosenthal fibres belong to glioma.

q.stem: A retinoblastoma specimen shows rings of cells bounded internally by a continuous membrane. These are:
q.explanation: Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes are rings of cells lined internally by a continuous membrane resembling the outer limiting membrane. Homer–Wright rosettes are multilayered rings of nuclei around eosinophilic fibrillary material. Fleurettes are fleur-de-lys photoreceptor-like structures, usually seen in irradiated tumours.

q.stem: Survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma carrying the abnormal gene are at increased risk of which tumour in early adult life?
options: Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid
q.explanation: The abnormal gene carries a risk of pineal tumour in childhood, soft tissue and osteogenic sarcoma in early adult life, and carcinoma later on. Modern treatment cures about 90% of retinoblastomas, which affect around 1 in 20,000 live births.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a differential diagnosis of leukocoria?
q.explanation: Besides retinoblastoma, the book lists Coats' disease, astrocytic hamartoma, retinopathy of prematurity, persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous, endophthalmitis and toxocara or toxoplasma retinitis. Choroidal melanoma is an adult tumour and is not on the list.

q.stem: What is the most common orbital malignancy of childhood, and its most common histological subtype?
q.explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest orbital malignancy of childhood. It usually presents before 20 with proptosis and squint, as tan-coloured fleshy tissue. Embryonal is the commonest subtype, and pleomorphic is rare and mostly seen in adults. MyoD1 immunohistochemistry helps diagnosis.

q.stem: Which statement about ocular adnexal lymphoma is correct?
options: Primary intraocular lymphoma is usually T-cell derived
Conjunctival lymphoma has the highest association with systemic disease
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (MALT-derived, low-grade B-cell) is the most common type
Follicular lymphoma is usually confined to the orbit
q.explanation: EMZL, a low-grade B-cell lymphoma from mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, is the most common ocular lymphoma. Conjunctival lesions have the lowest rate of systemic disease, compared with orbit (35%), lacrimal gland (40%) and eyelid (67%). Primary intraocular lymphoma is usually diffuse large B-cell type, and follicular lymphoma is usually part of systemic disease.

q.stem: In adults, metastatic tumours to the eye most commonly affect:
options: The uveal tract, often from breast, lung, prostate or gastrointestinal carcinoma
q.explanation: In adults, metastases usually go to the uveal tract, most often from carcinomas of the breast, prostate, lung or gastrointestinal tract. In children the orbit is involved more often, e.g. by neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma, Wilms' tumour and rhabdomyosarcoma.

q.stem: Orbital teratomas:
options: Are derived from lacrimal gland epithelium
Arise from totipotent germ cells and contain tissues of all three germ layers
Are usually malignant tumours of elderly patients
q.explanation: Orbital teratomas are rare, present in neonates with proptosis, and are mostly benign. They come from totipotent germ cells left behind in the midline during migration to the gonads. They contain tissues from all three germ layers, e.g. respiratory or GI epithelium, fat, cartilage, bone and neuroectoderm.

q.stem: Conjunctival papillomas are most often associated with:
q.explanation: Conjunctival papillomas are benign epithelial tumours, pedunculated or sessile, mostly associated with human papillomavirus. A benign squamous proliferation can also occur with the poxvirus of molluscum contagiosum. EBV is linked to Burkitt's and intraocular B-cell lymphoma.

q.stem: Which bacterial structure is responsible for conjugation, the transfer of DNA between bacteria?
q.explanation: Pili link bacteria so DNA can pass from one cell to another (conjugation). Flagella provide motility, the cell membrane is an osmotic barrier and enzyme site, and the capsule mainly helps resist host defences.

q.stem: An aerobic bacterium obtains most of its energy from respiration but can also use fermentation. How is it best described?
q.explanation: Aerobes that can also ferment are facultative anaerobes. Strict anaerobes depend entirely on fermentation; autotrophs are defined by using simple inorganic compounds, not by their energy pathway; obligate intracellular organisms (e.g. Chlamydia) need host cells.

q.stem: Which feature is characteristic of bacterial endotoxins rather than exotoxins?
options: They are highly potent proteins effective in tiny amounts
They are easily destroyed by heat
They are heat-stable lipopolysaccharides from the Gram-negative cell wall
They are mostly secreted by living Gram-positive bacteria
q.explanation: Endotoxins are heat-stable cell wall lipopolysaccharides released by dead or lysed Gram-negative bacteria, and large amounts are needed for an effect. Potent protein toxins that are heat-labile and usually made by Gram-positive organisms are exotoxins.

q.stem: Large doses of endotoxin cause intravascular coagulation through endothelial damage and platelet aggregation, mainly in the lungs and kidneys. What is this called?
q.explanation: This is the Schwartzman phenomenon. Tolerance is the loss of the fever response after repeated exposure, as antibody clears the toxin. The Mazzotti reaction is the inflammation caused by dying microfilariae, and the Nagler reaction is used to type C. perfringens.

q.stem: Which pairing of a bacterial enzyme with its action is INCORRECT?
options: Coagulase: promotes fibrin deposition that shields bacteria from complement
Collagenase: breaks down collagen in connective tissue
Streptolysin O: lyses red blood cells and tissue cells
q.explanation: Converting plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve fibrin clots is the action of streptokinase. Hyaluronidase hydrolyses hyaluronate in the connective tissue matrix, which helps the organism spread. The other pairings are correct.

q.stem: A patient with herpes simplex epithelial keratitis goes on to develop a bacterial keratitis from overgrowth of their own commensal flora. Which concept does this illustrate?
q.explanation: When one microorganism makes another more pathogenic, this is pathogenic synergy, and viral damage to the epithelium followed by commensal bacterial keratitis is the classic example. Antigenic drift, latency and tolerance are unrelated ideas.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: In the Gram staining procedure, which reagent is used to decolourize the specimen?
q.explanation: The sequence is crystal violet, then iodine, then acetone to decolourize, then carbol-fuchsin as the red counterstain. Gram-positive organisms keep the crystal violet; Gram-negative organisms lose it and take up the counterstain.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: Why do Gram-negative bacteria appear red after Gram staining?
options: Their thick peptidoglycan wall binds carbol-fuchsin more strongly than crystal violet
They lack a cell wall altogether
Their lipid-rich three-layer wall lets acetone wash out crystal violet, so they take up the carbol-fuchsin counterstain
Their waxy mycolic walls repel crystal violet
q.explanation: The three-layer Gram-negative wall contains lipid, so acetone removes the crystal violet and the cells are then stained red by carbol-fuchsin. A thick peptidoglycan wall is a Gram-positive feature. Absent walls describe mollicutes, and waxy walls describe mycobacteria.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: In the full (unmodified) Ziehl-Neelsen technique, which counterstain is used?
q.explanation: Ziehl-Neelsen uses heated carbol-fuchsin as the primary stain, then acid and/or alcohol to decolourize, then a counterstain. The counterstain is methylene blue in the full method and malachite green in the modified method. Crystal violet belongs to the Gram stain.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: In the laboratory workup of microbial keratitis, a modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain is mainly used to detect which organism?
q.explanation: In the keratitis protocol the modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain is aimed at weakly acid-fast Nocardia, and the full Ziehl-Neelsen stain at Mycobacterium. Acanthamoeba is detected by immunofluorescence and culture on E. coli-seeded agar, fungi by PAS, acridine orange or Sabouraud's agar, and Pseudomonas by Gram stain and agar culture.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: Gomori's methenamine silver stain and PAS are mainly used to show which of the following?
q.explanation: PAS and Gomori's methenamine silver pick out fungal elements such as hyphae. Acid-fast bacilli need a Ziehl-Neelsen stain, Chlamydia is detected by immunofluorescence or Giemsa, and treponemes are shown by dark-ground microscopy or the Levaditi silver method.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: A culture medium contains glycerol, malachite green and whole egg. Which organism is it designed to grow?
q.explanation: That recipe is Lowenstein-Jensen medium, which is used for mycobacteria. Gonococcus grows on enriched chocolate agar (Thayer-Martin), Acanthamoeba on non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli, and Candida on Sabouraud's agar.

q.section: Gram staining and classification of bacteria
q.stem: Why is Robertson's meat broth included in a standard microbial keratitis culture set?
q.explanation: In the keratitis protocol, meat broth is used for anaerobes. Acanthamoeba needs non-nutrient E. coli-seeded agar, fungi need Sabouraud's agar, and mycobacteria need Lowenstein-Jensen medium.

q.stem: Which organism is the most frequent commensal isolated from the normal eye?
q.explanation: S. epidermidis is found on about 40-45% of eyes, compared with roughly 25% for S. aureus. Streptococci are found on only 2-3%, and P. acnes is the commonest anaerobe rather than the commonest commensal overall.

q.stem: Which statement about the normal flora of the eye is FALSE?
options: The eye is sterile in utero and gains its flora during birth
Demodex is found on the lashes of most people over 70
Several viruses are normal commensals of the conjunctiva
Propionibacterium acnes is the most common anaerobic commensal
q.explanation: The eye has no viral commensals. The other statements are true: the eye picks up its flora at birth, Demodex colonizes the lashes of most people over 70, and P. acnes is the commonest anaerobe.

q.stem: Which laboratory test is classically used to tell pathogenic Staphylococcus aureus apart from Staphylococcus epidermidis?
q.explanation: S. aureus, including MRSA, is coagulase positive, while S. epidermidis is coagulase negative. Both are catalase-positive Gram-positive cocci in clusters, so catalase testing and Gram staining cannot separate them, and neither is acid-fast.

q.stem: Which Staphylococcus aureus product reduces phagocytosis and inhibits complement?
q.explanation: S. aureus makes protein A, which reduces phagocytosis and inhibits complement. Erythrogenic toxin comes from Streptococcus pyogenes, IgA proteases are a feature of Neisseria, and toxin A is made by Pseudomonas.

q.stem: The generalized erythematous rash of scarlet fever is caused by a toxin from which organism?
q.explanation: S. pyogenes, a Lancefield group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, makes the erythrogenic toxin behind scarlet fever. S. pneumoniae is an alpha-haemolytic diplococcus linked to meningitis and pneumonia, and B. cereus toxin causes food poisoning.

q.stem: Which Bacillus species produces the antibiotic bacitracin?
q.explanation: B. brevis produces bacitracin. B. anthracis is an encapsulated, exotoxin-producing organism that causes anthrax, and B. cereus causes food poisoning from reheated or lukewarm rice. 'Bacillus fumigatus' is not a real organism; fumigatus is an Aspergillus species.

q.stem: Tetanus toxin causes tonic spasm of voluntary muscle by acting on which structure?
q.explanation: The tetanus exotoxin targets the presynaptic terminals of inhibitory interneurons. Losing that inhibition produces tonic spasm. C. tetani forms terminal spores that give it a drumstick appearance, and it is sensitive to penicillin.

q.stem: What is the Nagler reaction used for?
options: Distinguishing different strains of Clostridium perfringens
q.explanation: The Nagler reaction identifies strains of C. perfringens, the main cause of gas gangrene and an occasional cause of necrotizing keratitis and panophthalmitis. Onchocerciasis is linked with the Mazzotti reaction, and local antibody production is assessed with the Goldmann-Witmer coefficient.

q.stem: Months after uncomplicated cataract surgery, a patient develops chronic low-grade endophthalmitis. The organism is an anaerobic, non-spore-forming Gram-positive rod that normally lives in the meibomian glands. What is it most likely to be?
q.explanation: P. acnes is an anaerobic, non-spore-forming commensal of the eyelids and meibomian glands that causes chronic blepharitis and low-grade post-cataract endophthalmitis. Clostridia and Bacillus both form spores, and Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative aerobe.

q.stem: A patient has chronic lacrimal canaliculitis, and yellow-white 'sulphur granules' are expressed from the punctum. Which organism is most likely responsible?
q.explanation: A. israelii is an anaerobic filamentous Gram-positive organism that commonly causes canaliculitis and dacryocystitis, and it forms sulphur granules. It is sensitive to penicillin. Nocardia is aerobic and is linked with keratitis and endophthalmitis instead.

q.stem: A corneal scraping shows branching, aerobic filamentous bacteria that are weakly acid-fast. Which organism is the most frequent cause of this kind of keratitis?
q.explanation: Nocardia are branching aerobic actinomycetes that are weakly acid-fast, and N. asteroides is the commonest cause of nocardial keratitis and endophthalmitis. Actinomyces is anaerobic, mycobacteria are rods rather than branching filaments, and Aspergillus is a fungus.

q.stem: A neonate develops profuse purulent conjunctivitis 3 days after vaginal delivery, and Gram-negative cocci are seen. Which culture medium is best for growing the likely organism?
options: Non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli
q.explanation: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum usually starts 2-3 days after birth, and gonococcus grows best on enriched chocolate media such as Thayer-Martin. Quick diagnosis matters because corneal ulceration can cause blindness, and both parent and child are treated with a cephalosporin or penicillin.

q.stem: Which statement about Pseudomonas aeruginosa keratitis is correct?
options: It readily penetrates intact, healthy corneal epithelium
Its growth does not depend on iron
Its proteases let it cross traumatized epithelium easily, though it penetrates healthy epithelium poorly
q.explanation: Pseudomonas does not get through healthy corneal epithelium well, but its many proteases let it pass through damaged epithelium. Risk factors are corneal trauma, thermal burns, vitamin A deficiency and immune suppression. It is aerobic and depends on iron to grow.

q.stem: Haemophilus needs X and V factors to grow. What is V factor?
q.explanation: X factor is haematin and V factor is NAD, which other bacteria can supply. This explains satellitism, where H. influenzae colonies grow around staphylococcal colonies on chocolate agar.

q.stem: A child with sinusitis develops orbital cellulitis after spread through the thin orbital walls. The organism is a capsulated Gram-negative bacillus that shows satellitism around staphylococcal colonies. What is the most likely organism?
q.explanation: H. influenzae type b causes upper respiratory infection and sinusitis that can spread into the orbit, and satellitism is characteristic of it. Its capsule increases virulence, and most strains are sensitive to cefotaxime and chloramphenicol. Neisseria are cocci, and neither Moraxella nor Serratia shows satellitism.

q.stem: The Koch-Weeks bacillus, a cause of endemic conjunctivitis, is which organism?
q.explanation: H. aegyptius is a non-encapsulated Haemophilus known as the Koch-Weeks bacillus, and it causes conjunctivitis. H. ducreyi causes chancroid and Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, and Moraxella is a Gram-negative diplobacillus that causes purulent conjunctivitis and ulceration.

q.stem: Which enteric organism is known for contaminating contact lens solutions and causing keratitis and endophthalmitis?
q.explanation: Serratia marcescens is an enteric organism that can contaminate contact lens solutions and cause infective keratitis and endophthalmitis. E. coli is best known as the commonest cause of urinary tract infection. Salmonella and Proteus are not linked with contact lens solutions.

q.stem: In the classification of enterobacteria, which organism is lactose fermenting and non-motile?
q.explanation: Lactose fermenters are split into the usually motile Escherichia and the non-motile Klebsiella. Proteus (urease positive) and Salmonella (urease negative) do not ferment lactose.

q.stem: Humans usually acquire Borrelia burgdorferi from which life-cycle stage of the Ixodes tick?
q.explanation: Humans are infected by infected nymphs, which feed in late spring and early summer. Rodents are the primary host needed at the nymph stage, and deer are where adult ticks mate and take the blood meal for egg production. Lyme disease is diagnosed by finding specific IgM and IgG with immunofluorescence or ELISA.

q.stem: Which syphilis test becomes positive first and stays positive after treatment?
q.explanation: The specific FTA-Abs test turns positive first and stays positive after treatment. The VDRL (reagin) and complement fixation tests return to normal after treatment, and the VDRL can give false positives. T. pallidum cannot be grown on artificial media.

q.stem: Why can mycobacterial cultures take up to 8 weeks?
options: Mycobacteria grow only inside host cells
Mycobacteria have a very slow generation time of about 12-24 hours
Mycobacteria have to form spores before they multiply
Lowenstein-Jensen medium suppresses growth for the first few weeks
q.explanation: Mycobacteria grow on Lowenstein-Jensen medium but divide only once every 12-24 hours, so cultures can take up to 8 weeks. They are non-sporing and are not obligate intracellular organisms. Their waxy walls stop them taking up the Gram stain.

q.stem: Which statement about Mycobacterium tuberculosis is correct?
options: Its typical lesion is a non-caseating granuloma made of lymphocytes
It causes uveitis only by direct spread from the conjunctiva
BCG, a live attenuated bovine strain, gives about 75% protection
q.explanation: BCG is a live attenuated bovine strain that prevents about 75% of cases. The typical TB lesion is a caseating granuloma made of macrophages and macrophage-derived cells. The waxy wall stops Gram staining, and TB reaches the choroid by the bloodstream to cause panuveitis.

q.stem: Mollicutes differ from other bacteria because they lack a cell wall. Which mollicute has been linked to the cause of Reiter's syndrome?
q.explanation: Mollicutes include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Mycoplasma hominis and Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Ureaplasma has been linked to Reiter's syndrome. Chlamydia are not classed as mollicutes in this scheme, and Treponema has a peptidoglycan wall.

q.stem: In viruses, which term describes small changes in antigenicity caused by point mutations in the viral genome?
q.explanation: Point mutations cause antigenic drift, a small change in antigenicity. Antigenic shift is a bigger change in which whole genome segments are swapped with other virus reservoirs. Transformation and latency are outcomes of chronic infection.

q.stem: In a chronic viral infection, the viral genome sits in the host DNA and does not replicate until something such as stress triggers it. What is this state called?
q.explanation: This is latency, and herpes simplex is the classic example. In persistence the virus keeps replicating at a very low rate, and in transformation the virus gives the cell new properties.

q.stem: Which statement about where viruses replicate is correct?
options: RNA viruses typically replicate in the nucleus using host RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
All DNA viruses depend entirely on host nuclear enzymes
Inclusion bodies are degenerating host organelles unrelated to viral synthesis
Most DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus and produce intranuclear inclusions
q.explanation: Most DNA viruses use host enzymes in the nucleus, so they produce intranuclear inclusions. RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm because host cells have no enzymes that copy RNA from RNA. Pox viruses are an exception among DNA viruses because they carry their own enzymes. Inclusion bodies are sites of viral synthesis.

q.stem: Which virus produces nuclear 'owl's eye' inclusion bodies as well as cytoplasmic inclusions?
q.explanation: CMV forms both cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions, and the nuclear ones are the 'owl's eye' bodies. Herpes simplex shows eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions with syncytial giant cells, but not this owl's eye pattern.

q.stem: How does herpes simplex virus type 1 avoid complement?
options: It makes a C3b-binding molecule that speeds breakdown of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb)
It makes IgA proteases that cleave complement
It has a polysaccharide capsule that does not activate complement
It suppresses MHC class I expression
q.explanation: HSV-1 makes a C3b-binding molecule that promotes breakdown of the C3bBb convertase. IgA proteases belong to Neisseria, non-activating capsules are a bacterial strategy, and suppressing MHC class I is how adenovirus avoids T cells.

q.stem: Which virus is typically transmitted by the faeco-oral route?
q.explanation: Enteroviruses spread faeco-orally. Paramyxoviruses spread through airborne respiratory droplets, hepatitis B spreads parenterally, and rubella can pass vertically across the placenta.

q.stem: When the Goldmann-Witmer coefficient is calculated on aqueous and serum samples, which value indicates local intraocular antibody production?
q.explanation: The coefficient compares the specific antibody ratio between ocular fluid and serum with the total IgG ratio between them. A value of 3 or more indicates that antibody is being made inside the eye, which points to local infection.

q.stem: In a positive complement fixation test for viral infection, what happens to the indicator erythrocytes?
options: They are lysed, because free complement is still available
They are not lysed, because the complement has already been used up by the antigen-antibody reaction
They agglutinate directly with viral antigen
They take up the fluorescent label
q.explanation: If the specific antibody is present, it binds the viral antigen and fixes the added complement. No complement is left to lyse the erythrocytes, so lack of lysis means a positive test.

q.stem: After primary infection at a peripheral site, how does HSV-1 reach the trigeminal ganglion to become latent?
options: Retrograde intra-axonal transport in sensory neurons
Anterograde axonal transport from the ganglion
Direct spread through the cerebrospinal fluid
q.explanation: HSV enters sensory nerve terminals and travels backwards up the axon to the neuronal cell bodies in sensory and autonomic ganglia, where it becomes latent. On reactivation, new virus travels anterogradely back to the periphery. Latency in lymphocytes is a CMV feature.

q.stem: Which viral structural protein enhances transcription of the immediate-early, early and late genes of herpes simplex?
q.explanation: VP16 is the HSV structural protein that boosts transcription of its regulatory (immediate-early), DNA replication (early) and structural (late) genes. E6 is an HPV oncoprotein, Tax regulates HTLV-1, and p24 is the HIV core protein.

q.stem: What is the main mechanism of herpes simplex disciform (stromal) keratitis?
options: Direct cytolysis of keratocytes by replicating virus
A hypersensitivity reaction to viral antigen
q.explanation: Stromal disease such as disciform keratitis comes from a hypersensitivity reaction to the highly immunogenic viral antigen, not from the virus itself. That is why it is not explained by active viral cytolysis or by any toxin.

q.stem: What mainly keeps varicella zoster virus latent in sensory ganglia?
options: Interferon secreted by the ganglion cells
q.explanation: Cell-mediated immunity keeps VZV latent. Reactivation, which can give herpes zoster ophthalmicus from the trigeminal ganglion, follows concurrent illness, immunosuppression or radiotherapy, all of which weaken cell-mediated immunity.

q.stem: In which cells does cytomegalovirus become latent?
options: B lymphoblasts only, which it transforms
