q.stem: Which factor is NOT described as contributing to the improvement in visual acuity after birth?
options: Development of the blue cone pigment, which is absent at birth
Cones becoming more densely packed at the fovea
Myelination of the visual pathway up to 4 months post partum
q.explanation: All three cone pigments are present at birth, though blue function lags behind. Postnatal cone packing, outer segment lengthening and completion of myelination by about 4 months post partum all contribute to better acuity.

q.stem: Regarding ocular axial length:
options: It is about 24 mm at birth and does not change
It is about 21 mm at birth and decreases at puberty
It reaches adult length by 6 months
It is about 18 mm at birth, increases in early childhood and again at puberty, settling at about 24 mm
q.explanation: The neonatal eye is hypermetropic with an axial length of about 18 mm, growing in the first years and again in puberty to an adult length of about 24 mm, so children often grow out of hypermetropia.

q.stem: Astigmatism present at birth in most infants:
options: Is due to the lens and resolves at age 10
Is usually gone by the end of the first year as adult corneal dimensions are reached
q.explanation: Most infants have astigmatism at birth, which typically resolves within the first year as the cornea reaches adult dimensions. It is a normal developmental finding.

q.stem: Why might the sclera be thinned in axial myopes?
options: The sclera is derived entirely from mesoderm
The sclera forms first posteriorly around the optic nerve
The posterior sclera is the last part to form, as sclera develops from the rectus insertions backwards
The choriocapillaris does not connect until after birth
q.explanation: Scleral development spreads from the rectus insertions, so the posterior portions form last, which may explain thinning in long myopic eyes. The sclera is mainly neural crest, not mesoderm, derived.

q.stem: Regarding infant visual fields:
options: They extend about 40 degrees either side of the vertical meridian at 3 months, and nasal fields lag behind temporal
Temporal fields lag behind nasal fields
They reach 80 degrees on each side by 3 months
q.explanation: At 3 months the field is about 40 degrees either side of the vertical meridian, reaching 80 degrees by 10 months, with nasal field development behind temporal.

q.stem: Stereopsis normally develops at what age?
q.explanation: Stereopsis develops between 3.5 and 6 months once the visual apparatus has matured enough for the brain to compare the two retinal images. Saccades, pursuit, vergence and accommodation are described as maturing after stereopsis.

q.stem: Which statement about newborn eye alignment and movement is correct?
options: Optokinetic nystagmus is present at birth, supporting it being a subcortical reflex
The angle between the optic nerve axes is 68 degrees at birth
Orthotropia is an involuntary reflex present at birth
q.explanation: Newborns have OKN, which supports its being an involuntary subcortical reflex. Most infants are exotropic at birth with optic nerve axes at 71 degrees, reaching the adult 68 degrees by 3 years, and orthotropia requires voluntary control.

q.stem: Which statement about infant colour and contrast vision is correct?
options: Contrast sensitivity is not measurable until 6 months
Only rod pigment is present at birth
Spectral sensitivity is independent of photoreceptor length
Infants can distinguish red from white by 2 months, but blue pigment function develops later than the others
q.explanation: Contrast sensitivity is measurable at 6 weeks and spectral sensitivity at 2 months, when red can be told from white. All cone pigments and rod pigment are present but blue lags; spectral sensitivity increases with photoreceptor length.

q.stem: The Hayflick limit refers to:
options: The maximum amplitude of accommodation in youth
The number of lens fibres laid down each year
Somatic cells dividing a finite number of times (about 40-60) before proliferation stops
The age at which macular development ceases
q.explanation: The Hayflick limit describes cells ceasing to divide after roughly 40-60 divisions, which limits genetic instability and malignant growth. It is a theory of cellular senescence, unrelated to accommodation or lens growth.

q.stem: An elderly patient has epiphora and foreign body sensation with a fold of redundant inferior bulbar conjunctiva overlapping the lid margin. The diagnosis is:
q.explanation: Conjunctivochalasis is a redundant fold of lower bulbar conjunctiva from mechanical stress that can block the inferior punctum and disrupt the tear meniscus; treatment is excision. A pinguecula is a yellow-white deposit, and entropion involves an inturned lid margin.

q.stem: Involutional ptosis is typically caused by:
options: Horizontal laxity of the lower lid
Dehiscence, disinsertion or stretching of the levator aponeurosis
Weakness of Muller's muscle from sympathetic loss
q.explanation: Age-related ptosis results from levator aponeurosis dehiscence, disinsertion or stretching. Horizontal lower lid laxity causes involutional ectropion, and the neurological causes are not involutional.

q.stem: Which feature distinguishes arcus senilis from the limbal girdle of Vogt?
options: Arcus is separated from the limbus by a clear zone and progresses circumferentially, whereas the girdle does not progress
Arcus is a form of subepithelial elastosis
The girdle is composed of cholesterol esters
Arcus begins in the medial and temporal cornea
q.explanation: Arcus is lipid (cholesterol esters, triglycerides, phospholipids) deposited peripherally, starting superiorly and spreading round with a 0.2 mm clear zone from the limbus. The limbal girdle sits at the medial and temporal limbus, is non-progressive, and is described as subepithelial elastosis.

q.stem: In cross-section, arcus senilis has an hourglass shape because lipid deposits:
options: Are densest in Bowman's layer and anterior to Descemet's membrane, extending towards each other
q.explanation: Deposits form anterior to Descemet's membrane extending forwards and in Bowman's layer extending backwards, meeting to give an hourglass profile. They are not confined to the epithelium, endothelium or mid-stroma alone.

q.stem: An iron line at the upper border of the tear film in the lower cornea is named:
q.explanation: The Hudson-Stahli line is a tidemark at the tear film's upper border. Ferry's line lies next to a trabeculectomy bleb and Stocker's line ahead of an advancing pterygium; Glaukomflecken are lens opacities after angle closure.

q.stem: Which histological feature is found in pterygium but not in pinguecula?
options: Location in nasal or temporal conjunctiva
q.explanation: Both lesions show actinic (solar) elastosis, occur nasally and temporally, and are more common in sunny climates owing to UV. Only pterygia additionally destroy Bowman's layer as they grow onto the cornea.

q.stem: Which proposed mechanism of presbyopia is described as disproved?
options: Reduced elasticity of the lens capsule
Lens hardening, since lenticular sclerosis predates presbyopia onset
Altered geometry between ciliary muscle root and lens changing zonular tension
Continued growth of the eye and its components
q.explanation: Presbyopia is the age-related fall in amplitude of accommodation, with no single cause. Capsular elasticity change and altered ciliary muscle-lens geometry from ongoing growth remain proposed mechanisms, but hardening of the lens is described as disproved because sclerosis occurs before presbyopia begins.

q.stem: Which is NOT listed as a known risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma?
q.explanation: Recognised POAG risk factors are age, raised IOP, race, family history, diabetes and myopia. Hypermetropia is not among the listed risk factors; myopia is.

q.stem: A hypermature cataract in which the liquefied cortex allows the hard nucleus to sink within the capsule is called:
q.explanation: In a Morgagnian cataract the cortex has liquefied so much that the nucleus sinks inferiorly in the bag. Brunescent describes a brown-black mature nuclear cataract, immature cataracts are only partly opaque, and Glaukomflecken are anterior subcapsular infarcts.

q.stem: Patients with cortical cataract often complain of glare because:
options: Increased nuclear refractive index causes myopia
Fluid entering between fibres has a lower refractive index than lens matter, scattering light
q.explanation: Cortical cataract follows osmotic changes (loss of potassium, retention of sodium, chloride and calcium) drawing water between fibres as spokes; the lower refractive index fluid scatters light. Urochrome and index myopia relate to nuclear cataract, and calcium hydroxyapatite to asteroid hyalosis.

q.stem: An elderly patient finds she can read without her glasses again as her vision for distance worsens. The most likely explanation is:
options: Nuclear sclerosis increasing the lens refractive index, causing index myopia
q.explanation: Nuclear cataract arises from post-translational protein modification with oxidation, crosslinking and aggregation; an increased refractive index induces myopia, the 'second sight of the aged'. Accommodation declines, not increases, with age.

q.stem: Glaukomflecken are best described as:
options: Posterior capsular plaques from hyaloid remnants
Focal infarcts of the anterior lens epithelium seen as grey-white anterior subcapsular opacities after angle closure
Haemosiderin deposits in the corneal epithelium
Pigment deposits on the corneal endothelium
q.explanation: Glaukomflecken are grey-white anterior subcapsular or capsular opacities within the pupil following acute or recurrent angle-closure glaucoma, representing focal epithelial infarcts. Posterior capsular plaques are Mittendorf dots and epithelial haemosiderin forms iron lines.

q.stem: In posterior vitreous detachment, separation of the posterior hyaloid typically begins:
options: Perifoveally, then spreads anteriorly towards the vitreous base
At the vitreous base, then spreads posteriorly
At the optic disc, then spreads to the macula
q.explanation: With age the vitreous liquefies (synchysis) and collapses (syneresis), and separation starts around the fovea and extends anteriorly. Detachment over the disc creates the Weiss ring, through which liquefied vitreous fills the retrohyaloid space.

q.stem: Asteroid hyalosis consists of:
options: Calcium hydroxyapatite, calcium phosphate and phospholipid opacities that are usually asymptomatic
Cholesterol crystals that settle inferiorly and cause severe visual loss
q.explanation: Asteroid bodies are age-related calcium hydroxyapatite, calcium phosphate and phospholipid deposits that move with eye movements, and patients are usually asymptomatic. Acid mucopolysaccharide cavities describe retinoschisis.

q.stem: In typical (degenerative) retinoschisis the neurosensory retina splits at which layer?
q.explanation: Typical retinoschisis splits at the outer plexiform layer, whereas reticular retinoschisis splits at the nerve fibre layer. It is most often inferotemporal and bilateral; separation of photoreceptors from RPE would be a retinal detachment.

q.stem: Lattice degeneration is characterised by:
options: Radial bands of retinal thickening at the posterior pole
Splitting of the retina at the outer plexiform layer
Circumferential areas of peripheral retinal thinning, often near the vertical meridian, with possible atrophic round holes
Drusen with loss of RPE at the macula
q.explanation: Lattice is demarcated, circumferentially oriented peripheral retinal thinning, usually adjacent to the vertical meridian, sometimes with small round atrophic holes and a risk of detachment. Retinal splitting describes retinoschisis and macular drusen relate to ARMD.

q.stem: Which statement about age-related macular degeneration is correct?
options: Neovascular ARMD accounts for about 85-90% of cases
Neovascular ARMD accounts for about 10-15% of cases
Dry ARMD is defined by choroidal vessels growing into the subretinal space
Bruch's membrane thickens in dry ARMD
q.explanation: Wet (neovascular) ARMD is 10-15% of ARMD, defined by choroidal vessel ingrowth into the RPE and subretinal space. Dry ARMD involves RPE and photoreceptor loss with thinning of the outer plexiform layer and Bruch's membrane and choriocapillaris atrophy.

q.stem: Which ocular structure absorbs most of the ultraviolet A (315-400 nm) radiation that reaches the eye?
q.explanation: UVA gets through the cornea and is strongly absorbed by the crystalline lens. The cornea and sclera absorb the shorter UVB and UVC wavebands, and the longer IRB and IRC. Without a lens (aphakia) or with a pseudophakic lens, UVA may reach and damage the retina.

q.stem: Which wavelength range corresponds to ultraviolet B?
q.explanation: UVB covers 280-315 nm. UVC is 200-280 nm, UVA is 315-400 nm and infrared A is 780-1400 nm. Visible light lies between 400 and 780 nm.

q.stem: A solar eclipse viewer presents with a central retinal burn. Which statement best explains how the damage happened?
options: Infrared light passes through the ocular media to the retina and causes a thermal injury
UVC passes through the cornea and causes a photochemical injury to the retina
IRC is focused by the lens and burns the retina
UVB is transmitted by the lens and causes the injury
q.explanation: The longer-wavelength infrared that reaches the retina can cause thermal effects such as eclipse burns. UVB and UVC are absorbed entirely by the cornea and sclera, and so are IRB and IRC, so none of these reach the retina.

q.stem: What optical phenomenon chiefly accounts for the transparency of the corneal stroma?
options: Diffraction at the endothelial cell borders
Destructive interference of light scattered by the regularly spaced collagen fibrils
Polarization of light by the stromal lamellae
q.explanation: The stromal collagen fibrils are evenly spaced, so light deviated by them is cancelled by destructive interference (waves half a cycle out of phase). Constructive interference would make the scattered light stronger, not weaker. Diffraction and polarization do not explain stromal clarity.

q.stem: Concerning diffraction through a circular aperture, which statement is correct?
options: Diffraction does not occur in the human eye
The Airy disc is a central dark spot surrounded by bright rings
Reducing the aperture size enlarges the central Airy disc
Diffraction becomes less important as the pupil gets smaller
q.explanation: The smaller the aperture, the larger the Airy disc, because diffraction is most marked with small apertures. The Airy pattern is a central bright disc surrounded by alternating dark and light rings. Diffraction happens in all optical instruments, and it is the main cause of image imperfection when the pupil is smallest.

q.stem: The limit of resolution is reached when two point images are separated so that:
options: The two Airy discs just touch at their edges
The centres of the two Airy discs coincide
The centre of one Airy disc falls on the first dark ring of the other
The first bright rings of the two patterns overlap completely
q.explanation: Two points can just be seen as separate when the middle of the second Airy disc lies on the first dark ring of the first disc. This sets the smallest angle of separation that can be resolved. The eye's resolving power is measured clinically with visual acuity tests.

q.stem: Which pairing of optical property and example is correct?
options: Birefringence - Polaroid sunglasses blocking misaligned waves
Birefringence - tourmaline giving a single polarized beam
Dichroism - Polaroid used in the Titmus test
Dichroism - quartz having two refractive indices
q.explanation: Dichroic materials such as tourmaline and Polaroid completely block waves that are not aligned with their molecular structure, so only one polarized beam comes out. Polarizing glasses are used to separate the two eyes in the Titmus test. Birefringent materials such as quartz split light into two polarized beams and have two refractive indices.

q.stem: The troland is a unit of:
options: Light reflected per solid angle per area, in candelas
Retinal illumination, based on a surface luminance of 1 cd/m2 viewed through a 1 mm2 entrance pupil
Radiant flux emitted from a point source, in watts
Luminous flux per square metre of a reflecting surface
q.explanation: The troland measures retinal illumination: a surface luminance of one candela per square metre seen through a one square millimetre entrance pupil, corrected for the Stiles-Crawford effect. Radiant flux is measured in watts. One lumen per square metre gives a luminance of one apostilb. Luminance is the light reflected per solid angle per area.

q.stem: How does the photometric system of light measurement differ from the radiometric system?
options: It quantifies only the visible spectrum, weighted by the visual response produced
Its unit of flux is the watt rather than the lumen
It measures the whole electromagnetic spectrum as absolute values
It ignores the visual response and measures energy only
q.explanation: Photometry deals only with the visible spectrum and measures light by the visual response it produces, with luminous flux in lumens. Radiometry measures the whole electromagnetic spectrum as absolute values, with radiant flux in watts.

q.stem: An object is viewed in a plane mirror. Which describes the image?
q.explanation: Light from the object appears to come from behind the mirror, so the image is virtual. It is also erect and laterally inverted. No real image forms because the reflected rays never actually meet.

q.stem: A plane mirror reflecting a fixed beam of light is rotated through 15 degrees. By how much does the reflected beam move?
q.explanation: When a mirror rotates, the reflected ray moves through twice the angle of rotation: 2 x 15 = 30 degrees. This follows because the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection each change by the rotation angle.

q.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with a radius of curvature of 40 cm. Where is the image, and what is its nature?
options: 60 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect, magnified x2
20 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted, same size
12 cm in front of the mirror, real, erect, diminished
60 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted, magnified x2
q.explanation: f = r/2 = 20 cm. Using 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (real distances positive): 1/v = 1/20 - 1/30 = 1/60, so v = 60 cm in front of the mirror. Magnification = -v/u = -60/30 = -2, so the image is real, inverted and twice the size. An object between F and C of a concave mirror always gives a real, inverted, magnified image beyond C.

q.stem: A convex mirror has a radius of curvature of 50 cm. Which statement is correct?
options: Its focal length is 100 cm and the image is virtual
Its focal length is 25 cm and the image is real and in front of the mirror
Its focal length is 50 cm and the image is real
Its focal length is 25 cm and the image of a distant object is virtual, behind the mirror
q.explanation: For a spherical mirror the focal length is half the radius, so 50/2 = 25 cm. A convex mirror reflects parallel rays away from the axis. The image is virtual and found by extending the reflected rays back behind the mirror. Only concave mirrors bring parallel light to a real focus.

q.stem: Light passes from air into glass. Which statement is correct?
options: Light speeds up in the glass and bends towards the normal
The incident and refracted rays lie in different planes
Light slows in the glass and bends away from the normal
Light slows in the glass and bends towards the normal
q.explanation: Absolute refractive index = speed of light in a vacuum / speed in the medium, so light slows in a denser medium. Going into a medium of higher refractive index, light bends towards the normal. The incident and refracted rays lie in the same plane, as with reflection.

q.stem: A ray in air strikes a flat glass surface (n = 1.5) at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees. What is the approximate angle of refraction?
options: 20 degrees exactly, since angles scale with refractive index
q.explanation: Snell's law gives n1 sin i = n2 sin r, so sin r = (1.0 x sin 30)/1.5 = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333 and r = 19.5 degrees. The ray bends towards the normal on entering the denser glass, so the angle must be less than 30 degrees. Snell's law relates the sines of the angles, not the angles themselves.

q.stem: Approximately what percentage of incident light is transmitted through a clean, parallel-sided pane of glass?
q.explanation: About 4% of light is reflected at each air-glass interface and 96% is transmitted. With two surfaces, about 92% gets through. This partial reflection lets glass act as a beam splitter, for example in the teaching mirror of an indirect ophthalmoscope.

q.stem: Taking the refractive index of the cornea as 1.376 and the radius of curvature of its anterior surface as 7.7 mm, what is the approximate power of the air-cornea interface?
q.explanation: Surface power = (n2 - n1)/r = (1.376 - 1.000)/0.0077 m = 0.376/0.0077 = about +48.8 D. Forgetting to convert millimetres to metres gives an answer ten or a thousand times too small. The air-cornea interface accounts for most of the eye's refraction (the net corneal power is lower because of the posterior surface). +58.6 D is the power of the whole reduced eye.

q.stem: Why is the iridocorneal angle not normally visible without a gonioscopy lens?
options: Light from the angle meets the cornea-air interface beyond the critical angle and is totally internally reflected
The limbus absorbs all light coming from the angle
Dispersion at the cornea separates the light into its colours
The angle lies behind the iris and is optically blocked
q.explanation: Rays from the angle strike the tear-air interface at more than the critical angle, so they are totally internally reflected back into the eye. A contact lens with a coupling fluid such as saline removes the corneal-air interface so the light can come out. The book gives critical angles of 48.5 degrees for water:air and 41 degrees for glass:air.

q.stem: Which is the approximate critical angle for a glass:air interface?
q.explanation: The critical angle for glass:air is about 41 degrees. For water:air it is about 48.5 degrees. At incident angles larger than the critical angle, total internal reflection occurs. Prisms, fibreoptics and gonioscopy all make use of this.

q.stem: Regarding dispersion, which statement is correct?
options: Red light is deviated more than blue light
All wavelengths share the same refractive index in a given medium
Dispersive power is directly proportional to refractive index
Blue light is deviated more than red light by a refracting medium
q.explanation: A medium's refractive index differs slightly for different wavelengths. Shorter (blue) wavelengths are bent more than longer (red) ones. Dispersive power is the angle between the red and blue light and is not related to the refractive index. Dispersion is the cause of chromatic aberration.

q.stem: A glass prism (n = 1.5) has a refracting angle of 10 degrees. At minimum deviation, what is the angle of deviation?
q.explanation: At minimum deviation D = (n - 1) x alpha = (1.5 - 1) x 10 = 5 degrees. So for glass of refractive index 1.5, the deviation is half the refracting angle. Minimum deviation occurs when the angles of incidence and emergence are equal.

q.stem: What image does a prism form of an object viewed through it?
options: Inverted, real, displaced towards the apex
Erect, virtual, displaced towards the base
Erect, virtual, displaced towards the apex
Inverted, virtual, displaced towards the base
q.explanation: Light is deviated towards the base, so the eye sees the object displaced towards the apex. The image is erect and virtual.

q.stem: Concerning how prisms are specified, which statement is correct?
options: In the Prentice position, deviation happens equally at both surfaces
Glass trial-frame prisms are specified in the Prentice position and plastic prism bars at minimum deviation
Glass trial-frame prisms are specified at minimum deviation
A prism has less power in the Prentice position than at minimum deviation
q.explanation: In the Prentice position one face is perpendicular to the incident light, so all the deviation happens at the second surface. The prism is more powerful in this position than at minimum deviation. Glass ophthalmic and trial-frame prisms are specified in the Prentice position, while plastic prism bars are specified at minimum deviation.

q.stem: A patient is given a 6 prism dioptre base-up prism and an 8 prism dioptre base-out prism, stacked in front of the same eye. What is the resultant prism power?
q.explanation: A horizontal and a vertical prism can be combined, and the resultant is found using Pythagoras: square root of (6 squared + 8 squared) = square root of 100 = 10 prism dioptres, with an oblique base. Simply adding them (14) or subtracting them (2) is wrong. Two prisms stacked in the same direction cannot simply be added either.

q.stem: An object 2 m from a prism appears displaced by 10 cm. What is the power of the prism?
q.explanation: One prism dioptre moves an object 1 cm at 1 m. At 2 m, each prism dioptre moves it 2 cm, so 10 cm / 2 cm = 5 prism dioptres. Equivalently, displacement per metre = 10/2 = 5 cm/m. Each prism dioptre gives roughly half a degree of apparent deviation.

q.stem: A patient has a symptomatic right hypertropia and the prism correction is to be split between the eyes. How should the prisms be orientated?
options: Right eye base-up, left eye base-down
Right eye base-down, left eye base-up
Right eye base-out, left eye base-in
q.explanation: For vertical deviations the prisms go in opposite directions in the two eyes: base-down in front of the higher (right) eye and base-up in front of the left. Esotropia is corrected with base-out prisms and exotropia with base-in prisms.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT a recognised use of prisms?
options: Base-in prism exercises to improve fusional reserve in convergence insufficiency
Fresnel prisms for temporary relief of diplopia
q.explanation: Therapeutic prisms for convergence insufficiency are used base-out during exercise periods, not base-in. The 4-dioptre prism test (microtropia), assessment of simulated blindness, and stick-on Fresnel prisms for immediate or temporary relief of diplopia are all listed uses.

q.stem: What is the power of a converging lens with a second focal length of 40 cm?
q.explanation: Power (D) = 1/second focal length (m) = 1/0.40 = +2.5 D. The sign is positive because a converging (convex) lens has a positive second focal length. Forgetting to convert to metres gives the wrong result.

q.stem: An object is placed 50 cm in front of a +5.00 D thin lens. Where is the image formed?
options: 33 cm in front of the lens (virtual)
q.explanation: Incident vergence U = 1/-0.50 = -2.00 D. Emergent vergence V = U + F = -2.00 + 5.00 = +3.00 D. Image distance = 1/3 m = 33 cm behind the lens, and it is real because the emerging light converges. 20 cm is the focal length, which applies only to an object at infinity.

q.stem: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a +5.00 D thin lens. What are the image position and linear magnification?
options: 6.7 cm in front of the lens, virtual, erect, magnified x0.67
20 cm in front of the lens, virtual, erect, magnified x2
10 cm behind the lens, real, inverted, same size
20 cm behind the lens, real, inverted, magnified x2
q.explanation: U = 1/-0.10 = -10 D, so V = -10 + 5 = -5 D, giving v = -20 cm (on the object side, virtual). Magnification = v/u = -20/-10 = +2, so the image is erect and twice the size. An object inside the first principal focus of a convex lens always gives a virtual, erect, magnified image. This is how a simple magnifier works.

q.stem: What dioptric power is needed for a simple loupe with a magnifying power of x5 (reference near point 25 cm)?
q.explanation: Magnifying power M = F/4, so F = 4M = 4 x 5 = +20 D. This follows from M = 0.25/f, comparing an object at its focal point with the same object at the 25 cm near point. An x8 loupe would need +32 D.

q.stem: A patient's line of sight passes 5 mm from the optical centre of a -6.00 D spectacle lens. What prismatic effect results?
q.explanation: Prentice's rule: P = F x D, with D in centimetres. P = 6 x 0.5 = 3 prism dioptres. Using millimetres gives 30, ten times too large. The prismatic effect grows towards the edge of the lens, which is also why spherical aberration happens.

q.stem: What image does a thin concave lens form of a real object?
q.explanation: A diverging lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object, on the same side as the object and within its second principal focus. A real inverted image needs a converging lens with the object outside F1. A virtual magnified image comes from a convex lens with the object inside F1.

q.stem: An object is placed exactly at the first principal focus of a convex lens. Where is the image formed?
options: At twice the focal length, real and inverted
At the second principal focus, real and inverted
q.explanation: Light from the first principal focus comes out of the lens parallel, so the image is at infinity, virtual and erect. Object and image subtend the same angle at the lens. A loupe uses this arrangement so the object can be seen at a much closer working distance than the 25 cm near point.

q.stem: How is the first principal focus (F1) of a thin lens defined?
options: The centre of curvature of the first lens surface
The point through which rays pass undeviated
The point where incident parallel rays are brought to a focus
The point from which rays come that leave the lens parallel to the principal axis
q.explanation: F1 is the point of origin of rays that come out parallel after refraction. Incident parallel light converges to, or diverges from, the second principal focus F2, and lenses are numbered by their second focal length. Rays pass undeviated through the nodal point.

q.stem: A plano-cylindrical lens has its axis at 90 degrees. In which meridian does it have its refracting power?
options: It has equal power in all meridians
q.explanation: A cylindrical lens has no power along its axis. Its power lies 90 degrees away from the axis, so a cylinder with axis 90 acts in the 180 (horizontal) meridian. It forms a line image (focal line) of a point object.

q.stem: A Maddox rod with its cylinders arranged horizontally is placed before the right eye, which views a distant spotlight. What does the right eye see?
q.explanation: The Maddox rod is a row of convex cylinders. The eye sees the spotlight as a streak at 90 degrees to the cylinder axes, so horizontal rods give a vertical line. That arrangement is used to test horizontal imbalance. The rod and spot present different images to the two eyes, which dissociates them.

q.stem: A patient views a spotlight with a Maddox rod (horizontal cylinders) before the right eye. The vertical line appears to the left of the spot. What is the diagnosis?
q.explanation: The eye behind the rod moves the opposite way to where the line appears. If it drifts outwards (exophoria), the line falls in the nasal field and appears to the left of the spot. A line to the right indicates esophoria. Because the eyes are dissociated, the deviation shown is a phoria, not a tropia.

q.stem: A Maddox rod is placed before the right eye with its cylinders vertical, so a horizontal line is seen. The patient reports the line lies below the spot. What does this indicate?
q.explanation: According to the book, a line below the spot means right hyperphoria (the right eye is deviated upward and the line appears in the opposite direction). A line above the spot means right hypophoria, which is the same as left hyperphoria. Esophoria is a horizontal deviation and shows as the vertical line lying to the right of the spot.

q.stem: What is the spherical equivalent of -1.00 DS / -1.50 DC x 180?
q.explanation: Spherical equivalent = sphere + half the cylinder = -1.00 + (-1.50/2) = -1.00 - 0.75 = -1.75 D. Adding the whole cylinder gives -2.50 D, which is the power of the stronger meridian. The spherical equivalent corresponds to the circle of least confusion of Sturm's conoid.

q.stem: For a toric lens forming Sturm's conoid, which statement is correct?
options: The circle of least confusion lies at the first line focus
The two line foci lie in parallel planes
The principal meridians of an ophthalmic toric lens lie at 45 degrees to each other
The circle of least confusion lies between the two line foci and corresponds to the spherical equivalent
q.explanation: A toric lens gives two line foci in perpendicular planes. The interval between them is Sturm's conoid, and the circle of least confusion sits between them. It matches the spherical equivalent (sphere plus half the cylinder). In ophthalmic lenses the principal meridians are exactly perpendicular.

q.stem: A +/-0.50 D Jackson cross-cylinder may also be written as:
q.explanation: A Jackson cross-cylinder is a sphero-cylinder whose cylinder is twice the sphere and of opposite sign. This is the same as two equal and opposite cylinders crossed at right angles. +0.50 in one meridian and -0.50 in the other is written +0.50 DS / -1.00 DC (check: +0.50 - 1.00 = -0.50). Its handle sits at 45 degrees to the axes.

q.stem: During subjective refraction, retinoscopy shows no astigmatism. How can the Jackson cross-cylinder confirm that no cylinder is needed?
options: Rotate the handle continuously until the patient sees scissoring
Use it to refine the spherical endpoint against the duochrome
Present it once at 180 degrees only
Present it at 90, 180, 45 and 135 degrees; if none improves vision, no cylinder is required
q.explanation: If no orientation gives better vision when the cross-cylinder is held at 90, 180, 45 and 135 degrees, it can be assumed that no cylinder is needed. Its usual role is to refine the axis (moving the trial cylinder towards the same-sign axis) and the power of a cylinder found on retinoscopy.

q.stem: On a toric surface, what is the 'base curve'?
options: The meridian at 45 degrees to the principal meridians
The principal meridian of minimum curvature (the weaker meridian)
The principal meridian of maximum curvature
The spherical back surface of the lens
q.explanation: A toric surface is curved in two perpendicular principal meridians. The flatter (minimum curvature, weaker power) meridian is the base curve. The steeper meridian is sometimes called the cross curve. In toric transposition the base curve stays fixed and the prescription is fitted to it.

q.stem: Transpose +1.00 DS / -3.00 DC x 10.
q.explanation: To transpose, add the sphere and cylinder for the new sphere (+1.00 + -3.00 = -2.00), change the sign of the cylinder (+3.00), and turn the axis through 90 degrees (10 becomes 100). Check: the original has +1.00 in the 10 meridian and -2.00 in the 100 meridian. The transposed lens has -2.00 + 3.00 = +1.00 in the 10 meridian and -2.00 in the 100 meridian, so they match. Keeping the old axis or the old cylinder sign gives a different lens.

q.stem: Which of these is a correct transposition of +3.00 DS / -1.00 DC x 90?
q.explanation: New sphere = +3.00 + (-1.00) = +2.00, the cylinder changes sign to +1.00, and the axis rotates 90 degrees to 180. Both forms give +3.00 D in the vertical (90) meridian and +2.00 D in the horizontal (180) meridian. The other options give different meridional powers.

q.stem: Focimetry of a spectacle lens gives -2.00 D in the vertical (90 degree) meridian and -4.00 D in the horizontal (180 degree) meridian. What is the prescription?
q.explanation: In minus-cylinder form the sphere is the more positive meridian (-2.00 D, acting in the 90 meridian). The cylinder is the difference (-2.00 D). The cylinder axis is the meridian where the cylinder has no power, which is 90. Check: 90 meridian = -2.00; 180 meridian = -2.00 - 2.00 = -4.00. The plus-cylinder equivalent would be -4.00 DS / +2.00 DC x 180.

q.stem: An unknown spectacle lens is moved side to side in front of a distant cross. The image moves against the lens, and no movement is seen once a -1.50 DS trial lens is held against it. What is the unknown lens?
q.explanation: An 'against' movement shows a convex (plus) lens, and a 'with' movement shows a concave lens. Neutralization uses a known lens of opposite sign: the point of no movement is reached with -1.50 D, so the unknown lens is +1.50 DS. If the lens were astigmatic, the arms of the cross would 'scissor', and each meridian would need to be neutralized separately.

q.stem: Which statement about the Geneva lens measure is correct?
options: It is accurate for any lens material without correction
It is calibrated for thin crown glass, so a correction is needed for other materials
It measures the back vertex power directly using a collimated beam
It uses two fixed pins and a fixed central pin
q.explanation: The Geneva lens measure has three contact pins, and the middle one is spring-loaded. It measures surface curvature, which is turned into surface power on a dial. It was designed for thin crown glass, so other materials need a correction. A collimated beam and back vertex power belong to the focimeter.

q.stem: Why does a focimeter use a green light source?
options: To make the target appear larger
To maximize the brightness of the target
q.explanation: The green source back-lights the target, usually a ring of dots, and is chosen to reduce chromatic aberration. The other components are the collimating lens, the moveable target on a dioptre scale, the viewing telescope with a graticule, and the lens under test.

q.stem: Concerning the focimeter, which statement is correct?
options: Focimeters measure the front vertex power of distance lenses
The lens under test is placed at the second principal focus of the collimating lens, back surface towards the target
The target reads zero when it is at the second principal focus of the collimating lens
The test lens is placed at the first principal focus of the viewing telescope
q.explanation: The instrument reads zero when the target sits at the first principal focus of the collimating lens, so that light comes out parallel. The test lens sits at the collimator's second principal focus. Because focimeters measure back vertex power, the back surface of the spectacle lens faces the target. Front vertex readings are used only to work out the near add of bifocals.

q.stem: When an astigmatic lens is measured on a focimeter, one meridian comes into focus as a set of sharp parallel lines. What does the orientation of these lines show?
options: The direction of the power in that meridian, not the cylinder axis
The direction of any prism base
The position of the optical centre
q.explanation: At each meridional end point the ring of dots is stretched into a focused 'stack of sticks'. Their orientation shows the direction of the power, not the cylinder axis. Measuring both meridians gives a power cross, which is then turned into the prescription. Prism shows up as displacement of the target, not as lines.

q.stem: On focimetry of a bifocal, the distance portion reads +1.25 D and the near portion reads +3.75 D (front vertex readings). What is the near addition?
q.explanation: The near add is the positive difference between the near and distance readings: +3.75 - (+1.25) = +2.50 D. For bifocals the front vertex power is measured in both zones, because the near add is a function of the anterior surface.

q.stem: What thickness does a single-layer anti-reflective coating need in order to cancel reflection of a given wavelength?
q.explanation: A quarter-wavelength coating puts the reflected light half a wavelength out of phase (a quarter shift going in and another coming out), so destructive interference occurs. A half-wavelength coating causes constructive interference and acts like a mirror.

q.stem: Which statement about tinted and photochromic lenses is correct?
options: Slit-lamp heat filters block ultraviolet rather than infrared radiation
Photochromic lenses become lighter in bright sunlight
A neutral density filter selectively absorbs blue light
Glass photochromic lenses darken because light dissociates silver halide crystals
q.explanation: Glass photochromic lenses contain colourless silver halide crystals in borosilicate glass. Incident radiation dissociates the silver and halogen, so the lens darkens in brighter light. A neutral density tint reduces all wavelengths equally and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Slit-lamp heat filters protect against infrared.

q.stem: Regarding chromatic aberration in the human eye, which statement is correct?
options: The difference between red and blue focus is about 0.25 D
Peak spectral sensitivity at 450 nm is focused on the retina
Red light is focused in front of the retina in an emmetrope
The dioptric difference between red and blue focus is about 2 D, and the retina lies between them
q.explanation: Red and blue light are dispersed about 2 D apart in the eye. The retina sits between them, near the focus for 550 nm (green), where the eye is most sensitive. Blue, which is bent more, focuses in front of the retina and red focuses behind it. The pupil and lens nucleus also help reduce chromatic aberration.

q.stem: A myopic patient's new glasses cause eyestrain. On the duochrome test, the letters on the green background are much clearer than those on the red. What is the most likely problem?
options: The myopia has been over-corrected (too much minus)
The patient is red-green colour deficient, so the test is invalid
q.explanation: Too strong a minus lens makes the eye effectively hypermetropic. The focus moves back so green is better focused, and the patient has to accommodate, which causes strain. Reducing the minus until red is clearer corrects this. Because the patient only has to say which panel is clearer, the duochrome works even in colour-blind patients.

q.stem: An emmetropic patient views the duochrome chart. A +1.00 D lens is placed before the eye. What happens?
options: The letters on the green panel become clearer
The red and green panels change positions
The letters on the red panel become clearer
q.explanation: A plus lens moves the dispersed spectrum forward, so red comes closer to the retina and the red letters become clearer. A -1.00 D lens has the opposite effect and makes green clearer. The duochrome has a red top panel and a green bottom panel.

q.stem: How does an achromatic doublet correct chromatic aberration while keeping a useful focusing power?
options: Two lenses of identical material and opposite power are cemented together
A lens of high dispersion is combined with a lens of identical dispersion but higher refractive index
A lens of high refractive power and low dispersion is combined with an opposing lens of low refractive power and high dispersion
A single aspheric surface is used to flatten the periphery
q.explanation: Dispersion and refraction are independent properties, so materials can be paired. One element with high refractive power and low dispersion is combined with an opposing element of low refractive power and high dispersion. The colour dispersions cancel while net power remains. Two equal and opposite lenses of the same material would have zero total power.

q.stem: Which of the following does NOT help to reduce spherical aberration in the human eye?
options: The higher refractive index of the lens nucleus compared with the cortex
The peripheral cornea being steeper than the central cornea
q.explanation: The cornea acts as an aplanatic surface because its periphery is flatter, not steeper, than the centre, which reduces peripheral power. A small pupil (best at 2-2.5 mm) limits light to paraxial rays. The higher-index nucleus offsets the prismatic effect on peripheral rays. The Stiles-Crawford effect reduces the response to obliquely incident light.

q.stem: A patient wearing a high-powered convex spectacle lens looks at a square. What type of distortion is seen?
q.explanation: The increasing prismatic effect towards the edge of a strong plus lens bows the sides of a square inwards (pin-cushion). This is also seen with aphakic spectacles. Concave lenses produce barrel distortion, which bows the edges outwards.

q.stem: How is oblique astigmatism of spectacle lenses reduced?
options: Tilting the lenses away from the face and using a biconvex form
Giving the lenses a pantoscopic tilt and using a meniscus (rather than biconvex) form
q.explanation: Oblique astigmatism happens when the line of sight passes obliquely through the lens. It increases with lens power and is worse in biconvex or biconcave lenses. A pantoscopic (downward) tilt and the equivalent meniscus form reduce it, and best-form lenses are designed to minimize it.

q.stem: Which aberration is described as a combination of oblique rays and spherical aberration, in which an off-axis point appears as an elongated blurred shape?
q.explanation: In coma, light from off-axis points passes obliquely through the centre and periphery of the lens, giving two focal points. A main image is overlaid by a blurred, elongated one, so a circular target looks comet-shaped. In the eye it is reduced by limiting rays to near the principal axis and is usually negligible.

q.stem: In a thick lens system, when do the nodal points coincide with the principal points?
options: Only when the lens is biconvex
When the media on either side of the system are the same
Only when the object is at infinity
q.explanation: The nodal points lie at the principal points only when the media in front of and behind the system are the same. In the eye, air is in front and vitreous is behind, so the nodal points (about 7.1-7.3 mm) lie well behind the principal points (about 1.35-1.60 mm).

q.stem: Why is back vertex power, rather than equivalent power, used when prescribing spectacles?
options: Back vertex power gives the distance from the back surface at which parallel light is focused, which must match the eye's far point
Equivalent power cannot be calculated for thick lenses
Back vertex power ignores lens thickness and so is more accurate
Back vertex power is always equal to the sum of the surface powers
q.explanation: Back vertex power is the reciprocal of the back vertex focal length, which is where parallel light focuses measured from the back surface. It is the value that matters for correcting the eye. Equivalent power comes from the two surface powers with a correction for thickness, and the difference can cause errors in high-power spectacles or contact lenses. Focimeters measure back vertex power.

q.stem: According to Gullstrand's schematic eye, which refractive index is correct?
q.explanation: Gullstrand's values are: cornea 1.376, aqueous and vitreous 1.336, and lens 1.386 (cortex) to 1.406 (core). Because the cornea and aqueous have such similar indices, the posterior corneal surface contributes little refraction.

q.stem: In the reduced schematic eye, what are the approximate total power, aphakic (corneal) power and crystalline lens power?
q.explanation: The reduced eye has a single refracting power of about +58.6 D. Without the lens (cornea only) the eye has about +43 D, so the crystalline lens provides about +15 D. The cornea is more powerful because of the large refractive index difference at the air-tear interface.

q.stem: Why can a small posterior subcapsular cataract cause marked visual symptoms?
options: It changes the refractive index of the aqueous
It lies close to the nodal points, where the cone of light entering through the pupil is narrow
It is located at the first principal plane, 1.35 mm behind the cornea
It lies at the first principal focus of the eye
q.explanation: The nodal points (about 7.08 and 7.33 mm behind the cornea) lie near the posterior pole of the lens. Here the pupil allows only a narrow cylinder of light, so a small central opacity blocks a large part of it. The principal planes lie much further forward, at about 1.35-1.60 mm.

q.stem: A -2.00 D myope (uncorrected) has a near point of 10 cm. What is the amplitude of accommodation?
q.explanation: Amplitude = 1/near point - 1/far point. Near point = 0.10 m gives 10 D. The far point of a -2.00 D myope is 0.50 m, which gives 2 D. Amplitude = 10 - 2 = 8 D. Using the near point alone (10 D) is correct only for an emmetrope, whose far point is at infinity (0 D).

q.stem: What is the amplitude of accommodation of an emmetrope whose near point is 25 cm?
q.explanation: Amplitude = 1/NP - 1/FP = 1/0.25 - 1/infinity = 4 - 0 = 4 D. So to change focus from infinity to 25 cm, an emmetrope must accommodate 4 D.

q.stem: Using the heterophoria method, find the AC/A ratio: IPD 6 cm; 2 prism dioptre exophoria at distance; 8 prism dioptre exophoria at 1/3 m.
q.explanation: AC/A = IPD (cm) + (near deviation - distance deviation)/D, with exo as negative. = 6 + (-8 - (-2))/3 = 6 + (-6/3) = 6 - 2 = 4. The near fixation distance of 1/3 m is 3 D. A ratio of about 4:1 is normal.

q.stem: Using the gradient method at a fixed distance, a patient has a 2 prism dioptre esophoria without lenses and a 14 prism dioptre esophoria through -3.00 D lenses. What is the AC/A ratio?
q.explanation: AC/A = (deviation with lens - deviation without lens)/lens power = (14 - 2)/3 = 4. Eso deviations are positive and exo deviations negative. The -3.00 D lens is taken to cause 3 D of accommodation. 12 is the change in deviation before dividing by the lens power.

q.stem: Which statement about the AC/A ratio is correct?
options: A high AC/A ratio typically causes a distance esotropia with straight eyes at near
The normal AC/A ratio is about 1:1
The gradient method gives a lower value than the heterophoria method, mainly because of proximal convergence
AC/A ratios typically fall with age
q.explanation: The heterophoria method includes proximal convergence, so it gives higher values than the gradient method. The normal ratio is about 4:1, and it tends to rise with age as accommodation declines. A high AC/A gives a convergence excess esotropia: straight for distance and esotropic for near, often managed with bifocals.

q.stem: Which statement about the Purkinje-Sanson images is correct?
options: The third image, from the posterior cornea, is used in keratometry
All four images are erect and virtual
The fourth image, from the posterior lens surface, is real and inverted
The first image comes from the anterior lens surface
q.explanation: Images I to IV come from the anterior cornea, posterior cornea, anterior lens and posterior lens. The first three are erect virtual images from convex reflecting surfaces. Image IV is real and inverted because it forms at the concave posterior lens surface. Image I is used in keratometry, Placido disc assessment and strabismus assessment.

q.stem: Which of the following is an example of refractive (index) myopia rather than axial myopia?
q.explanation: In refractive or index myopia the eye is a normal length but its dioptric power is too high. Examples are keratoconus and nucleosclerosis. Axial myopia (a long eye) is the most common form. Aphakia causes refractive hypermetropia, and a short eye causes axial hypermetropia.

q.stem: Regarding hypermetropia, which statement is correct?
options: Hypermetropes usually need presbyopic correction later than emmetropes
Refractive hypermetropia is the most common form
Manifest hypermetropia can only be revealed with cycloplegia
Latent hypermetropia is the extra correction needed to overcome remaining ciliary tone, and needs cycloplegia to reveal it in children
q.explanation: Manifest hypermetropia is the correction needed for clear distance vision. Latent hypermetropia is the extra amount hidden by ciliary tone, and children need cycloplegic refraction to reveal it fully. Axial hypermetropia is the most common form. Because hypermetropes are always accommodating, they need presbyopic correction earlier.

q.stem: In which type of astigmatism does one principal meridian focus in front of the retina and the other behind it?
q.explanation: In mixed astigmatism the two focal lines lie on either side of the retina. In simple myopic or simple hypermetropic astigmatism one meridian focuses on the retina. In compound forms both meridians focus on the same side of the retina, either in front (myopic) or behind (hypermetropic).

q.stem: The principal meridians of a patient's astigmatism are not perpendicular to each other. How is this classified?
options: Oblique astigmatism, which can be corrected with spectacles
Irregular astigmatism, which cannot be corrected with spectacles
q.explanation: If the principal meridians are not at 90 degrees to each other, the astigmatism is irregular and spectacles cannot correct it. Oblique astigmatism has perpendicular meridians that do not lie at 90 and 180 degrees. Regular astigmatism has perpendicular principal meridians.

q.stem: In anisometropic amblyopia, which eye usually becomes amblyopic?
q.explanation: Accommodation acts equally on both eyes, so they cannot accommodate by different amounts. The more hypermetropic eye stays blurred and becomes amblyopic. Anisometropia of more than about 1 D is a common cause, and myopes tolerate larger differences.

q.stem: An uncorrected myope can see clearly no further than 40 cm. Ignoring vertex distance, what lens corrects the distance vision?
q.explanation: The far point of the eye must coincide with the focal point of the correcting lens. A far point of 0.40 m needs a lens of focal length -0.40 m, which is 1/-0.40 = -2.50 D. Concave lenses make parallel light diverge so that it seems to come from the far point.

q.stem: An aphakic patient is fully corrected by a +15.00 D spectacle lens at a back vertex distance of 14 mm. What power of contact lens is needed?
q.explanation: F2 = F1/(1 - dF1) = 15/(1 - 0.014 x 15) = 15/(1 - 0.21) = 15/0.79 = +18.99, which is about +19 D. A plus lens moved closer to the eye must be stronger to keep the same focal point. Leaving the power unchanged ignores the vertex effect.

q.stem: A myope wears -8.00 D spectacles at a back vertex distance of 12 mm. What is the approximate contact lens power?
q.explanation: F2 = F1/(1 - dF1) = -8/(1 - 0.012 x -8) = -8/(1 + 0.096) = -8/1.096 = -7.30 D, about -7.25 D to the nearest quarter dioptre. A minus lens moved closer to the eye needs less power. Getting the sign of the denominator wrong gives about -8.75 D.

q.stem: A high hypermetrope's spectacles slip forward down the nose (further from the eye). What is the effect?
options: There is no change in effective power
q.explanation: Moving any lens away from the eye moves the image forward. For a hypermetrope this adds to the lens's effect, so the effective plus power rises. For a myope, moving a minus lens forward reduces its effect, so stronger minus is needed. That is why myopes dislike glasses that slip forward.

q.stem: During refraction with several lenses in the trial frame, which practice is correct?
options: Lens position in the trial frame never affects the effective power
The back vertex distance is only needed for lenses under 5 D
The higher-power lens goes in the back cell and the back vertex distance is recorded
The higher-power lens goes in the front cell
q.explanation: Lenses over about 5 D must sit in the back of the trial frame, because their distance from the cornea makes a significant difference. With more than one lens, the stronger one goes at the back. The back vertex distance is measured with the scale on the trial frame and recorded.

q.stem: Which correction of aphakia gives the least image magnification?
options: Spectacles at the anterior focal point (about x1.36)
q.explanation: Relative spectacle magnification for aphakia is about 1.36 at the anterior focal point (23.23/17.05) and about 1.33 at the usual 14 mm. It is about 1.1 with a contact lens and about 1.0 with an IOL. This is why unilateral aphakia corrected with spectacles causes an unacceptable size difference between the eyes.

q.stem: A patient wearing high-plus aphakic spectacles notices objects suddenly appearing and disappearing at the edge of vision. What causes this?
options: A ring scotoma from the prismatic effect at the lens edge
Uncorrected oblique astigmatism of the eye
q.explanation: The strong prismatic effect at the edge of aphakic spectacles (usually +10 D or more) creates a ring scotoma. Objects pop in and out of it (the 'jack in the box' effect), and the scotoma moves with the eye. These lenses also cause pin-cushion, not barrel, distortion. Patients adapt by turning the head rather than the eyes.

q.stem: In refractive (rather than axial) ametropia corrected with spectacles, which statement about relative spectacle magnification (RSM) is correct?
options: In refractive hypermetropia the RSM is less than 1
In refractive myopia the RSM is less than 1, even with the lens at the anterior focal point
Moving the lens closer to the eye makes the image smaller
RSM is exactly 1 when the lens is at the anterior focal point
q.explanation: In refractive ametropia the corrected image is never the same size as the emmetropic one, even at the anterior focal point. RSM is above 1 in refractive hypermetropia and below 1 in refractive myopia. Bringing the lens closer to the eye makes the image larger, and moving it away makes it smaller. RSM equals 1 at the anterior focal point only in axial ametropia.

q.stem: In the SRK formula, approximately how much does a 1 mm error in axial length change the calculated IOL power?
q.explanation: Axial length is multiplied by B = 2.5 in the SRK formula, so a 1 mm error gives about a 2.5 D error in IOL power. This is why axial length must be measured along the visual axis, and why an inter-eye difference of more than 0.5 mm should be rechecked.

q.stem: A posterior chamber IOL was planned, but an anterior chamber IOL has to be inserted. How should the IOL power be adjusted?
options: Reduce the power by the difference between the two lenses' A constants
Increase the power by 2.5 D for every millimetre the lens moves forward
Increase the power by the difference between the A constants
q.explanation: An anterior chamber lens sits further forward, so a weaker lens is needed. The power is reduced by the difference between the A constants, since the A constant reflects the lens's position in the eye.

q.stem: According to the book, what is the approximate amplitude of accommodation at about 45 years and at about 60 years?
options: About 14 D at 45 years and about 4 D at 60 years
About 8 D at 45 years and about 4 D at 60 years
About 1 D at 45 years and 0 D at 60 years
About 4 D at 45 years and about 1 D at 60 years
q.explanation: Accommodation can be up to 14 D in infancy. It declines with age, falling faster around 45 years (about 4 D) to about 1 D by 60. Causes include stiffening of the lens and capsule and weakening of the ciliary body.

q.stem: An uncorrected +3.00 D hypermetrope wants to read at 33 cm. How much accommodation is needed?
q.explanation: 3 D is needed to cancel the hypermetropia, and another 3 D (1/0.33 m) to focus at 33 cm, making 6 D in total. A -3.00 D myope needs no accommodation at 33 cm, because that is their far point. This is why presbyopia affects hypermetropes earlier and more severely.

q.stem: In a standard bifocal, where is the near line-of-sight point (LOSN) placed relative to the distance line-of-sight point (LOSD)?
options: About 2 mm below and 8 mm nasal
About 15 mm below and directly in line
About 8 mm below and 2 mm nasal
About 8 mm below and 2 mm temporal
q.explanation: The LOSN is usually about 8 mm below and 2 mm nasal to the LOSD. This follows the convergence of the eyes when reading. The top edge of the segment is usually lined up with the inferonasal corneal limbus, so it does not interfere with distance vision in primary gaze.

q.stem: Executive bifocals for a child with convergence excess esotropia. Which statement is correct?
options: The segment top should be well below the lower lid margin
They are used to increase accommodation for near
They are fused bifocals with a small flint-glass button
They are solid one-piece bifocals, with the segment top aligned to the lower edge of the pupil
q.explanation: Executive bifocals are a type of solid bifocal in which the near add takes up the whole lower half. For convergence excess esotropia, the segment top is set at the lower pupil margin to maximize use of the add. This reduces accommodation, and so convergence, at near. Fused bifocals use a higher-index flint-glass button.

q.stem: Which statement about bifocal prismatic effects is correct?
options: Most patients tolerate up to 5 D of vertical prismatic imbalance
Monocentric bifocals remove prismatic jump because the distance and near optical centres coincide at the segment junction
Prismatic jump is worse with low-powered additions
Slab-off (biprism) is used to correct horizontal prism in high myopia
q.explanation: Prismatic jump is the sudden image shift when the eye crosses from the distance part into the near segment, and it grows with the refractive change. In monocentric bifocals the optical centres coincide at the junction, so there is no jump. Slab-off corrects the vertical imbalance caused by high anisometropia, since only about 1.5 D of vertical imbalance is tolerated.

q.stem: Concerning progressive addition (varifocal) lenses, which statement is correct?
options: Unwanted astigmatism lies within the power progression corridor
Harder designs have the widest progression corridor
Softer designs have a wider progression corridor, smaller distance and near zones, and less peripheral aberration
Varifocals cause more prismatic jump than bifocals
q.explanation: Varifocals have no prismatic jump and no visible segment line. Astigmatism and aberration occur on either side of the power progression corridor (PPC), not within it. 'Soft' designs widen the PPC and shrink the distance and near zones, which reduces aberration in the peripheral zones. High astigmatism or a strong near add make varifocals harder to tolerate.

q.stem: Which activity is a direct contraindication to bifocal use?
q.explanation: Bifocal hazards relate to dangerous activities. Working at heights is a direct contraindication, and caution is needed with dangerous chemicals, hot objects and vertigo. A computer user may simply need an intermediate add.

q.stem: Which statement about a Galilean telescope used as a low vision aid is correct?
options: Its lenses are separated by the sum of their focal lengths
It increases the field of view in proportion to magnification
It has a convex objective and a concave eyepiece separated by the difference of their focal lengths, giving an erect image
It has a concave objective and a convex eyepiece giving an inverted image
q.explanation: A Galilean system has a plus objective and a minus eyepiece separated by the difference of their focal lengths. It gives an erect, magnified image that is not much affected by peripheral aberration or astigmatism. Like all optical magnifiers, higher magnification narrows the field of view and reduces depth of focus.

q.stem: A simple convex lens magnifier (about +5 D) is used as a low vision aid. Which statement is correct?
options: Its power is greater than a standard x8 loupe
Increasing magnification increases the depth of focus
The object is placed beyond F2, giving a real inverted image
The object is placed between the lens and F1, giving a magnified virtual image
q.explanation: The magnifier lets the object be held closer than normal, so it subtends a larger angle at the eye and forms a bigger retinal image. With the object inside F1, the image is virtual and magnified. At about +5 D it is much weaker than an x8 (+32 D) loupe, acting like a stronger reading correction. Magnification reduces depth of focus and field of view.

q.stem: Topically instilled eye drops can produce marked systemic effects mainly because the drug is:
options: Absorbed through the nasal and nasopharyngeal mucosa, bypassing first-pass hepatic metabolism
Absorbed across the corneal endothelium directly into the choroidal circulation
Concentrated in the vitreous and then released slowly into the blood
Converted into more potent metabolites by corneal enzymes
q.explanation: Drops draining through the nasolacrimal system are absorbed by nasal and nasopharyngeal mucosa straight into the systemic circulation, escaping first-pass metabolism and so achieving high bioavailability. Topical drugs penetrate the posterior segment poorly, and corneal metabolism does not explain the systemic effects.

q.stem: Which statement about first-order drug kinetics is correct?
options: Elimination proceeds at a fixed rate regardless of plasma concentration
It typically arises when hepatic metabolizing enzymes become saturated
The rate of drug transfer is proportional to the amount of drug present, so the half-life is constant
It describes only a small minority of clinically used drugs
q.explanation: First-order (linear) kinetics means transfer rate is proportional to the amount of drug, giving a constant half-life, and most drugs behave this way. A fixed elimination rate limited by body capacity, such as saturated liver enzymes, is zero-order kinetics.

q.stem: In zero-order (saturation) kinetics, which of the following is true?
options: The half-life is constant at all doses
The rate of drug handling depends on a functional capacity of the body rather than on drug concentration
The size of the administered dose has little clinical relevance
Active transport systems convert first-order kinetics into zero-order kinetics
q.explanation: Zero-order kinetics reflects a limited body capacity (e.g. liver enzymes) so unmetabolized drug persists at high doses, making dose important. A constant half-life is a feature of first-order kinetics, and the book states active transport changes kinetics from zero to first order, not the reverse.

q.stem: Binding of atropine to uveal melanin would be expected to:
options: Increase both efficacy and duration of action
Increase efficacy but shorten duration of action
Have no effect on its pharmacokinetics
Reduce the drug's efficacy but prolong its duration of action
q.explanation: Tissue binding (e.g. melanin binding of atropine and pilocarpine) sequesters drug so it is unavailable, lowering efficacy while lengthening the time it is retained in the compartment. Binding is therefore not pharmacokinetically neutral.

q.stem: Bioavailability of a drug is best defined as:
options: The time taken for plasma concentration to fall by half
The peak plasma concentration achieved after a dose
The fraction of drug bound to albumin
The area under the curve of (log) plasma concentration against time
q.explanation: Because rapid absorption gives a high peak but rapid elimination may still give low availability, bioavailability is expressed as the area under the concentration-time curve. Half-life and peak concentration are separate measures, and protein binding is unrelated to the definition.

q.stem: According to Fick's law, the rate of diffusion of a drug across a membrane is inversely proportional to:
q.explanation: Fick's law gives rate = K x A x (concentration difference) / D, where D is membrane thickness, so thicker membranes slow diffusion. Area, concentration gradient and the diffusion coefficient (set by lipid solubility, ionization and molecular size) all increase diffusion rate.

q.stem: Local anaesthetics are weak bases. At acidic pH they will be:
options: Mostly ionized (BH+), reducing passive diffusion through lipid membranes
Equally ionized at every pH because their pKa equals tissue pH
q.explanation: By the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship a weak base is mostly ionized (BH+) at acid pH and mostly unionized (B) at alkaline pH. Since unionized drug is the lipid-soluble form that diffuses passively, ionization in acid tissue reduces penetration.

q.stem: The pKa of a weak acid or base is the pH at which the drug is:
q.explanation: The pKa is the pH at which a compound is half ionized and half unionized, and it determines the degree of ionization at any given pH. It has nothing to do with protein binding.

q.stem: Facilitated diffusion differs from active transport in that facilitated diffusion:
options: Is carrier-mediated but requires no energy because it does not move solute against a concentration gradient
Does not involve a carrier molecule
Moves solute against its concentration gradient using ATP
q.explanation: Both processes use carriers, but active transport is energy-dependent while facilitated diffusion proceeds down the concentration gradient without energy. Pinocytosis is a separate route across membranes.

q.stem: Which statement about plasma protein binding of drugs is correct?
options: Binding to albumin usually involves irreversible covalent bonds
Only the bound fraction is filtered at the glomerulus
Bound drug is inactive and acts as a reservoir that dissociates as free drug is eliminated
Each albumin molecule has a single binding site for all drugs
q.explanation: Albumin is the main binding protein; binding is usually non-covalent and reversible, the bound drug is inactive and forms a store that buffers falls in free concentration. Glomerular clearance relates to the unbound fraction, and albumin has multiple sites for acids and bases.

q.stem: Phase 1 drug biotransformations are mainly carried out by:
q.explanation: Phase 1 reactions (hydroxylation, dealkylation, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) are performed by the heterogeneous cytochrome P450 group, present in liver and some peripheral organs including the eye. Glucuronidation is a phase 2 conjugation; xanthine oxidase and MAO are other enzyme systems with specific substrates.

q.stem: Which of the following is listed as a hepatic enzyme INHIBITOR?
q.explanation: Chloramphenicol, isoniazid, metronidazole, warfarin and carbon monoxide are listed as enzyme inhibitors. Rifampicin, phenytoin, barbiturates, phenothiazines and nicotine are enzyme inducers.

q.stem: Regarding renal handling of drugs, which statement is correct?
options: Lipid-soluble drugs are excreted faster because they cannot cross back into plasma
Protein-bound drug is freely filtered at the glomerulus
Tubular secretion cannot be affected by other drugs
Acidic drugs are excreted faster in alkaline urine because they remain ionized and are poorly reabsorbed
q.explanation: Only unionized weak acids and bases are reabsorbed, so alkalinizing urine ionizes acidic drugs and speeds their elimination. Lipid-soluble drugs return to plasma more readily and are excreted more slowly, filtration depends on the unbound fraction, and drugs compete for secretory carriers.

q.stem: Enterohepatic circulation of a drug involves:
options: Excretion of volatile drug via the lungs
Biliary excretion of a conjugate, hydrolysis in the gut and reabsorption of active drug
Glomerular filtration followed by tubular reabsorption
Secretion of drug into breast milk
q.explanation: Conjugated drugs concentrated in bile reach the intestine, where hydrolysis may release active drug that is reabsorbed and recirculated. The other options are different excretion routes.

q.stem: Pharmacodynamics is best described as the study of:
options: The relationship between drug concentration and its effect
The time course of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion
q.explanation: Pharmacodynamics concerns drug effects and the concentration-response relationship. The time course of ADME is pharmacokinetics.

q.stem: Pilocarpine is listed as which type of agent at muscarinic receptors, compared with acetylcholine?
q.explanation: Table 9.3 lists pilocarpine as a partial agonist at muscarinic receptors with acetylcholine as the full agonist; a partial agonist cannot elicit the maximal tissue response. Prenalterol and impromidine are the partial agonists listed for beta and H2 receptors respectively.

q.stem: A drug that achieves the maximal response but only at high doses has:
q.explanation: Efficacy is the maximal response a drug can produce, whereas potency is the amount needed for a given response. A drug reaching full effect only at high doses is efficacious but of low potency; a partial agonist cannot achieve the maximal response at all.

q.stem: Atropine blocking the effect of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, overcome by raising the agonist concentration, is an example of:
q.explanation: Agonist and antagonist compete for the same site and form short-lived combinations, so more agonist surmounts the block - reversible competitive antagonism. Irreversible competitive antagonism is insurmountable; chemical and physiological antagonism are non-competitive forms.

q.stem: Phenobarbital reducing the anticoagulant effect of warfarin by inducing hepatic enzymes is an example of:
options: Indirect antagonism via a downstream receptor
q.explanation: Pharmacokinetic antagonism lowers the concentration of the active drug at its site of action, as with enzyme induction. Chemical antagonism is direct combination (e.g. EDTA chelating lead); functional antagonism uses an opposing receptor (e.g. adrenaline vs histamine bronchoconstriction).

q.stem: Adrenaline reversing histamine-induced bronchoconstriction by acting on its own receptor is an example of:
q.explanation: In functional antagonism the antagonist is an agonist at a separate receptor producing an opposing effect. It does not compete for the histamine receptor, alter histamine concentration, or combine with histamine chemically.

q.stem: Which layer is the most important barrier to corneal penetration of water-soluble (ionized) drugs?
q.explanation: The lipid-rich epithelium (with desmosomes and Bowman's layer beneath) is impermeable to electrolytes but passes fat-soluble agents. The stroma favours water-soluble drugs, and the endothelium offers little resistance so stroma and aqueous act as one compartment.

q.stem: Why must a drug ideally exist in both ionized and unionized forms to cross the cornea effectively?
options: The stroma is lipid rich and blocks ionized drugs
The cornea is a lipid-water-lipid sandwich: epithelium and endothelium favour lipid-soluble forms and the stroma favours water-soluble forms
The endothelium actively pumps only ionized drug into the aqueous
Bowman's layer only transmits ionized molecules
q.explanation: Epithelium and endothelium contain about 100 times more phospholipid than the stroma, while the stroma (90% of corneal substance, GAGs and water) passes ionized water-soluble drugs more freely. Hence biphasic solubility is needed; the endothelium is not an active drug pump in this sense.

q.stem: Which of the following is a weak base existing in both ionized and unionized forms within the normal tear pH range?
q.explanation: Tropicamide, cyclopentolate and atropine are cited as weak bases present in both forms at tear pH (6.5-7.6), aiding corneal penetration. The other options are a dye, a preservative and a tear substitute polymer.

q.stem: Why is the pH of an eye drop adjusted to near that of the tear film?
options: To ensure the drug is fully ionized for epithelial penetration
To prevent precipitation within the anterior chamber
Acidic or alkaline drops irritate, increasing blinking and lacrimation and so clearing the drug faster
To inactivate the preservative after instillation
q.explanation: Irritant drops stimulate tearing and blinking, which shortens residence time. Full ionization would actually impair epithelial penetration.

q.stem: Benzalkonium chloride increases ocular drug absorption by:
options: Compromising corneal epithelial integrity and increasing permeability
q.explanation: As a cationic surfactant, benzalkonium disrupts the corneal epithelium and so raises corneal permeability to drugs. It does not act as a viscosity agent or block drainage.

q.stem: Penetration of drugs given by sub-Tenon's or subconjunctival injection across the sclera is limited by:
options: Impermeability of sclera to large molecules
Trans-scleral outflow, which depends on IOP
q.explanation: The sclera is tough but porous even to large molecules; the limit on drug penetration is outward trans-scleral flow dependent on IOP. The sclera has no epithelium.

q.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a factor influencing topical ocular drug absorption?
options: Blink rate and tear film stability
q.explanation: Listed factors include environment (temperature, humidity), drop volume, formulation (pH, preservative, vehicle), blink rate, tear film and surface health, nasolacrimal drainage and conjunctival vessel absorption. Serum albumin is relevant to systemic protein binding, not topical absorption.

q.stem: Muscarinic agonist drops can reduce their own ocular residence time by:
q.explanation: Muscarinic stimulation increases lacrimal gland secretion; the extra tear flow washes out the drug faster. The other options would, if anything, prolong residence.

q.stem: The human conjunctival sac holds about 15-30 microlitres. What is the consequence of instilling a second drop immediately after the first?
options: Longer contact time of the first drop
No increase in ocular bioavailability but greater risk of systemic toxicity
q.explanation: A single drop (10-75 microlitres) already exceeds sac capacity so most is spilled; extra drops do not raise bioavailability but add nasolacrimal mucosal absorption and systemic toxicity.

q.stem: Which manoeuvre is recommended to reduce systemic absorption of eye drops?
options: Instilling two drops of the same drug
Digital pressure over the lacrimal sac
Tilting the head forward after instillation
q.explanation: Punctal/lacrimal sac pressure, the pouch method (evert lower lid, close eye 2 minutes), more viscous preparations and smaller drop volume all reduce systemic absorption. Extra drops and less viscous vehicles increase it.

q.stem: When two different eye drops are prescribed, the recommended interval between them to avoid a washout effect is about:
q.explanation: Leaving about 5 minutes between different drops avoids the second washing out the first. The tear film turns over at roughly 15% per minute.

q.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a suspension from a colloid?
options: Colloid particles are larger and sediment rapidly
In a suspension the solute is fully dissolved
Suspension particles (usually >1 micrometre) settle with time; colloid particles are smaller and do not settle
q.explanation: Suspensions are heterogeneous with particles large enough to sediment, requiring agitation; colloids have smaller evenly dispersed particles that stay suspended. In a true solution the solute is dissolved and not present as a solid.

q.stem: In the classification of colloids, a liquid dispersed in a liquid continuous phase is termed:
q.explanation: Liquid in liquid is an emulsion (e.g. milk). A sol is solid dispersed in liquid (e.g. blood), a gel is liquid in solid, and an aerosol is liquid in gas.

q.stem: Compared with drops, ophthalmic ointments are:
options: Cleared faster from the conjunctival sac
Retained longer on the ocular surface but more likely to blur vision and cause contact dermatitis
Free of hydrocarbon or polymer bases
q.explanation: Ointments are viscous semi-solids (hydrocarbons, mineral oils, lanolin, polymers) that stay on the surface longest, at the cost of blurring and contact dermatitis.

q.stem: Ocular inserts used for slow drug release consist of:
options: A single layer of cross-linked collagen alpha helices
Two outer ethylene vinyl acetate layers enclosing a drug/alginate core
A lipid bilayer vesicle with an aqueous core
A hydrophilic soft contact lens polymer
