q.explanation: Ocular inserts are flexible elliptical three-layer devices with ethylene vinyl acetate outer layers around a drug/alginate mix. Collagen shields are made of alpha-helical chains with controllable crosslinking; liposomes are lipid vesicles.

q.stem: Which property is described for liposomes as an ocular drug-delivery system?
options: They carry hydrophilic drugs better than lipophilic ones
They are solid particles that sediment over time
They are irritant and cause marked blurring
They carry lipophilic drugs more easily than hydrophilic drugs and do not blur vision
q.explanation: Liposomes are lipid-membrane vesicles with an aqueous interior; they carry lipophilic drugs more readily, are easily prepared, non-irritant and do not blur vision.

q.stem: In an inflamed eye with endophthalmitis, intravitreal aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are:
options: Retained longer because the retinal pump is damaged
Cleared only through the retinal vasculature
Cleared more rapidly, because they are eliminated via the aqueous circulation
q.explanation: Aminoglycosides leave via aqueous circulation and are cleared faster from inflamed eyes. It is water-soluble penicillins whose half-life is prolonged because the retinal pump mechanism is damaged.

q.stem: Unilateral topical timolol lowering IOP in the fellow, untreated eye illustrates:
options: Systemic absorption of a topically applied drug
Direct passage through the optic chiasm
q.explanation: Topical drugs reach the systemic circulation and can act on the contralateral eye; timolol is the classic example and may also worsen asthma and cardiac disease.

q.stem: Ligand-gated ion channels are classified into three superfamilies. Which receptor belongs to the cys-loop superfamily?
q.explanation: Cys-loop receptors include GABA-A, glycine and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. NMDA, AMPA and kainate are ionotropic glutamate receptors, P2X is ATP-gated, and metabotropic glutamate receptors are G-protein coupled.

q.stem: Compared with ionotropic receptors, metabotropic receptors:
options: Form an ion channel within the receptor itself
Mediate fast synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Act more slowly but produce longer-lasting and more widespread effects
Open within milliseconds and close equally rapidly
q.explanation: Metabotropic receptors do not form channels; they work through second messengers (often G-proteins), so channels open more slowly but may stay open seconds to minutes with broader intracellular effects. Fast synaptic transmission is ionotropic.

q.stem: G-protein coupled receptors characteristically have:
options: Seven transmembrane domains with a G-protein binding domain on the third intracellular loop
Four transmembrane subunits surrounding a water-filled pore
A single transmembrane domain with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity
An intracellular receptor that binds DNA
q.explanation: GPCRs span the membrane with seven hydrophobic domains, a ligand binding domain, and a G-protein binding site on the third intracellular loop. Pore-forming multi-subunit structures are ion channels, and intrinsic kinase activity describes RTKs.

q.stem: Which receptor is NOT a G-protein coupled receptor according to the classification given?
q.explanation: GABA-B (amino acid class), prostaglandin (lipid class) and TSH (glycoprotein class) receptors are GPCRs. The nicotinic receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel.

q.stem: On binding a growth factor, a receptor tyrosine kinase first:
options: Dimerizes with adjacent receptors and autophosphorylates its own tyrosine residues
q.explanation: Ligand binding triggers RTK dimerization, activating cytoplasmic kinase domains whose first substrate is the receptor itself; phosphotyrosines then recruit proteins such as Src and phospholipase C-gamma. VEGF receptors are an example.

q.stem: Regarding local anaesthetic nerve block, which is correct?
options: Large fibres are blocked before small fibres
Myelinated fibres are more easily blocked than unmyelinated fibres
Deep pressure sensation is the first to disappear
Pain is lost first because it is carried by small myelinated and unmyelinated fibres
q.explanation: Small fibres are blocked before large ones and myelinated fibres are more resistant, so pain goes first, followed by temperature, touch and deep pressure.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: In the parasympathetic supply to the eye, the postganglionic neurotransmitter and receptor are:
q.explanation: Preganglionic fibres synapse in the ciliary ganglion releasing ACh onto nicotinic receptors; postganglionic fibres release ACh onto muscarinic receptors at the effector. Noradrenaline is the sympathetic postganglionic transmitter.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Which cycloplegic leaves NO residual accommodation?
q.explanation: Atropine leaves nil residual accommodation. Cyclopentolate leaves 1-2D, homatropine 0.5-2D and tropicamide 1.6-3.2D.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Full recovery from atropine 1% cycloplegia typically takes:
q.explanation: Atropine 1% takes 7-14 days for full recovery. Cyclopentolate 1% recovers in about 24 hours, tropicamide in about 6 hours and homatropine in 10-48 hours.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Cyclopentolate is less effective and slower to act in patients with:
q.explanation: Residual accommodation varies with number of drops, age and iris colour; cyclopentolate is less effective and slower in dark irides, consistent with melanin binding reducing available drug.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Which is NOT a mechanism by which cycloplegics help in anterior uveitis?
options: Increasing aqueous humour production to flush inflammatory cells
Dilating the pupil to break synechiae
q.explanation: Cycloplegics relieve iritis by paralysing inflamed muscle, dilating the pupil (breaking synechiae) and reducing vessel permeability, decreasing outpouring of cells and protein. Increasing aqueous production is not a listed mechanism.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Why is adrenaline not used for routine mydriasis in ophthalmology, whereas phenylephrine is?
options: Adrenaline's beta activity is unnecessary for pupil dilation and causes more systemic side effects
q.explanation: Pupil dilation needs only alpha-1 stimulation of the dilator; phenylephrine is selectively alpha-1. Adrenaline also stimulates beta receptors, adding systemic effects without helping mydriasis. Sympathomimetics have no cycloplegic action.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: A sympathomimetic alone may give incomplete pupillary dilatation because:
options: The iris sphincter lacks muscarinic receptors
The dilator pupillae is a weak muscle
q.explanation: The dilator pupillae is not powerful, so alpha-1 stimulation alone can leave dilatation incomplete; combining with an antimuscarinic is more effective.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Pilocarpine lowers IOP principally by:
options: Constricting the iris sphincter, which pulls on the trabecular meshwork
Reducing aqueous production by the ciliary epithelium
Contracting longitudinal ciliary muscle, pulling the scleral spur and opening the trabecular meshwork
q.explanation: Muscarinic stimulation of the longitudinal ciliary fibres pulls the scleral spur posteriorly and inwards, opening the meshwork. Iris miosis has no direct effect on IOP, and ciliary contraction may actually reduce uveoscleral drainage.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: The most troublesome ocular side effect of pilocarpine, especially in young patients, is:
q.explanation: Ciliary spasm (up to about 5D increased accommodation, lasting 2-3 hours after each drop) with brow ache is the most troublesome effect and is worse in the young. Iris darkening relates to prostaglandin analogues and verticillata to systemic drugs like amiodarone.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Ecothiopate differs from physostigmine in that ecothiopate:
q.explanation: Both are indirectly acting cholinergic agonists, but physostigmine (eserine) blocks acetylcholinesterase reversibly whereas ecothiopate does so irreversibly. Pilocarpine and carbachol are direct agonists.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Cholinergic miotics should be avoided in neovascular or uveitic glaucoma because they:
q.explanation: Cholinergic miotics cause blood-aqueous barrier breakdown, so they are avoided in inflamed eyes, neovascular and uveitic glaucoma.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Thymoxamine is used to reverse sympathetic mydriasis because it is:
q.explanation: Thymoxamine blocks alpha-1 receptors on the dilator pupillae, reversing sympathomimetic (e.g. phenylephrine) mydriasis.

q.section: Ocular drugs and the autonomic nervous system
q.stem: Stimulation of alpha-1 receptors in Müller's muscle causes:
q.explanation: Müller's muscle is sympathetically innervated via alpha-1 receptors; contraction elevates the lid (retraction). Miosis and accommodation are muscarinic effects.

q.stem: Which topical beta-blocker has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity?
q.explanation: Carteolol is the only topical beta-blocker with ISA, theoretically reducing bradycardia and systemic effects. Betaxolol is relatively beta-1 selective ('cardioselective'); timolol and levobunolol are non-selective.

q.stem: Topical beta-blockers are contraindicated in which patient?
options: A patient with a dark iris
q.explanation: Beta-2 blockade can cause bronchospasm, so asthma and COPD are contraindications, as are bradycardia, heart block and heart failure. Sulphonamide allergy is a contraindication to carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.

q.stem: Which IOP-lowering drug is a lipophilic prodrug converted to adrenaline by ocular enzymes?
q.explanation: Dipivefrine crosses the cornea more easily than adrenaline, allowing lower concentrations. Latanoprost is also a prodrug but of a prostaglandin acid; brimonidine and apraclonidine are alpha-2 agonists.

q.stem: Why is apraclonidine licensed only for short-term IOP control, unlike brimonidine?
options: It is a strong beta-1 antagonist
Its IOP-lowering effect wanes over about 4 weeks
q.explanation: Apraclonidine loses efficacy over about 4 weeks. Brimonidine is more alpha-2 selective, also enhances uveoscleral outflow and is licensed long term. Alpha-2 agonists have minimal cardiovascular effects.

q.stem: Prostaglandin F2-alpha analogues such as latanoprost lower IOP mainly by:
q.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues act on the FP receptor to increase non-conventional (uveoscleral) outflow; bimatoprost may also increase trabecular outflow. Reduced aqueous production is the mechanism of beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists and CAIs.

q.stem: Which adverse effect is characteristic of prostaglandin analogue drops?
q.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues increase iris stromal melanin and cause eyelash growth and darkening, plus initial hyperaemia. Paraesthesia is a systemic CAI effect, bradycardia a beta-blocker effect, and orange lens staining is rifampicin.

q.stem: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors should be used cautiously when:
q.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase is present in corneal endothelium; inhibition acidifies the cells, so CAIs are not recommended with compromised endothelium. Asthma is a beta-blocker concern.

q.stem: Which is a recognized systemic side effect of oral acetazolamide?
options: Paraesthesia of the hands and feet
q.explanation: Acetazolamide causes paraesthesia, taste disturbance, headache, fatigue, an early diuresis and less commonly renal calculi, blood dyscrasias and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Bronchospasm relates to beta-blockers.

q.stem: Oral glycerol is unsuitable for lowering IOP in which patient?
options: A patient with a pseudophakic eye
q.explanation: Glycerol has a high calorific value, so it cannot be given to diabetics. It lowers IOP within an hour but briefly, and can cause dehydration, headache and vomiting.

q.stem: NSAIDs exert their anti-inflammatory effect by inhibiting:
q.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and thus prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis from arachidonic acid. Steroids prevent membrane phospholipid breakdown; lipoxygenase produces leukotrienes; methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.

q.stem: Aspirin may exacerbate asthma because cyclo-oxygenase blockade:
options: Increases histamine release from mast cells
Increases leukotriene production via the lipoxygenase pathway
q.explanation: With cyclo-oxygenase inhibited, arachidonic acid is shunted to lipoxygenase, raising leukotrienes and worsening asthma.

q.stem: Glucocorticoids reduce eicosanoid production by:
options: Preventing breakdown of cell membrane phospholipids to arachidonic acid
q.explanation: Steroids act upstream, preventing phospholipid breakdown so less arachidonic acid is available for prostaglandins and thromboxane. NSAIDs act at cyclo-oxygenase.

q.stem: Which is a recognized LOCAL side effect of topical glucocorticoids?
q.explanation: Topical steroids can raise IOP, cause cataract, slow epithelial healing, precipitate corneal melt, predispose to HSV and fungal infection and cause ptosis. Verticillata and orange tears are effects of other systemic drugs.

q.stem: Methotrexate suppresses the immune response by:
options: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase as a folic acid antagonist
Inhibiting IL-2 production and stimulating TGF-beta
Blocking de novo purine synthesis selectively in lymphocytes
q.explanation: Methotrexate antagonizes folic acid by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, suppressing DNA synthesis. Ciclosporin inhibits IL-2 and stimulates TGF-beta, mycophenolate selectively blocks lymphocyte purine synthesis and infliximab/etanercept target TNF.

q.stem: Which immunosuppressant selectively blocks de novo purine synthesis in lymphocytes?
q.explanation: Mycophenolate mofetil blocks de novo purine synthesis and is selective for lymphocytes. Azathioprine inhibits purine synthesis more generally, tacrolimus inhibits IL-2 and infliximab is a chimeric anti-TNF-alpha antibody.

q.stem: Pegaptanib is thought to carry a lower risk of systemic vascular events than ranibizumab and bevacizumab because it:
q.explanation: Pegaptanib binds only VEGF165, whereas ranibizumab and bevacizumab block all isoforms. However, visual results with ranibizumab and bevacizumab are better.

q.stem: Bevacizumab was originally approved for intravenous use in:
q.explanation: Bevacizumab was licensed as an adjuvant in metastatic colorectal cancer and used off-label for choroidal neovascularization because ranibizumab is expensive.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Lidocaine is longer acting than tetracaine and oxybuprocaine because it:
options: Has an amide rather than an ester link, making it resistant to hydrolysis
Has an ester link resistant to cholinesterase
q.explanation: Lidocaine's amide link resists hydrolysis, prolonging action and allowing use in allergy to ester-linked agents (tetracaine, oxybuprocaine, proxymetacaine, cocaine).

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Which topical anaesthetic stings least, is popular for children and must be refrigerated?
q.explanation: Proxymetacaine stings least and has the best toxicity profile but is the least stable and needs refrigeration. Cocaine is the worst for stinging and toxicity; tetracaine can irregularize the corneal surface.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Cocaine applied topically dilates the pupil because it:
options: Blocks muscarinic receptors on the sphincter
Blocks noradrenaline reuptake into sympathetic nerve endings
q.explanation: Cocaine is an indirect sympathomimetic, preventing noradrenaline reuptake so more transmitter acts on the dilator.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Local anaesthetic agents produce nerve block by:
options: Blocking sodium entry through voltage-gated channels
q.explanation: They block sodium transport into the nerve fibre, preventing generation and conduction of the action potential, and are active in their cationic form.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Which is NOT a recognized problem with prolonged topical anaesthetic use?
options: Increased corneal permeability to other drugs
Reduced bacterial replication affecting swab results
q.explanation: Topical anaesthetics abolish (not enhance) the blink reflex. They impair epithelial cell motility, increase epithelial permeability, and reduce bacterial and viral replication, affecting cultures.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Healthy corneal epithelium does not stain with fluorescein because:
options: Fluorescein fluoresces only in acidic solution
Its high lipid content resists water-soluble fluorescein
q.explanation: Fluorescein is water soluble; intact lipid-rich epithelium excludes it. Defects allow entry to Bowman's layer and stroma, glowing green under cobalt blue. Fluorescence occurs in alkaline solution (pH >7).

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: During intravenous fluorescein angiography, which is correct?
options: About 80% of fluorescein is bound and only unbound dye leaks from normal retinal vessels
The choriocapillaris normally prevents all fluorescein leakage
Bound fluorescein crosses intact retinal vessel walls
q.explanation: Fluorescein is about 80% bound to plasma proteins and red cells. The choriocapillaris leaks both bound and unbound dye, while retinal vessels release only unbound dye unless the barrier is damaged. Excretion in urine takes up to 48 hours.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: An advantage of indocyanine green over fluorescein angiography is that ICG:
options: Is excreted unchanged in the urine within an hour
Fluoresces through pigment and haemorrhage and is largely retained in the choriocapillaris
q.explanation: ICG is retained in retinal vessels and choriocapillaris and can fluoresce through pigment and blood, unlike fluorescein. Rose Bengal stains devitalized cells red.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Rose Bengal staining is used to show:
options: Devitalized corneal and conjunctival cells and mucus
q.explanation: Rose Bengal 1% stains dead cells and mucus red, e.g. in dry eye; it is irritant so topical anaesthetic is used first.

q.section: Topical anaesthetics, tear substitutes and diagnostic agents
q.stem: Which tear substitute component gives a longer retention time and improves tear film stability?
q.explanation: Hyaluronic acid has even longer retention than polyvinyl alcohol or celluloses. Saline is a base; benzalkonium and thiomersal are preservatives that harm epithelial stability.

q.stem: Mast cell stabilizers such as sodium cromoglicate must be started before allergen exposure because they:
options: Prevent mast cell degranulation but cannot reverse it once it has occurred
q.explanation: Stabilizers prevent histamine release by stabilizing mast cell membranes; once degranulated, they are ineffective. H1 receptor blockers are antihistamines such as olopatadine.

q.stem: Which of the following is a topical H1 antihistamine rather than a mast cell stabilizer?
q.explanation: Azelastine, antazoline, emedastine, epinastine, levocabastine and olopatadine are listed antihistamines. Cromoglicate, lodoxamide, nedocromil and ketotifen are listed mast cell stabilizers.

q.stem: Histamine H2 receptor activation results in:
options: Activation of adenylyl cyclase and second messenger production
A rise in intracellular calcium in bronchial muscle
Opening of a ligand-gated chloride channel
q.explanation: H2 activation stimulates adenylyl cyclase (stomach, heart, uterus); H1 activation raises intracellular calcium, as in bronchial muscle. Topical ocular antihistamines target H1.

q.stem: A predictable unwanted effect of a drug at therapeutic dose, such as sedation with antihistamines, is termed:
q.explanation: Side effects are unavoidable, predictable actions. Secondary effects result from the drug's action (e.g. thrush after antibiotics), and idiosyncratic effects occur only in susceptible individuals.

q.stem: Regarding the LD50, which statement is correct?
options: It is the dose killing 50% of treated animals over a short period and gives no information on long-term effects
It is the dose producing 50% of the maximal response
q.explanation: LD50 is a crude measure of acute lethality; animal results do not reliably predict human effects, as thalidomide limb defects showed.

q.stem: Benzalkonium chloride is inactivated by soaps and calcium/magnesium salts, so which is often added?
q.explanation: EDTA chelates divalent cations that would otherwise inactivate benzalkonium. Benzalkonium is most effective at alkaline pH (about 8).

q.stem: Orange discoloration of tears and soft contact lenses is caused by:
q.explanation: Rifampicin discolours tears and lenses orange and may cause uveitis. Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, chloroquine maculopathy and amiodarone verticillata.

q.stem: A patient on ethambutol develops reduced vision and red-green colour defect. The likely cause is:
q.explanation: Ethambutol causes retrobulbar optic neuritis with red-green defects; safe dose is quoted as 15 mg/kg/day.

q.stem: Which drug binds melanin in the RPE and uveal tract and can cause maculopathy, verticillata and lens deposits?
q.explanation: Chloroquine binds melanin and causes maculopathy, verticillata and lens deposits; hydroxychloroquine has fewer side effects. Tamoxifen causes crystalline macular deposits; digoxin reduces acuity and colour vision.

q.stem: White/yellow macular deposits and cystoid macular oedema in a patient taking >40 mg/day for over a year suggest toxicity from:
q.explanation: High-dose tamoxifen causes white-yellow macular deposits, CMO and sometimes optic neuritis. Chlorpromazine causes pigment granules, penicillamine myasthenia, and gold corneal verticillata.

q.stem: Which drug causes myasthenia presenting with ptosis and diplopia?
q.explanation: Penicillamine can induce myasthenia with ptosis and diplopia. Amiodarone and indometacin cause verticillata; digoxin affects acuity and colour vision.

q.stem: Which drug group may precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma through anticholinergic effects?
q.explanation: Anticholinergics including tricyclics, antihistamines, ipratropium, scopolamine and atropine cause dry eye and may precipitate angle closure. Oral contraceptives are linked to vascular occlusion and tetracyclines to conjunctival deposits.

q.stem: Light emerging from the partially transparent mirror of a laser tube is best described as:
q.explanation: Laser output is in phase (coherent), of a single wavelength (monochromatic) and made of parallel rays (collimated). Spontaneous emission, by contrast, is incoherent and travels in all directions; laser light is not polychromatic.

q.stem: In laser physics, the state in which more atoms of the active medium have electrons in an excited state than in the ground state is called:
q.explanation: Population inversion describes an excess of excited atoms, the prerequisite for net stimulated emission. Pumping is the delivery of energy that creates this state; mode locking and Q-switching are methods of producing intense pulses.

q.stem: When an excited atom in a laser medium is struck by a photon of the wavelength it would naturally emit, what happens?
options: It becomes ionised and forms a plasma
It emits an incoherent photon travelling in a random direction
It absorbs the photon and rises to a higher energy level
It drops to a lower energy level, emitting a photon coherent with the stimulating photon
q.explanation: This is stimulated emission: the atom falls to a lower level and releases light in phase with the incoming photon. Random-direction incoherent light comes from spontaneous emission, and plasma formation is the ionising tissue effect of some lasers, not the lasing mechanism.

q.stem: Why is the separation of the two mirrors at the ends of a laser tube important?
options: It controls the colour of the aiming beam
It determines which pumping source can be used
If it is a multiple of the emitted wavelength, resonance can occur
It sets the pulse duration of a Q-switched laser
q.explanation: Mirror spacing that is a multiple of the emitted wavelength allows the reflected stimulated emission to reinforce itself in phase (resonance). The pumping source, Q-switch pulse and aiming beam are not determined by this spacing.

q.stem: Which laser is correctly matched with the physical state of its active medium?
q.explanation: Lasers are named after their active medium: dye lasers use a liquid, argon, krypton and CO2 lasers use gases, and Nd:YAG uses a solid crystal (neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet).

q.stem: Which statement about the energy output of a laser is correct?
options: Most light from the active medium is produced by stimulated emission
Laser beams are perfectly parallel in practice
Energy is evenly distributed across the width of the beam
The emitted luminous flux is only a small fraction of the energy pumped in
q.explanation: A great deal of energy must be pumped in to obtain a few coherent waves, so efficiency is low; brightness comes from concentrating the flux in a fine beam. Most emitted light is actually spontaneous, the beam is slightly divergent, and energy is concentrated at the beam centre.

q.stem: Output of an argon photocoagulation laser is quoted in watts, whereas that of a Nd:YAG laser is quoted in joules. Why?
options: The argon laser is Q-switched, whereas the YAG is continuous
The argon laser produces a continuous beam, whereas the YAG delivers a peak of power over a fixed period
Joules are used only for lasers with a He:Ne aiming beam
The YAG laser emits visible light, whereas argon emits infrared
q.explanation: A continuous argon beam is described by power (energy per unit time, watts), whereas the YAG delivers a pulse of energy over a fixed time, so energy (joules) is quoted. It is the YAG that is Q-switched, and it emits infrared (1064 nm), not visible light.

q.stem: In a Q-switched laser, what occurs while the shutter in front of one mirror is closed?
options: The medium is pumped and population inversion builds up, but lasing cannot occur
The medium returns to its ground state, preventing further pulses
Longitudinal modes are phase-locked by an acousto-optic modulator
Light resonates between the mirrors and is released continuously
q.explanation: With the Q-switch closed, energy is stored in the medium as population inversion; lasing begins only when the switch opens, releasing a strong short pulse (giant pulse formation). Phase-locking with an acousto-optic modulator is active mode locking, a different technique.

q.stem: In the Nd:YAG laser, the Q-switch is made of a material that:
options: Mechanically rotates one of the mirrors
Becomes more transmissive once light intensity exceeds a threshold
Absorbs all wavelengths shorter than 1064 nm
Converts infrared light into a red aiming beam
q.explanation: The Nd:YAG Q-switch material increases its transmission above an intensity threshold, then returns to its closed state after the pulse so the next pulse waits until the gain medium is replenished. The red aiming beam comes from a separate He-Ne laser.

q.stem: Why does the slight divergence and central concentration of real laser beams matter more for YAG capsulotomy than for argon photocoagulation?
options: YAG energy is concentrated peripherally in the beam
Photodisruption needs energy focused to a point, whereas diffuse continuous delivery is little affected
Photocoagulation relies on ionisation, which needs a sharp focus
q.explanation: For continuous diffuse delivery such as argon photocoagulation, beam divergence matters little, but photodisruption must focus energy at a point to have a disruptive effect. Energy is greatest at the centre of the beam, and photocoagulation is thermal, not ionising.

q.stem: The discrete set of self-regenerating frequencies formed by standing waves between the two mirrors of a laser cavity are called:
q.explanation: Constructive and destructive interference in the resonant cavity creates standing waves at a discrete set of frequencies, the longitudinal modes; all other frequencies are suppressed. Transverse electromagnetic modes describe intensity variations across the beam.

q.stem: A laser in which each longitudinal mode oscillates with a fixed phase relative to the others, periodically producing an intense burst of light, is described as:
q.explanation: Fixing the phase relationship between modes makes them constructively interfere periodically (mode or phase locking). In continuous-wave lasers with many independent modes, interference averages out; Q-switching stores energy behind a shutter.

q.stem: Inserting a saturable absorber into a laser cavity is an example of:
options: Optical pumping by a second laser
q.explanation: A saturable absorber behaves differently depending on light intensity and achieves mode locking passively. Active mode locking modulates the signal, for example with a standing-wave acousto-optic modulator.

q.stem: Retinal photocoagulation raises tissue temperature by approximately how much?
q.explanation: Photocoagulation produces a localised burn with a temperature rise of about 10-20 degrees C. Temperatures above 100 degrees C, as produced by CO2 lasers, vaporise tissue.

q.stem: Which ocular pigment absorbs blue and shorter wavelengths more than red or green light and is concentrated at the macula?
q.explanation: Macular xanthophyll preferentially absorbs blue and shorter wavelengths. Melanin absorbs most of the visible spectrum and haemoglobin absorbs blue, green and yellow; rhodopsin is not cited as a laser-absorbing pigment.

q.stem: Tissue disruption by a Nd:YAG laser is mainly due to:
options: Vaporisation of water at over 100 degrees C
Ionisation producing a rapidly expanding high-temperature plasma
q.explanation: Nd:YAG (and ArF excimer) lasers strip electrons from molecules, forming a hot plasma whose rapid expansion causes mechanical shock. Photochemical damage occurs with long exposures, and thermal coagulation/vaporisation describe argon and CO2 lasers respectively.

q.stem: Regarding photochemical laser damage, which statement is correct?
options: It occurs only with pulses shorter than 1 nanosecond
It is caused by plasma expansion
Red light is the most hazardous wavelength
Blue and UV light cause damage at lower irradiance than longer wavelengths
q.explanation: Photochemical injury results from toxic free radicals with long exposures (over 10 seconds), and shorter wavelengths such as blue and UV are harmful at lower irradiance. Plasma expansion is the mechanism of ionising lasers.

q.stem: According to the effects of wavelength on ocular tissue, which colours are preferred for photocoagulation in the eye?
q.explanation: Shorter wavelengths are absorbed more by the cornea, lens and macular xanthophyll and are more harmful, so red or green light is preferred. Blue light should not be used at the macula.

q.stem: A CD player containing a fully enclosed laser belongs to which laser safety class?
q.explanation: Class 1 lasers are safe because the light is contained in an enclosure. Class 2 includes laser pointers, Class 3b includes CD/DVD writers and ophthalmic lasers, and Class 4 can burn skin.

q.stem: Which laser safety class is defined as carrying a small risk of damage within the time of the blink reflex, with power up to 5 mW?
q.explanation: Class 3a lasers (up to 5 mW) carry a small risk within the blink reflex time. Class 2 is up to 1 mW and safe in normal use; Class 3b (up to 500 mW) can cause severe eye damage; Class 4 can burn skin.

q.stem: Staff using therapeutic ophthalmic lasers protect their eyes with goggles. Which statement is correct?
options: Ophthalmic lasers fall within Class 3b and goggles absorb a particular wavelength
Ophthalmic lasers are Class 2 and goggles are optional
Goggles are needed only for Class 1 lasers
q.explanation: Ophthalmic lasers are grouped with Class 3b, and workers with Class 3b and 4 lasers wear goggles designed to absorb light of a specific wavelength. Goggles are wavelength-specific, not universal blockers.

q.stem: The argon laser used for photocoagulation emits at which wavelengths?
q.explanation: Argon lasers operate at 488 nm (blue), 514 nm (green) or a mixture. 633 nm is the He:Ne aiming laser, 810 nm the diode, and 1064 nm the Nd:YAG.

q.stem: Why is the blue component of the argon laser contraindicated when treating near the macula?
options: It is absorbed only by melanin
It cannot be focused through the slit lamp
It is absorbed by xanthophyll in the inner macular layers
q.explanation: Blue light is absorbed by xanthophylls in the inner macula, risking damage to the inner retina, whereas photocoagulation should act on the outer retina. Scleral penetration and melanin-only absorption describe the diode laser.

q.stem: A low-power laser emitting visible red light at 633 nm, used as an aiming beam for lasers with invisible output, is the:
q.explanation: The He:Ne gas laser produces red 633 nm light and serves as an aiming beam, for example for the Nd:YAG. The diode emits infrared at 810 nm and the excimer UV at 193 nm.

q.stem: Which laser is suitable for transscleral cyclophotoablation in glaucoma and can photocoagulate retina even when the view is obscured?
q.explanation: The 810 nm infrared diode laser penetrates sclera, is absorbed only by melanin, is efficient and portable, and can photocoagulate retina even when it is obscured. Argon light does not penetrate sclera, excimer light is absorbed by cornea, and He:Ne is only an aiming beam.

q.stem: A patient with posterior capsule opacification after cataract surgery needs a capsulotomy. Which laser and wavelength are used?
q.explanation: The Q-switched Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm infrared) is used for posterior capsulotomy and for iridotomy in shallow angles; it must be focused before use. Excimer lasers are for corneal ablation, and argon and diode for photocoagulation.

q.stem: The excimer laser used in photorefractive keratectomy:
options: Emits 810 nm light absorbed only by melanin
Causes tissue removal mainly by photocoagulation
Uses an argon-fluorine medium emitting 193 nm ultraviolet that is highly absorbed by the cornea
Uses a neodymium crystal emitting 1064 nm infrared
q.explanation: The ArF excimer laser emits 193 nm UV that the cornea absorbs strongly, giving precisely controlled ablation for PRK, LASIK and PTK. The other options describe Nd:YAG, diode and thermal lasers.

q.stem: Which laser-wavelength pairing is INCORRECT?
q.explanation: The diode laser emits at 810 nm; 1064 nm is the Nd:YAG wavelength. The other pairings are correct.

q.stem: How does a confocal microscope improve image contrast and resolution compared with a conventional microscope?
options: It uses ultrasound echoes from tissue interfaces
It floods the object with light from every angle
Point illumination and a pinhole in a conjugate plane exclude out-of-focus light
It uses polarised light and tissue birefringence
q.explanation: Confocal optics use point (laser) illumination and a pinhole in front of the detector at an optically conjugate plane to remove out-of-focus scattered light; scanning enlarges the field. In ophthalmology it is used to view corneal layers. Polarised light describes scanning laser polarimetry.

q.stem: Which statement about optical coherence tomography (OCT) is correct?
options: Scattered light forms the image, while reflected light causes glare
It uses ultraviolet light to achieve greater depth than confocal microscopy
Its resolution is inferior to that of ultrasound
It is an interferometric technique using near-infrared light with a resolution of about 10 micrometres
q.explanation: OCT uses interferometry with near-infrared light, penetrates 1-2 mm (deeper than confocal microscopy) and resolves around 10 micrometres, better than MRI or ultrasound. Reflected light forms the image; scattered light only adds glare.

q.stem: Compared with time-domain OCT, frequency (spectral/Fourier) domain OCT:
options: Uses visible blue light for better penetration
Requires a separate exposure for every depth point
Moves the reference arm longitudinally in time
Acquires broadband interference with spectrally separated detectors, improving signal-to-noise ratio
q.explanation: In frequency-domain OCT a dispersive element spreads optical frequencies onto a detector stripe so all depth information is obtained in one exposure, improving the signal-to-noise ratio. Moving the reference arm in time is the time-domain method.

q.stem: The GDx nerve fibre analyser measures retinal nerve fibre layer thickness using:
options: Scanning laser polarimetry based on the birefringence of the nerve fibre layer
q.explanation: Scanning laser polarimetry projects polarised laser light; birefringent tissue (cornea and RNFL) slows it (retardation), and after compensating for the cornea this change is converted into RNFL thickness. The RNFL is the first structure damaged in glaucoma.

q.stem: Which statement about the direct ophthalmoscope is correct?
options: It allows easy examination of the far peripheral retina
It gives a virtual, erect image with a field of about two disc diameters and no stereopsis
It requires a hand-held 20D condensing lens
It gives a real, inverted image and a wide stereoscopic view
q.explanation: The direct ophthalmoscope, invented by Helmholtz in 1851, gives a virtual erect image without a condensing lens, views about two disc diameters at a time and is monocular. A real inverted image with a 20D lens describes indirect ophthalmoscopy, which is better for the periphery.

q.stem: With a direct ophthalmoscope, which change will enlarge the field of view?
options: Increasing the distance between examiner and patient
Reducing the distance between examiner and patient
Using a smaller hole in the mirror
q.explanation: The field of view is set by the mirror aperture or the pupil, whichever is smaller, and is enlarged by dilating either pupil or by moving closer to the patient. Constriction, a smaller aperture or greater distance all reduce it.

q.stem: With the direct ophthalmoscope, compared with an emmetropic eye, the image of the fundus appears:
options: Smaller in myopia and larger in hypermetropia
The same size in all refractive states
Larger in myopia and smaller in hypermetropia
Inverted in myopia and erect in hypermetropia
q.explanation: Image size is larger in myopia and smaller in hypermetropia than in emmetropia. The direct ophthalmoscope always gives an erect image.

q.stem: In binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy with a 20D lens, the image the examiner sees is:
options: Real, inverted vertically and horizontally, and formed between the lens and the observer
Virtual and erect, formed behind the patient's eye
Real and erect, formed within the patient's eye
q.explanation: The condensing lens refracts light from the retina to form a real image between the lens and the examiner, inverted in both meridians. The lens is held so that the patient's and examiner's pupils are conjugate foci.

q.stem: In indirect ophthalmoscopy, the field of illumination is:
options: Largest in hypermetropia and smallest in myopia
Limited only by the power of the condensing lens
Largest in myopia, smallest in hypermetropia, and always limited by the subject's pupil size
q.explanation: The field of illumination is greatest in myopia and least in hypermetropia, and in every refractive state the subject's pupil size limits it.

q.stem: During retinoscopy, an image of the illuminated retina is formed at the subject's far point. Which stage of retinoscopy is this?
q.explanation: Retinoscopy has three stages: illumination (light shone onto the retina), reflex (image of the illuminated retina formed at the far point) and projection (the examiner views the image and watches how the reflex moves).

q.stem: Light leaving the retina of an uncorrected hypermetropic eye emerges from the eye as:
options: Rays focused at the examiner's pupil
q.explanation: From a hypermetropic eye emerging rays are divergent; from an emmetropic eye they are parallel; from a myopic eye they converge to a far point in front of the eye.

q.stem: During retinoscopy at 2/3 m, a patient with -3.00 D of myopia will show which reflex?
options: A 'with' movement, because the image lies behind the subject
A 'with' movement, because the image lies behind the examiner
An 'against' movement, because the image lies between subject and examiner
q.explanation: When myopia exceeds the working-distance equivalent (1.5 D at 2/3 m), the far-point image lies between patient and examiner and appears inverted, giving an against movement. Hypermetropes and low myopes (under 1.5 D) show a with movement.

q.stem: Working at 2/3 m, you neutralise the retinoscopy reflex with a +3.00 D lens. What is the patient's distance refraction?
q.explanation: At 2/3 m the dioptric equivalent of the working distance is 1.5 D (1/0.67), which is subtracted from the neutralising lens: +3.00 - 1.50 = +1.50 D. Adding it instead (+4.50) or using 1 D for 1 m distance (+2.00) are common errors.

q.stem: Working at 1 m, you neutralise the reflex with a -2.00 D lens. What is the patient's distance refraction?
q.explanation: At 1 m the working-distance correction is -1.0 D, so the result is -2.00 + (-1.00) = -3.00 D. The -3.50 answer wrongly uses the 1.5 D correction for 2/3 m.

q.stem: A -1.00 D myope is examined by retinoscopy at 2/3 m. What reflex is seen and what lens neutralises it?
q.explanation: Because this myopia is less than the 1.5 D working-distance equivalent, the far-point image lies behind the examiner and a with movement is seen. Neutralising lens = refraction + working-distance equivalent = -1.00 + 1.50 = +0.50 D.

q.stem: In a compound microscope, which statement is correct?
options: The final image is erect without the need for prisms
The objective's image lies far from the eyepiece's focal plane
The objective is a concave lens and the eyepiece a convex lens
The object lies outside the anterior focal point of the objective, and the final image is inverted
q.explanation: A compound microscope uses two convex lenses; the objective forms a real, magnified, inverted image that falls at or near the eyepiece focal plane, and the eyepiece magnifies it further as a loupe. The final image is inverted, so slit lamps use Porro prisms to re-erect it.

q.stem: The binocular stereoscopic view of a slit lamp is provided by:
options: A single microscope with a beam splitter
A Hruby lens held in front of the eye
Two Galilean telescopes set at 45 degrees
Two compound microscopes set at about 13-14 degrees to each other
q.explanation: A slit lamp consists of two compound microscopes angled about 13-14 degrees apart, giving stereopsis, plus an illumination system focused at the same point as the microscope.

q.stem: Which slit-lamp illumination technique is best for examining the corneal endothelium?
q.explanation: In specular reflection the illuminating and viewing arms are placed at equal angles either side of the normal, and examining the light reflected off a surface this way is the best method for the endothelium. Sclerotic scatter uses internal reflection within the cornea; transillumination shows iris defects.

q.stem: Which slit-lamp technique is used to check the patency of a laser iridotomy?
options: Transillumination with co-axial illuminating and viewing systems
q.explanation: In transillumination, light shone through the pupil reflects from the retina, so iris defects such as atrophy or a patent iridotomy appear as a red reflex. Sclerotic scatter is for the cornea, and specular reflection for the endothelium.

q.stem: Which slit-lamp fundus lens produces a virtual, erect and diminished image of the retina?
q.explanation: The Hruby lens, held in front of the eye, focuses the otherwise parallel light leaving the eye into the slit lamp's focal range, forming a virtual erect diminished image. The 90D and 78D lenses work like indirect ophthalmoscopy (inverted image), and the panfundoscope forms a real inverted image inside the lens.

q.stem: Why is a contact lens needed to view the anterior chamber angle?
options: The lens magnifies the angle by a factor of 90
The cornea absorbs light from the angle
The angle lies outside the field of the slit lamp
Total internal reflection at the cornea-air interface prevents light from the angle reaching the examiner
q.explanation: Light from the angle undergoes total internal reflection at the cornea. A gonioscopy lens with a higher refractive index than the eye, coupled with saline or gel, removes the cornea-air refracting surface so the light can pass to the examiner.

q.stem: Why does the Goldmann applanation tonometer use a contact area 3.06 mm in diameter?
options: At this diameter, corneal rigidity and tear-film surface tension cancel out
It is the corneal thickness in micrometres divided by 100
It is the diameter of the normal pupil
It displaces exactly 1 ml of aqueous
q.explanation: At 3.06 mm the effects of surface tension and corneal rigidity balance, so force is directly proportional to IOP and the volume displaced is negligible. Larger areas make rigidity more important; smaller areas make tear-film surface tension a source of error.

q.stem: During Goldmann applanation tonometry, the correct end point is reached when:
options: The inner edges of the two semicircles just touch
The outer edges of the two semicircles just touch
The semicircles separate by one ring width
q.explanation: Two prisms with bases opposite split the contact circle into two laterally displaced semicircles; when their inner edges just touch, the contact diameter is 3.06 mm and the reading is proportional to the applied force.

q.stem: A patient has 8 D of corneal astigmatism. If Goldmann tonometry is done with the prism in the standard horizontal position, the approximate error is:
q.explanation: High corneal astigmatism gives an error of about 1 mmHg per 4 D of astigmatism, so 8 D gives about 2 mmHg. To correct this, the prism is rotated so the minus cylinder value lies at the red line, taking the reading at 43 degrees to the meridian of lower corneal power.

q.stem: Which statement about pachymetry is correct?
options: Optical pachymetry is more accurate than ultrasound pachymetry
The tilt of the glass plate is inversely proportional to corneal thickness
The Jaeger pachymeter uses a Placido disc
Optical pachymeters use Purkinje-Sanson images from the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces
q.explanation: Optical pachymeters double the image of the anterior and posterior corneal reflections; the tilt needed to align them is proportional to corneal thickness. Ultrasound pachymetry is more accurate and more widely used clinically.

q.stem: Looking through a Placido disc at an astigmatic cornea, the reflected rings appear:
options: Closer together in the steeper meridian
Closer together in the flatter meridian
q.explanation: The smaller the radius of curvature (the steeper the cornea), the closer the reflected rings, much like contour lines on a map. The examiner views through a central aperture containing a +2 D lens.

q.stem: How do the von Helmholtz and Javal-Schiotz keratometers differ?
options: Only the Javal-Schiotz uses image doubling
Von Helmholtz uses a fixed object size with an adjustable image; Javal-Schiotz uses an object of variable size
Von Helmholtz measures peripheral cornea; Javal-Schiotz measures central cornea
Von Helmholtz uses coloured step-shaped mires
q.explanation: Both measure only the central zone (about 3 mm) and both use doubling. Von Helmholtz keeps the object fixed and adjusts the image with tilting glass plates, while Javal-Schiotz varies the separation of two mires (one step-shaped, one rectangular, differently coloured).

q.stem: Using the keratometric formula D = (1.3375 - 1)/r, with r in metres, what is the corneal power for a central radius of curvature of 7.5 mm?
q.explanation: D = 0.3375 / 0.0075 m = 45 D. The keratometric index 1.3375 stands in for the tear/cornea medium and 1 is air; using 1.376 or forgetting to convert mm to metres gives wrong answers.

q.stem: For the data set 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 10, 26, what is the median?
q.explanation: Ordered from smallest to largest, the middle (4th of 7) value is 5. The mode is 3 (most frequent), and the mean is 56/7 = 8, pulled upward by the outlier 26.

q.stem: For the data set 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 10, 26, what is the arithmetic mean?
q.explanation: The mean is the sum (56) divided by the number of values (7), giving 8. The median is 5 and the mode is 3; the mean is larger because the outlier 26 skews the data to the right.

q.stem: Which is a disadvantage of the median as a measure of average?
options: It is distorted by skewed data
It cannot be calculated for an odd number of values
It ignores most of the information in the data
q.explanation: The median is robust to outliers and skew but ignores most of the data, is not algebraically defined and has a complicated sampling distribution. Distortion by outliers and skew are disadvantages of the mean.

q.stem: Which measure of average is easiest to determine for categorical data?
q.explanation: The mode, the most frequently occurring value, is easily found for categorical data, though it ignores most of the information and is rarely used. Standard deviation is a measure of spread, not an average.

q.stem: The interquartile range is:
options: The range containing the central 95% of observations
The difference between the largest and smallest values
The square root of the variance
The difference between the 25th and 75th percentiles, containing 50% of observations
q.explanation: The IQR spans from the 25th to the 75th percentile and holds the middle half of the data, excluding outliers. The central 95% range is often called the normal range; the square root of the variance is the standard deviation.

q.stem: The interval that excludes 2.5% of observations above and 2.5% below, containing the central 95%, is often called the:
q.explanation: The range containing the central 95% of observations is often referred to as the normal (reference) range. The IQR contains the central 50%.

q.stem: Which statement about the standard deviation is correct?
options: It is the square root of the variance and is in the same units as the data
It is measured in the square of the data units
It equals the standard error multiplied by the sample size
It falls markedly as sample size increases
q.explanation: Variance is in squared units and the SD, its square root, is in the original units. Both change little with sample size. The standard error (SD divided by the square root of n) is the quantity that falls as n increases.

q.stem: A sample of 36 eyes has a mean central corneal thickness with a standard deviation of 12 micrometres. What is the standard error of the mean?
q.explanation: SEM = SD / square root of n = 12 / 6 = 2 micrometres. Dividing by n (12/36 = 0.33) instead of by its square root is a common mistake.

q.stem: Which feature does NOT apply to a normal (Gaussian) distribution?
options: It becomes flatter if the variance increases
The mean is greater than the median
It is symmetrical about the mean
q.explanation: A normal distribution is symmetrical and unimodal, with equal mean and median; increasing variance flattens it and changing the mean shifts it sideways. A mean greater than the median indicates right skew.

q.stem: In a positively (right) skewed distribution, how are the mean, median and mode arranged?
q.explanation: With the long tail to the right, the mean is pulled toward the tail, the mode stays at the highest peak, and the median lies between them, so mode < median < mean. Negative skew reverses this order.

q.stem: Which asymmetrical distributions are characterised by their degrees of freedom?
options: The t-distribution and the chi-squared distribution
q.explanation: The t and chi-squared distributions are given as examples of asymmetrical distributions, both characterised by degrees of freedom. The normal distribution is symmetrical.

q.stem: A survey records how many residents of a town have glaucoma on a single day. This is best described as a:
q.explanation: Cross-sectional studies are observational and carried out at one time point, such as a survey or census, and are used to measure point prevalence. Cohort studies follow people over time; case-control studies look back from outcome to exposure.

q.stem: In a cross-sectional survey of 1500 adults, 30 have diabetic retinopathy on the day of examination. What is the point prevalence?
q.explanation: Point prevalence = number with the disease at a time point / total studied at that time = 30/1500 = 0.02, or 2%.

q.stem: In a cohort study, 20 of 200 smokers and 10 of 400 non-smokers develop cataract over 10 years. What is the relative risk of cataract in smokers?
q.explanation: Risk in exposed = 20/200 = 0.10; risk in unexposed = 10/400 = 0.025; RR = 0.10/0.025 = 4. An RR of 1 would mean the same risk in both groups.

q.stem: Which is an advantage of a cohort study over a case-control study?
options: It is better for very rare diseases
There is no loss to follow-up
Incidence and the time sequence of events can be measured
q.explanation: Cohort studies measure incidence/risk, show temporal sequence and reduce recall and selection bias. However, they need long, expensive follow-up, very large samples for rare diseases, and suffer loss to follow-up; speed, cost and rare diseases favour case-control designs.

q.stem: Which is a recognised disadvantage of a case-control study?
options: Recall bias, because cases may remember past exposures differently
It requires long and expensive follow-up
It is unsuitable for rare diseases
Participants are frequently lost to follow-up
q.explanation: Case-control studies are quick, cheap, good for rare diseases and have no follow-up losses, but are prone to recall and selection bias and are unsuitable when the exposure is rare.

q.stem: In a case-control study of uveal melanoma, 60 of 100 cases and 20 of 100 controls report a particular exposure. What is the odds ratio?
q.explanation: Odds of being a case among exposed = 60/20 = 3; among unexposed = 40/80 = 0.5. OR = 3/0.5 = 6. Simply dividing the proportions exposed (0.6/0.2 = 3) gives a ratio of proportions, not the odds ratio.

q.stem: Case-control studies are best described as:
q.explanation: Case-control studies are observational and retrospective: cases with the outcome are compared with controls without it, looking back at exposures. Experimental studies, such as clinical trials, involve an intervention.

q.stem: In a randomised controlled trial, stratified randomisation is used to:
options: Hide treatment allocation from the assessor
Allocate groups of people rather than individuals
Balance factors such as age between the treatment and control groups
q.explanation: Stratified randomisation controls for factors such as age to spread them equally between groups. Restricted randomisation ensures equal group numbers, cluster randomisation allocates clusters, and blinding prevents assessment bias.

q.stem: A trial in which neither the patients nor the doctors know who received the active drug is:
q.explanation: Blinding both patients and doctors (double-blind) avoids assessment bias. If only the patient is blinded the trial is single-blind.

q.stem: An 'intention to treat' analysis means that:
options: All patients are analysed in the group to which they were originally allocated, whether or not they followed treatment
Patients are analysed according to the treatment they actually received
Only patients who completed treatment are analysed
Patients who withdraw are replaced by new recruits
q.explanation: Intention to treat keeps every analysed patient in the original randomised group regardless of adherence, which helps avoid bias. Analysing by treatment actually received or only completers can reintroduce bias.

q.stem: A factor that is associated with the outcome and with another exposure, producing a false association or masking a real one, is a:
q.explanation: A confounder relates to both the outcome and other exposures, creating spurious associations or hiding real ones; careful study design and analysis reduce its effects.

q.stem: In a questionnaire study, patients give answers they think the researcher wants to hear. This is an example of:
options: Reporter bias, a form of information bias
q.explanation: Information bias arises when exposure or outcome data are wrongly recorded; reporter bias (patients answering in the direction they think the researcher favours) is one type. Publication bias concerns reporting only positive results, and selection bias concerns unrepresentative participants.

q.stem: Phase III clinical trials are:
options: Larger studies evaluating the effect of a new treatment
Small studies whose main aim is to assess safety
q.explanation: Phase I/II trials are small studies evaluating effect and safety; phase III trials are larger studies of the treatment's effect. All trials compare treatment with a control (standard treatment or placebo).

q.stem: A P value of 0.03 is obtained with a pre-set significance level of 0.05. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 97% chance the treatment works
The null hypothesis is rejected; the result is significant at the 5% level
A type II error has occurred
q.explanation: The P value is the probability of obtaining the results if the null hypothesis is true; a value below the pre-chosen significance level (0.05) means the null is rejected. It does not give the probability that the treatment works.

q.stem: A study concludes that a new drug lowers IOP when in fact it has no effect. This is a:
q.explanation: A type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis, concluding there is an effect when none exists. A type II error is accepting a false null hypothesis, missing a real effect.

q.stem: The power of a study is:
options: The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
q.explanation: Power is the chance of detecting a real, statistically significant effect, i.e. rejecting a false null hypothesis. Rejecting a true null is a type I error.

q.stem: Which change will INCREASE the power of a study?
options: Looking for a smaller effect of interest
Reducing the variability of the observations
q.explanation: Power increases with larger sample size, lower variability, a larger effect of interest and a larger significance level. Each of the other options reduces power.

q.stem: Which is NOT needed to calculate the sample size for a study?
options: The P value the study will obtain
q.explanation: Before a sample size calculation, the power, significance level, variability (standard deviation) and smallest effect of interest must be defined, often from pilot or published data. The P value is only known after the study.

q.stem: The non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test is the:
q.explanation: The Wilcoxon signed rank test compares paired observations. The Mann-Whitney U-test (and the Wilcoxon rank sum test) is the non-parametric equivalent of the unpaired t-test.

q.stem: Non-parametric tests should be used when:
options: The data are normally distributed with a large sample
The data are not normally distributed or the sample is too small
Two means from independent normal samples are compared
q.explanation: Parametric tests (e.g. the t-test) assume normally distributed data; when that fails or the sample is small, non-parametric tests rank the observations and analyse the ranks.

q.stem: Which statement about the chi-squared test is correct?
options: It is used on frequency data and a value of zero means observed and expected frequencies do not differ
It compares two means from independent groups
It should be calculated from percentages
A larger value makes the null hypothesis more likely to be true
q.explanation: The chi-squared test uses actual counts (not percentages) in a contingency table; zero means no difference between observed and expected, and larger values make the null hypothesis less likely. Comparing two independent means is the unpaired t-test.

q.stem: Before and after treatment, the same patients are classified as having or not having dry eye symptoms. Which test compares these paired proportions?
q.explanation: McNemar's test compares proportions in two related (paired) groups using a chi-squared statistic. The ordinary chi-squared test is for unpaired categorical data, and ANOVA compares a numerical outcome across more than two groups.

q.stem: Which test is suggested to compare a numerical variable across more than two groups?
q.explanation: For numerical data, one group uses a t-test, two groups a paired or unpaired t-test (or Wilcoxon rank sum), and more than two groups ANOVA. McNemar's and z tests are for categorical data.

q.stem: A new glaucoma screening test is applied to 200 people with glaucoma and is positive in 180. What is its sensitivity?
q.explanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease correctly identified by the test: 180/200 = 90%. The 20 diseased people who test negative are false negatives.

q.stem: The same screening test is applied to 800 people without glaucoma, of whom 760 test negative. What is the specificity?
q.explanation: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease correctly identified as negative: 760/800 = 95%. The remaining 40 are false positives.

q.stem: A test gives 180 true positives, 40 false positives, 20 false negatives and 760 true negatives. What is the positive predictive value?
q.explanation: PPV = true positives / all positives = 180/(180+40) = 180/220, about 82%. 90% is the sensitivity, 95% the specificity, and about 97% the negative predictive value.

q.stem: A test gives 180 true positives, 40 false positives, 20 false negatives and 760 true negatives. What is the negative predictive value?
q.explanation: NPV = true negatives / all negatives = 760/(760+20) = 760/780, about 97%. The other values are the specificity (95%), sensitivity (90%) and PPV (about 82%).

q.stem: A test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 95%. What is the likelihood ratio for a positive result?
q.explanation: The likelihood ratio compares the chance of a given result in people with versus without the disease. For a positive result: sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.90/0.05 = 18.

q.stem: A patient without keratoconus is incorrectly told by a topography screening program that they have it. This patient is a:
q.explanation: A false positive is a normal individual incorrectly diagnosed with the disease; a false negative is a diseased individual incorrectly called normal.

q.stem: Two variables have a clearly non-linear relationship and a measure of association is required. Which is most appropriate?
q.explanation: Spearman's coefficient is the non-parametric counterpart of Pearson's and is appropriate when the relationship is definitely non-linear. Pearson's measures closeness to a linear relationship; t-tests compare means rather than measure association.

q.stem: Regression in which y is modelled as depending on two or more x variables is termed:
q.explanation: Univariate regression relates y to a single x; with two or more x values it is multivariate, and ANOVA can be used in the analysis.

q.stem: The number of new cases of a disease per unit population per unit time is the:
q.explanation: Incidence counts new cases per population per time, whereas prevalence counts all cases, old and new, at a particular time.

q.stem: Giving aspirin after a transient ischaemic attack is an example of:
q.explanation: Tertiary prevention prevents the consequences of disease that has already developed, as with aspirin after a TIA. Primary prevention (e.g. health education) stops disease occurring; secondary prevention detects and treats disease before symptoms.

q.stem: A public health education campaign designed to prevent a disease from occurring is an example of:
q.explanation: Primary prevention aims to stop disease occurring at all, with health education as an example. Secondary prevention detects and treats early disease before symptoms, and tertiary prevention limits the consequences of established disease.
